																I backed this game on Kickstarter, cause it seemed interesting. And I liked that they didn't ask for a butt load of money and they delivered on their promise. It's getting rarer and rarer these days... I just wish they improved on the formula a little. - no random encounters
- pretty 2D art, especially the dialogue heads
- interesting battle mechanics

Con:
- story all over the place, characters with bipolar disorders
- ugly 3D art
- lack of polish

Posted: March 28, 2020
																This game isn't not bad for what it is, and there are some really good parts in there, however it does have several shortcomings that prevent it from truly shining.

Most prominently, it fails to fully take advantage of the post apocalyptic future setting. Things that you would expect from a modern princess maker game, such as electronics, computers, public schools, or clubs, are noticeably absent. Also absent is any form of romance, or really romantic prospects in general, given that there are only three other characters of your daughter's age.

It does have some improvements though. Gone is the almost stalker like approach you had to take in order to keep up your relationships in PM5. Making friends and raising relationships in this game is much more simple and straightforward, as is focusing on a career path thanks to the inclusion of a handy class tree that shows what are the requirements for each task you want to take.

If I had to guess, I'd say that the devs have only played PM2 before working on this game, and independently decided to iterate from that, which resulted in what can best be described as one step forward, one step back. It's better in some ways than PM5, but the shortcomings are really glaring, and you'll really miss some of the verisimilitude that PM5 offers. It does have a comparable length as PM5, though, so that is a plus.

Even so, this game is really good for what it is, so if you are into raising sims like Chinese Parents or the princess maker series, this will not be a bad purchase. Just don't expect it to be Princess maker 5, because it really isn't.

Posted: January 31
																Once again, a game that proves Valve really really needs to add a "Neutral" or "Mixed"  review option.  
TL/DR --  It's like STS in some ways but isn't as complex, for better or for worse. With its current level of content, I'd suggest getting it on sale instead of the full $20.   It's fun for some quick playing, but replay value is iffy. 



The game can be fun in short bursts, but don't expect - in its current state - a lot of complex synergies and playstyles like you can get out of Slay the Spire or Monster Train.
Even after receiving some balancing passes, the game still is a bit lopsided against you. There's times where you can do something to slow that down, but other times the game just simply decides it hates you and wants you to lose. Throwing an Elite battle against you where multiple enemies are attacking from two paths simultaneously and near constantly and any time you play a unit they get reinforcements with a very short time before the dangerous waves spawn?  Well, sometimes that happens in RNG-based games like this but unlike Slay The Spire, which this game seems partially inspired by, you can't dodge Elites - you HAVE to fight them to continue.

There's also not a terribly good variety in cards and artifacts/relics as of right now, so each run tends to feel pretty 'samey',  even if you change Heroes.

																This is my second go at Legrand Legacy. I had the opportunity to test it several months back but not the opportunity to actually review it. For a nod to JRPGs, Legrand gets a lot of things right. The map movement reminds me of FF7 without the random encounters. You can actual attempt to avoid different mobs if you are suffereing from low health or just trying to rush through an area. The art style is very unique. It takes what looks like hand painted images as the background with characters and interactable items done differently. It really helps everything POP out and when put together, looks quite pleasing to the eyes.

Combat is classicly turn based with a twist. Instead of just choosing your action and waiting for it to resolve, there is a mini-game for each attack/defense that occurs. This game of skill can infer bonuses or penalties based on how you do in each game. You need to get good at it too, as there are times when nailing a "good" or "perfect" will get you out of a sticky situation... instead of sending you to the Game Over screen... I'm talking to you boss battles!

I would like to see some voice work done for the game though... especially for the bigger cut scenes... like when you first meet Lazarus. I would also like to see some balancing done for certain enemies. I shouldn't really have to grind for 5 levels so I don't die in 1 hit to a mini boss. I understand grinding is all a part of JRPGs, but even after running an area repeatedly, you should be trounced so quickly...

Overall though, Legrand Legacy is enojoyable and I found myself wanting to continue playing it late into the night when I started this review.

																My Lovely Daughter is a... Unusual game. You play an anmesiac father trying to bring his daughter back from a soulless state, which as a whole sounds very noble and fatherly. A real family motive, if you will. Yet it's a rather dark descent as you bring forth homunculi to cultivate different aspects of her soul; namely: fear, joy, anger, and sorrow. You cultivate the soul by sending the homunculi to work for a week at different jobs, giving them experience and your wallet money. Money spent on buying more ingredients for homunculi, repairing the house, or preventing your daughter's body from rotting away.

Gameplay wise, it's very very repeatative. You go week in and week out doing the same activities to raise homunculi that will likely be "farmed" for their essense in a matter of days. Yet, the charm comes from the interactions between the homunculi and yourself, who they see as a father figure. Which is logical considering that you gave them life.

The music is alright, and generally fits the mood/tone of the game. And the graphics are ok for a cartoonish art style. The scenes that occur througout the game are very well done, and provide a nice visual to go along with the killings. Though I believe there is a limit to these since the total combinations of homunculi is based on a combination of 2 material types, material quality, and combination of materials.

																Coffee Talk is a game that I didn't see myself playing. I am not a huge fan of games like these, so I thought it was strange when it popped into my recommended feed. After 4 hours of gameplay I have come to the conclusion that this game is very close to a masterpiece. Each character has their own unique personality that makes them feel like real people who have real world issues. There are no real "choices" in the game, but you can decide on what drinks to serve your customers, because it's about giving the customer what they need, because what they want and what they need aren't the same. The only real mountain that you need to climb, is that the drinks are not laid out for you. Sometimes you need to rely on how the customer is feeling to get the drink, and sometimes they will tell you outright the drink. In the game you don't really get to bud into people's lives, because that isn't your job, your job is to give them their drinks, and listen to their problems. 

This game reminds me of why indie games are special, because each game can have their own special feel to them that makes them different from the others.

The only real complaint that I've seen is the fact that the politics that are in the game are supposed to align with current issues that are facing the world at the moment, so if you don't like politics, this might not be the game for you, but I would still recommend that you give this game a try.

Overall, I would give this game a solid 9/10, because latte art isn't easy, and because finding the correct drink combo could take a few tries and maybe even a few save states.

																DreadOut 2 was a disappointment to me in many ways, from the more action oriented gameplay, poor story to general lack of polish combined with absurd amount of bugs ranging from minor annoyances to potentially game breaking.

Overall scope of the game is much bigger than the first game and Keepers of the Dark - there are multiple locations featuring both daytime setting as well as an "alternate world" horror environment. Unlike the first game, DreadOut 2 is heavily combat focused and some of the chapters very much feel like moving from boss encounter to another with some minor monsters between them. Unfortunately this also means that the pacing is rather poor and the game never quite manages to get that horror atmosphere right.

Much like the first game, some of the combat revolves around the Fatal Frame inspired fighting ghosts by taking their pictures, but as a new addition the game also features a Silent Hill inspired melee combat. Unfortunately the heavier focus on the combat also highlights how bad the combat design and especially the boss encounters in the game are.

Boss encounters for the most part are badly designed, poorly balanced and buggy as hell. Some of the bigger issues include:
- Camera hitbox / hit registration is incredibly bad
- Ghost bosses are often fought in tiny spaces, where they can easily clip through walls and keep attacking you without giving you the chance to register a camera hit properly.
- One boss in particular, a tiger is so poorly balanced that you will most likely either resort to cheesing it out or winning by luck.
- Many of the bosses can chain several hits while player is waiting for the main character to get up after being hit.
- Some of the bosses can be stunlocked by the player if you time your hits out, making them totally trivial.
- Many of the bosses can be tricked in to certain attack loops that completely trivialize them.

That being said, there were things I liked about DreadOut 2 but I have to admit that I didn't have a whole lot of fun during my playthrough of the game which took me roughly 6 hours - which of about an hour was redoing things after losing progress with bugs.

Which brings me to the last point, DreadOut 2 is incredibly buggy. If I'd have to do a rough count of bugs I encountered during the playthrough I would estimate it being in the region of 50-100 from small things like visual glitches, incorrect subtitles, missing subtitles to more serious issues such as broken collision that could only be bypassed by attacking through it, boss fights breaking and requiring reload, progress blocking bugs that require restart and as a final bonus, even the end credits themselves bugged out.

In general, I would not recommend DreadOut 2 in its current state: It is a buggy mess that desperately needs several patches to fix bugs, balancing and the english localization.

																A strong and really amazing RPG adventure, with some frustrating parts as well.

The story is pretty good; it's nothing amazingly innovative but a lot of stuff is foreshadowed well and by the end you begin to care about most of the characters. There's a lot of dialogue to go around but most of it works towards giving characters some life to them. Finn starts off pretty meek but grows as time goes by, and ends as a good protaganist who I could identify with. Each character in your party gets development time and it doesn't suffer the same problem a lot of JRPGs have where characters join your party and then just kinda exist. Everybody pitches into the story and has their say.

While technically the game isn't cutting edge, the art style is still pretty good and I'm glad the devs didn't try and beat Witcher graphics and then end up with a game an hour long. The character art is gorgeous; one of the main highlights I feel is the Live 2D system which just looks absolutely amazing in this game. Even though it's a bit text heavy, the animations still do a really amazing job of getting you involved with the character. Hopefully we'll see more games using the system as well as Legrand Legacy. The battle arenas are in pretty basic 3D, but the rest of the game uses really nice looking 2D art. About the only criticism I have is that most dungeons take place outside and don't have standout features to them.

Onto the gameplay, which I think is probably gonna be the sticking point for a lot of people. The QTE in battle didn't bother me, but I can understand how it would turn people off.  I would implore the devs to add an option to turn it off (as much as I prefer RPGs with one standard difficulty level, when you've made a small indie game it's risky to alienate people who hate QTE even if I admire sticking to your guns about it) Many dungeons have a gimmick to them, most of which prevent movement; it can be frustrating at times.

The other more aggravating flaw is certain sections are a bit of a slog (towards the end, more specifically) and mainly that there's a strategy game element that pops up fairly frequently in game. Whilst I managed to beat them in a couple of tries, they left a sour taste in my mouth since they felt too disconnected from the game itself and it feels unfair to throw a different genre at a player and expect them to pass it. My advice to those stuck is to flank flank flank flank (never attack an enemy face on, a side attack deals much more damage and they can't strike back at you most of the time)

Those problems weren't enough to make me dislike the game; I fell in love with Legrand Legacy (and also thanks to the devs for making a demo, which inspired me to buy this day one) even though it has some irritating parts (but like all RPGs, will be easier on subsequent playthroughs now I know what to expect)

																I was really going to wait until I got more game time in before reviewing, I think I have somewhere around 3 hours b/c I was playing offline a bit. But I honestly have had very little drive to even start playing it again. 

This game is basically a very bad version of VA-11 Hall-A. I'm a sort of a-political moderate, I am not conservative by any definition of the word, but I get irritated by the overly meta political commentary that do literally nothing provocative for the story. I am pretty interested in feminism and issues of diversity- but when a game just kinda screeches, "RACISM IS BAD. SEXISM IS BAD," over and over again, it really doesn't add anything all that interesting or provocative. I can't deal with another, "It's like romeo and juliet! But with RACISM," story. This game makes these uninspired political/sociological criticisms that do nothing to add to the subjects they are seeking to address. The nuances of systemic racism, for example, are completely missed by these over the top, 1950's-esque racists who 99% of people think are bad. Same with some of the issues of sexism that are addressed, though barely. 

VA-11 Hall-A was exceptionally interesting to me because it also addresses a lot of different topics that are relevant today in new and interesting perspectives that the setting/characters/tone really add to. Here, I feel like the theme and setting of the story add nothing to the commentary that the creators are trying to make. 

I play a lot of games with clear political alignments, I have no issue with it as long as it is done well. Here, it isn't done very well. It's the equivalent to me writing a fantasy story where two goblins are complaining about how the orc king wants to build a wall to make sure all the dirty immigrants can't get in. I think I can definitely make a commentary about the absurdity of anti-immigration and xenophobia without it being so... boring and obvious. There's just something extremely un-engaging about the rhetoric in this game. Most of it is overly obvious, like I'm too stupid to understand where they're getting at. If this were a satirical piece, I'd get that and it might actually be decent. But it's not satirical. 

If you're going to make a story based game, I wish you wouldn't be so afraid to go out on a limb and allow the players to kinda build together your overall message through engaging storytelling (like in VA-11 Hall-A) instead of just going from one topic to the next that's going on in modern media and giving your blatant opinion about it through your characters. I just feel like I'm reading a high school essay on modern politics. 

The art and music is great, though, which really bums me out because it is so nice to look at and listen to. 

Another flaw in the game is the complete irrelevancy of the gameplay. In VA-11 Hall-A, you have a money system and some incentive to play it like a game. This game is a bait-and-switch. It has some minimal amount of interaction that, as far as I can tell, has no impact on anything except some dialogue. There's no money system and no real choices you can make. It's essentially just a visual novel. 

I'm not one to hate on a game for being overly political. I think VA-11 Hall-A had some even more controversial and interesting questions on modern politics than this game. I just think that they did it in such a boring way that I am basically just reading someone's opinion on various different hot topics right now. I even agree with most of them. I just don't really think it's interesting.

																The Antithesis of the "Princess Maker" type of games. This game is of mature subject matter, and while nothing explicit is shown or stated outright, it is there inbetween the lines.

Aside from the obvious murdering of your faux daughters.

Things to Expect:
    Repetition without a mix-up of gameplay.
    A decidedly gothic story for a gothic setting.
    You play as a villainous character.
    A game length of roughly 4-5 hours, more if you chase after achievements.
    Waifus? If you're into that sort of thing. You do have to murder them to complete the game.
Story
The driving force of the whole process of murder is Faust's desire to restore life to his deceased daughter. There is little to the game's story beyond that and it's ultimate conclusion. There are small tid-bits of world building given by the villiagers. But ultimately the narrative focuses on Faust and his mad science. There is little left for self-interpretation, and the tone of the story is constant through the whole of the game. Make no mistake, this is a horror story.

Gameplay
The core of the game is resource management. You have Gold, various alchemical ingrediants, various gifts, ritual items, and the monster daughters to keep an eye on. Gold pays for ingrediants, ingrediants are combined into monster daughters, gifts are given to the daughters to make them happy, you make them work for gold to buy everything but more monster girls.

Your faux daughters are then sacrificed to begin a "High-Low" guessing game. Finding the exact amount of Joy, Sadness, Anger, and Fear needed to constitute a soul completes the game. There are a few ways to completely lose, in which the game auto-deletes your save file and forcing you start over from the beginning. Those ways are:
    Letting your daughter's body (the non-monster) rot totally.
    Treating 20 monster daughters poorly enough that they run away from your home.
    Failing to complete tasks taken by villagers, thus killing their trust in you. (Have yet to test or see if this is an end state.)
Aesthetics
The game does not perpetuate any sort of mood beyond somber, horrific, and unsettling. The art is appropriately dismal but with a hint of elegant wonder. There are a couple instances of flounder mouth, but does not ruin the art. The music is a simple loop of a single track, sparing a couple of differing scores to fit various cutscenes. It does its job.

Conclusion
I'd reccomend this game only to those that enjoy horror, and aren't terribly emotional over losing female characters they name. If you ever wanted to be a mad scientist and execute horrible experiements on a whim, this may tickle you. The story had me intrigued enough to finish it, and while the ending sort of threw me for a loop, I can appreciate what the writers were attempting. It was fitting, if clumsily executed.

																TL;DR at the bottom.
I'm writing this review a little earlier than a normally would; usually I take a retrospective look the games I play, but it will be awhile before I can do that here and I want to give Ciel Fledge its best chance at making the front page of Steam.

Ciel Fledge: A Daughter Raising Simulator is Studio Namaapa's second project, and is a life sim/management in the same genre as the Princess Maker series of games. Your job is to raise Ciel, an eight-year-old girl with no memory, into an adult. Your time with her is broken into week-long chunks during which she will attend classes, make new friends, learn about her past, and make decisions about her future. The story has barely gotten started at the point of my review, but I expect great things as I played Studio Namaapa's previous title Nusakana, and despite the translation issues with the previous game, it managed to become one of my most-loved games for all time. 
Let's get down to details...

Gameplay:
Most of the week occurs on "autopilot" after you select a set of activities for Ciel to focus on during the week. Watching Ciel perform her weekly activities takes about five seconds per day (except for decision points, dialogues and random battles), but there is a speed multiplier you can use when watching her bounce around the city and gain stat points inevitably gets old.
Battles are a somewhat different take on the match-3 genre where you can have Ciel perform skills based on the matches you have made and call for help from her friends. These match-3 battles are not limited to physical conflicts but also include tests of intelligence, following directions, and social skills, which is why the starting skills include things like "spin" and "think" alongside "drop-kick."
Between weeks, you rest at home. Here you can discuss new information or people with Ciel, though as I'm still in the tutorial section most of the conversations have been short and meant to help move you through the tutorial weeks. You can also see and alter your parenting style, whether you'll be working or spending time with Ciel during the week, and plan out Ciel's next week. Each day has room for one activity, and the choices you make will alter Ciel's stats in the form of things like intelligence, creativity, strength, logic, spirituality, and how much she develops relationships with others. There are multiple ways of influencing each stat, so you can be a little more fluid in your discipline and activity choices without worrying that you've borked yourself over for the future. This is not a kinetic novel, so the choices you make will affect and change Ciel's story.

Controls and UI: 
This game has support for the controller, keyboard and mouse. The keyboard controls are kind of wonky to start out with, but they are all rebindable and most players will prefer to use the simple mouse-driven UI anyway. You may have to click on the screen in order to get it to recognize your cursor at first.
The game explains its mechanics very well, neither leaving anything out nor repeating itself in a way that would make it annoying. I have found it easy to get into, despite having little experience with the princess-maker genre as a whole.

Audio and graphics:
The music for Ciel Fledge is very good; you will come to love it if you spend time listening to it while playing. Jasmine Cooper has a special talent for scoring tracks that speak very well to the settings they accompany, and that only get better the more you hear them. 
The graphics are... well, I'd rate it a mediocre thus far if I had to use a technical scale, but they're servicable and I personally enjoy them because they remind me of the style of Nusakana, which as I mentioned earlier is among my favorite games of all time.

Story and characters: 
Unfortunately while it is the meat of the game, I can't give a proper review to the story and characters as I have yet to complete most of the game for myself. I can share that my expectations are high, as the writer and project leader is the same person as for Nusakana. It will take awhile before I can actually play enough of Ciel Fledge to let it speak on its own merits, but the characters in Nusakana were ALL unique and well-written, a major feat in itself with a cast of more than 30 characters. They were actually deep and interesting enough that I enjoyed spending time with all of them, and went well beyond the usual character stereotypes you'd expect from an anime life-sim with much less dialogue than you'd think they'd need.
Those who played Nusakana may be worried about poor grammar due to translation difficulties, as it was an unfortunate plague on the previous game. To my great relief, I have seen no such issues present in the hour I have played Ciel Fledge, and so I can confidently expect none in the future.

TLDR; I am recommending Ciel Fledge partly because the merits of its predecessor inspired enough confidence in me to expect greatness of this game, but also because all that I have seen so far of the game has me genuinely excited to discover its own merits. And because indie studios in a niche genre have such a difficult time making it to the front page as it is, I don't want to wait a few weeks until I finish the last chapter to give it my thumbs-up.

																Coffee Talk is a story focused barista game that was released on the 29th of January 2020. What I mean by “story focused barista” is that you are a barista in a coffee shop, and you listen to the stories of the customers. The stories of these customers are what the game focuses on. Coffee Talk plays half like a visual novel and half like and an arcadey coffee making game. The visual novel part is straight forward. You just listen to the customers talk. This is the main way the story moves forward. The customers will also order drinks. This is where the arcadey coffee making part come in. Drinks are made from 3 ingredients. There are 5 base ingredients and 6 additional ingredients. To keep track of everything happening, you have a phone you can use. The phone has an app to keep track of all the drinks that you can make. Another app keeps track of customers and information about them. There is also an endless mode.

The graphics are nicely done. The characters have a lot of detail and expression. The coffee shop is well done for what it is. The drinks themselves looks good and some of the drinks actually looked delicious. The music of the game is good but blended into the background after a while.

Coffee Talk is not a game for everyone. The story may be too slow for some. The gameplay may be too boring or slow for others, but if you are patient enough and like a really good story, Coffee Talk is 100% worth it.

																Just a heads up: at the time of writing this review, I had only cleared the main story once and I hadn't played the endless mode.

I have a lot of mixed feelings about this game, but I ended up recommending it mainly because I had quite a lot of fun with it in the long run. With that said, there are some negatives to consider, so don't take my first sentence as a fact immediately.

Coffee Talk takes places in an alternate universe where creatures that we normally associate with fantasy exist, like for example werewolves, elves, vampires, succubi, and so and so forth. In this world is a humble little cafe in Seattle owned by you, the self-insert protagonist. Throughout the game you serve customers drinks and listen to their stories. It's very similar in concept to VA-11 Hall-A, though instead of a bar it's a coffee shop.

The game is fairly short, I finished it in about 7½ hours or so. For what content there is, it's a pretty entertaining read, though maybe a bit on the shorter side. All the characters are well written and they're all pretty memorable. Because there are so many characters, some of them have their own story arcs as well. The only problem I had with most of those story arcs is that they felt way too short. Before you know it, you run out of days and the story is over. That was a little upsetting for me honestly, but compared to what was given to me in the first place, I don't see much reason to complain. I'm decently satisfied.

Gameplay wise... Well, I have some gripes to say the least, but let me first explain how the game works. A customer will order a drink, they will either give the name of the drink or the ingredients to make it. You then look up the drink and put it together with the required ingredients and serve it. There are some instances that someone will ask for a drink, but you might have to give them something else instead, which you have to determine from what you think the customer might really need. If you've played VA-11 Hall-A before, you should be familiar with how it works.

But this is where we get to my gripes with the game. You start off the game with instructions on how to make only a few drinks, the rest you have to discover for yourself. On top of that, the game can be incredibly picky about the order of the ingredients. You have three slots for those: the base, as well as primary and secondary ingredients. Sometimes customers will tell you to make a drink with certain ingredients, let's say for this example the character asks for a drink with "tea, ginger and milk." So you go start brewing it by adding them in the order the character said it in, but when you serve it, the game tells you that the drink isn't quite right, because you put ginger in before milk, as according to the order the customer themselves said them in. I think that's a bit cheap of the game to start pulling stuff like that out of nowhere.

But that's not the end of it. Sometimes, customers will ask for a specific drink, and if you haven't discovered it earlier, you're kinda screwed if they don't give you a few hints at least. Because what ends up happening is that you'll be given two ingredients and you're just left to your own devices to figure out what that last ingredient is, not to mention you have to figure out the order of input as well. It doesn't help that you can only trash a drink 5 times before you have to serve the drink you made most recently. I could see that working if you have a failure condition, but there kinda is none. Not in the story at least, especially since you can just save before brewing the drink and then loading the game if you screw up (which, at least it has that, so good). But that doesn't change the fact that you'll be spending most of your time figuring out what the correct drink is through trial and error. It's by far the most annoying part of the game and the only way to bypass it directly is to look up a walkthrough.

To give you an example of how bad it can get, there is a moment where a customer asks for a certain drink, and you think that they would need something else entirely. This other drink is a very specific drink that would guarantee a certain significant event to happen. The problem? The game never gives you any instructions or hints on how to make it. Never. The only reason I knew about the drink was because I had looked at a brewing guide before and I happened to see it on the list. This sort of trial and error design is one of those reasons that made me have severe mixed feelings about this game.

The story, though short, is pretty enjoyable. The brewing, while it seems easy, is plagued with some mind numbing design decisions. But despite that, I'm willing to give the game a recommendation, if only to show some support for the devs. It's not a perfect game, but for what it's worth, it was enjoyable.

																LEGRAND LEGACY: Tale of the Fatebounds by Semisoft Studios is a newly released JRPG, offering a fresh experience in a new fantasy world. If you are a fan of role playing games, especially those similar to Tales of Vesperia, Chrono Cross/Trigger, or The Last Remnant, then this game may fit your interests. This review will cover gameplay and story for the first three chapters.

The story begins with our protagonist, Finn, fighting for his life in an arena. He is an amnesiac, who has some sort of magical potential that purposefully marks him as special. A mysterious old man buys Finn’s freedom and employs him as a temporary bodyguard. As circumstance would have it, tragedy befalls our hero, and he chooses to use his newfound freedom to finish his master’s mission: to save his daughter. After the disaster, we are introduced to Aria, a noblewoman from the north on a quest to end a blood feud. After discovering that prophecy has foretold of the imminent return of other worldly invaders, Aria’s mission ultimately becomes Finn’s. Along the way, they make unlikely allies and colorful companions to aid them in their pursuit of destiny.

While I am not too crazy about the plot, seeming a little cliché, it does get more interesting as you become more invested in the journey itself. The villains fall a little flat, too, but the writers do subvert expectations every now and then. There are many themes of freedom, superfluity of destiny, justice, and the corrupting influence of power. I cannot help but feel like these are the usual tactics of the unlikely hero storyline we know all too well. I also feel as though Finn could have been written a little better, mostly because he comes across as a little too good. There are moments that capture his insecurities, but they do not capture any major flaws that he needs to overcome – just amnesia. The rest of the supporting cast members are written very well. I think Aria may be my favorite character, while being a strong leader, she overlooks certain issues and underestimates some enemies, to the point that she learns from the experiences from each chapter. The majority of characters join the party out of reluctance or caused to join by necessity, but they undergo changes and become heroes. Kael, for instance, is a clever rogue, and even he has a dynamic character arch that I personally enjoyed.

The characters, themselves, are very well designed in both dialogue profiles (that are animated) and in combat avatars. The art style is very cool, making me excited to engage in as much dialogue as possible. The world map, and local areas are well crafted as well. Occasionally I would have trouble navigating some areas because of the camera angle, but nothing game-breaking. The grimoire animations are flashy and cool, though I wish there could be more variety of attacks. The monsters are also put together very well. They just feel like they belong in a JRPG. These creatures will drop items that you may sell in bulk or use to craft items.

There are many different aspects to gameplay, some of which catch you by surprise. The prologue even throws you into the fight for your life knowing that you have no idea how to play yet. Combat is easy to pick up after a couple battles, and you tend to learn what strategies work since you fight the same enemies over and over again in the beginning. What is especially nice is that you can save up your AP, and when the gauge is full you can unleash an ultimate ability. Every character has one, not all necessarily designed to deal damage. Eris is the only character so far whose ultimate ability heals and buffs allies in play. It is best to use these abilities sparingly depending on the situation. Every time you commit to an action you need to hit “W,” “A,” “S,” or “D” at a specific moment to maximize effectiveness. If you play it poorly, then you will either do insignificant damage, or none at all. Be sure that you are using an attack that will affect the enemy effectively, based on elemental weaknesses or other vulnerabilities.

Chapter 3 (my favorite chapter so far) brings more gameplay to the table. I will avoid spoiling the plot, but there is a massive battle, in which multiple NPCs are engaging each other. So, you can engage some of these PCs in sort of microcosm of a battle in relation to the bigger battle going on around you. This war scenario turns into a brief turn-based strategy game as you command your heroes as individual units around a grid. I found that part of the game to be an interesting change in pace.

The soundtrack fits the world and the themes superbly – perhaps one of my favorite tracks among JRPGs that I have played in recent years, because it reflects that dark-fantasy/adventure vibe the developers may have had in mind. Battle music is very reminiscent of something out of Final Fantasy. It feels classic. The different settings also include their own music, like the desert theme from the beginning, the shanty theme at the harbor, and the harp melody from Shapur. They stick in your head for a little bit, and it’s nice to have that ambiance as you visit new places.

I am still having a relaxed time playing Legrand Legacy, and I’m engaged in the adventure wondering how the story will continue now that most of the party has been assembled and there has been a lot of development between the characters. This is an experience that I enjoy, especially since I grew up with classic Final Fantasy turn-based combat games. I think a fair score for this title is an 8.5 out of 10, because it delivers closely to what I am looking for in an RPG in general, but I think the audience of the genre would appreciate building the world more, subverting expectations in characters and the story, and making a defining staple for the Legrand series.

Pong, Lethal League, and Street Fighter walk into a barThis arcade sports game is a kind of throw back on retro fighting games with a bit of a twist. Imagine playing pong but you have freedom of movement anywhere on the screen. There are ten characters to play as. You can try your hand at the story on two different difficulties or kick back and unfold chaos with friends in multiplayer. 

Each interestingly crafted character has their own story, statistics, and special. Players move around the screen smacking a ball in whatever direction they hit the ball at and it changes into that team's color. The goal is to knock out your opponents health crystal which is guarded. As long as the ball is your team's color it can not hurt your defenses. The ball can increases in speed after multiple hits or when a stronger character hits it.

Retro game, retro difficultyAs simple as the mechanics are to learn they are pretty hard to master. In the story mode you will face off against some pretty tough opponents including at one point two at once. Battles can turn and be instantly lost with some abilities and lucky bounces used against you. There are two difficulties to the main single player mode. Playing with friends may increase your ability and understanding of the mechanics but they are still something that require some patience to be able to utilize well.

80s A E S T H E T I C SBetween the synthwave and house music or the bright colored characters and exaggerations this has some pretty neat aesthetics. It's also really awesome to boot up a game and hear music by Manami Matsumae. 

So this game has some pleasing aesthetics, fun mechanics, and room for a player to improve their abilities. The game supports up to four players and can be pretty chaotic. It is not exactly a fighting game but it does some kind of mechanic mixing that makes for a pretty intuitive title. The story and extra content may fall a bit short for the asking price, but if you can gather some friends it can make for a pretty good multiplayer session. I can recommend it for being something different than what I normally play and doing a good job of it.

Posted: 10 March, 2020

																OverviewDreadOut 2 is an adventure / horror game acting as sequel to DreadOut, and continues the story of Linda, the first game's protagonist, after she returns to a relatively normal life following the tragedy that fell on her and other classmates. Both blessed and cursed by the ability of seeing and exorcising ghosts, as well ostracized by most people due to the events she has gone through, Linda will soon find herself entangled in a new spiral of death and disaster, as literal ghosts from her past come back into her life.

?? Pros
Well done environments, atmosphere and art direction, emphasizing a lot the sense of dread when needed.
Good gameplay variety that includes investigation, exploration, puzzles, combat and bosses.
The usage of Indonesian settings and folklore delivers places and enemies not often seen in games.
Combat, on the good side, has a very satisfying hit feeling and the right pacing.?? Cons
Animations are janky, stiff and often ridiculous, breaking immersion during more complex actions. 
The story is a confusing mess, nothing that happens is ever explained properly, without any additional clue to understand it either.  
Combat system is gimmicky, unreliable and has several balance problems.
Most boss fights are either too easy or badly designed, only few of them result engaging and done properly.
Noticeable general lack of polishing and attention to finer details in characters and locations. Rating: DecentClick here for the complete Rating Chart


	
	
		Linda can use her phone to see supernatural events such as ghost apparitions, and if necessary banish them using the device as a weapon. 
		A Screenshot of DreadOut 2
		By: Tamaster
		
					
	


On the good side, DreadOut 2's biggest strength is the excellent environmental art direction, that manages to deliver realistic locations from urban areas to rural Indonesia landscapes, without forgetting the blood-soaked, dark places of the alternate dimension. This results in greater immersion especially during exploration sequences. The variety of gameplay is more than decent, as it alternates combat and horror segments with more relaxed exploration, and a middle point being ghost exorcisms, which though become much more dangerous later on. 

The game's setting is very unusual and probably there isn't another title with the same one, this ensures most players will not have a sense of "already seen" when facing challenges and visiting locations. The combat is not the best but has some good points, the best being the meaty, violent feeling of hits upon enemies and the right pacing to it, mostly on the slow side, as it is in most survival horrors.

The bad side also has a lot on its part, the largest flaw being animations of human NPCS and the protagonist herself, often resulting comedic and totally breaking immersion. The story is another weak point, because even by paying attention, seeing the "story before" intro to DreadOut 1's events, I still have no idea as to why or how most critical events happened: it's a confusing mess. Combat might be satisfying but is also gimmicky, with Linda's stun being OP and easily stagger-locking most enemies including bosses.

Some boss fights are good enough but most end up being too easy because of how OP the stun mechanic is, or badly designed to the point of stun-locking you into their attack cycles until death. Last but not least, the lack of polishing and attention to finer details is noticeable, with empty stores pretending to be open or NPCs pretending to watch their phone when they are holding nothing.

Overall DreadOut 2 is a decent horror game that manages to deliver an interesting and unusual experience for the genre that will be enjoyed by horror and paranormal fans, but the problems make it less appealing for other types of players. It took me 7 hours to complete the game while also doing all the side content I managed and exploring each area thoroughly. For the price of 16,79€, and low replay value, decent quality, I would suggest waiting for a sale even for fans of the genre.

Liked this review, and want to see more of the same quality? Check out Tamaster's Review Archive to see all my Reviews in a single, convenient location.

	
	
		Combat has a good feel of weight behind hits and feels satisfying, but is also clunky and gimmicky especially during boss fights. 
		A Screenshot of DreadOut 2
		By: Tamaster
		
					
	


In-Depth Breakdown?? Gameplay Analysis
The gameplay of DreadOut 2 is divided into Exploration, Quests, Combat and Puzzles. 

Exploration
Is always done on foot, Linda can either jog, run for a limited time, or walk to be silent when needed. The game is divided into several fully open areas such as city center, school and a rural village, to name some. At times you will enter an alternate dimension populated by hostile monsters, with its own map layout. Fast travel between locations is available most of the time, and certain quests or events can be only active at specific times of the day or as the main story progresses. There are no collectibles or other things making exploration worthwhile, other than collecting side quests or seeing some events unfolding. 

Quests
Are either given by NPCs directly or instead are curious rumors you hear from random people. Either way, they mostly are in your same area and might be retrieving an item or finding someone. A few quests are more complex and need more work to complete, in multiple areas. During the alternate dimension, most quests involve defeating a boss or getting items to progress.

Combat
Is two fold: while in the normal dimension Linda can use her phone as a "gun" to banish spirits, but only at specific moments when the screen glitches: you have to get used to it and with some enemies this system proves unreliable. While in the other dimension, you'll need to find actual weapons, as the phone only can stun enemies, the area stun is very potent and spammable, it can cheese through most enemies and even bosses, making combat a gimmick. Stunned enemies can be executed to inflict high damage. The absence of a dodge and the fact some bosses can perma-stun lock you to death can be frustrating.

Puzzles
Are not many and generally consist in logic-based enigmas such as rotating panels to form an image. Or chasing an enemy through the right path. They are generally decently done but presented few times.


	
	
		Environments have great atmosphere and depict Indonesian rural and city areas accurately. There is however a lack of finer details. 
		A Screenshot of DreadOut 2
		By: Tamaster
		
					
	


?? Technical
PC Specs: RTX2080Ti, Ryzen 3900X, 32GB RAM DDR4
There are no critical stability, performance or other issues to note. The game runs well in 1440p with an average GPU utilization of 70% at 85Hz. There are slight pop-in issues with distant elements especially while using the phone camera, while environments can take several seconds to fully load even on an SSD after transitions. Rarely doors can glitch and become stuck for some time. Some distortion effects such as motion blur or aberration cannot be disabled individually in the graphics menu. 

Final ThoughtsA decent horror title that delivers varied gameplay, enjoyable but clunky combat, and well done atmosphere in a setting not often seen in games. The lack of polishing and messy story however prevent it from being much better.

																This game was developed by an indie studio (if the publishers weren't a giveaway) combined with a kickstarter so I will give them slack when it comes certain aspects but overall Legrand Legacy is a game that perfectly replicates all the aspects that all the greatest JRPG have in common. This means the pros and the cons as well. This game is still being updates as we speak of so the developers are dedicated to improve the player experience as we speak of so some aspects might be different for me at the moment. The story especially is still being rewritten, more specifically the dialogue.

The world of Legrand Legacy is your classical middle age like world where magic exists, it's also a world where corruption and war are at it heights even though long ago the world was already saved by a group of heroes, showing that even though they prevented the world from its destruction they didn't actually save it. You play as the protagonist who doesn't know anything about his past suddenly comes into the companionship of a person destined to be the person who gathers the Fatebounds, a group of individuals who are destined to fullfill the same obligation of saving the world from its destruction once again although this time they are there to actually save it this time.

The gameplay itself is turn based so it will feel familiar to those who have played quiet a bit of (J)RPG games. But where Legrand Legacy sets itself appart is the amount of mechanics inspired by the classics. One of the biggest giveaway is its interactive, time based battle system, this is most recognizable from Legend of the Dragoon. There are of course more mechanics where Legrand Legacy took its inspiration from as this game is first and foremost a loveletter to all the classic JRPGs.

The game isn't simple though and stragety is required, the solution may not always come immeatidely and this might sometimes be frustrating but the challenge makes the game that more satisfying when it finally works. Though I do admit I had my fair share of frustrating moments. But there's a friendly a discord group that are always willing to lend a helping hand when needed, one which consists of the actual developers of the game so there's communication with its community.

https://discordapp.com/invite/ai (If the link doesn't show then just go to their twitter page, there should be a discord link for those who either want to ask for help or even perhaps ask questions about the game itself, like its story and such )

There are also several minigames which gives much needed variation and does help to setup the pace once again. But except for one, the rest are optional. It also gives you several chances to earn rare items which of course is very helpful.

The graphics are quiet alright, especially considering its an indie game. While the animation can be rough around the edges it has its charm and is more than enough to convey the story. I personally like the portrait faces that appear with the dialogue as the facial expressions convey much more information than a static image could do. As you know, a picture can say a thousand words but cgi rendered facial animations can say a million more.

The music is quiet good, there are certain tracks that are just fantastic and make me stop and listen to the music. My personal favorite is the theme of Belfas, it's pleasant.

This game doesn't have that much requirements so it should be able to play on even a low-end-pc.
Of course, if you are unsure and this review hasn't convinced you yet, then you can try the demo for free and see if this game is for you.

TLDR; It's an enjoyable love letter to JRPGs of the ps1 and ps2 era so there are a lot of things to enjoy. While it does have its rough edges it gives you a nice experience. If unsure, just download the demo and see if its something for you. Join their discord channel for discussions  or a helping hand when needed.

																As beautiful as this game is in terms of art and music, I cannot stand by the game design itself. This game holds both your hands, leaving nothing for you to figure out on your own. It might be excusable for a children's game, but it really underestimates the intelligence of the player regardless of their age. Everything is pointed out to you, either by blinking indications of where you should click, or told to you straight up in dialog. 

Not to mention that this game feels like 80% dialog and 20% gameplay. The dialog sections are far too long and beat around the bush instead of getting to the point. It seems like this is done in attempt to introduce the personalities of each character and to make you form some emotional attachment to them. The problem is that this could have been done in 5 lines instead of 25; it's just too much back and forth that serves little purpose. The animations of the firefly moving between different screens cannot be sped up (e.g. by double clicking) and combined with the loading time and the long dialog, progress can feel excruciatingly slow. 

I appreciate the additions of the hidden carvings as well as the "get slapped by the mushroom 10 times" and "scare orchids with snails" achievements, since these are the few parts of the game that involves exploration. And as mentioned earlier, the graphics are gorgeous. The art style is consistent, appropriate for the mood of the game and features a harmonious color palette. The character designs are creative and interesting as well. The music compliments the art very nicely, making the game an esthetically wonderful experience.

That is why it pains me to say that I don't recommend this game. As beautiful and relaxing as the esthetic aspects are, these should be a positive addition instead of the primary strong point of a game - the cherry on top of the already delicious sundae, not its saving grace. A game should be a game first and foremost, and I don't believe telling the player exactly what to do at all times is what that entails.

This is where the useability issues starts.

To recover 3-4 man points in a round of combat, you need to press 15 keyboard strokes for a team of 3 allies. After 11 hours, the game has reached a point where progress is slow and my hands are extremely tired because of excessive keyboard pressing. My hands are numbed, and I would most likely giveup on this game, unless the developer fixed the useability issues.

																I must have been one of the lucky ones because aside from the janky combat I was able to finish the game without any game breaking bugs. 

In my opinion Dreadout 2 embodies the saying bigger isn't always better.  A lot of the nuance from the earlier games is simply gone. There are very few puzzles in this game. And one of them actually requires that you use your camera.   If I'm being honest nothing is super memorable from the game. Remember DreadOut's Possessed Ira conversation or the mirror fights with the 2nd Sister? Those were very interesting and fun sequences but nothing close to that ever happens in DreadOut 2. It's painfully linear and honestly this game could largely benefit from some kind of HUD. You can't really gauge your health outside of the color fading from the screen and the number of hits before that cue even triggers varies based on who you fight. While the game world is expanded its admittedly bland and doesn't offer a whole lot. On top of this you can freely fast travel from place to place as soon as a new location is opened which kind of mutes the wide scope. The biggest issue i have with the game is: 

The removed Limbo from the death/checkpoint system. This was probably the most iconic part of DreadOut and its taken out of the gameplay loop an made into a section of a cutscene toward the end with no explanation. Its odd that no other reviewer or players have mentioned this I was honestly upset when I died and saw a continue screen pop up. I genuinely hope it gets patched into the game as IMO its the most unique part of the series


Combat is the same hit or miss dance as its always been. The enemies in this game have highly aggressive AI and they will stun lock you to death if you aren't careful. There's also the issue with the cam not registering hits on the enemies unless you get their good side (IE: a perfect center face picture of whatever ghost is in your way). In addition to this there is a couple seconds of delay between when you can snap another picture. Combine this with some of the more evasive ghosts and you will be on full tilt in seconds. Its rough but not completely impossible. the addition of physical combat is a fun addition and its clearly something they put a lot of thought into, though this is a bit overpowered. I only wish that we could mix up between snapping pictures and using physical items.

That all being said the game is still a step up from the previous titles in other areas. UE4 is a boon to this series and the Developers are really able to let their imaginations go ham with some enemy designs, Linda looks much better also. As a whole the game has many quality of life improvements. Linda gets bloody as she gets hurt, even scarred up a little bit. The vignette system is replaced with a bracelet that glows red/blue and we get a cool little phone glitch whenever enemies are close, a la Silent Hill. The game having actual controller support is nice as well. 

TL;DR the plot is paper thin and half baked but the gameplay was solid enough and the game never bugged out to the point that it was unplayable for me. Combat leans to unfair in most boss fights but if you can stay patient you can win. It's not the best game out there but these guys tried.  Also, I have to shout out Digital Happiness for discounting the game as an apology for releasing the game a day late. To me that shows a love to the community that shouldn't be overlooked and yeah that gives them an extra point on this review. 

All in all  I had fun and I'd give it a 7/10.

																Coffee Talk is a fun little narrative game with a few stumbling blocks that don't ruin the over-all experience.

The first thing anyone will do is to compare this game to Va11-Hall-A because...well, it should be obvious. It's a visual novel about making drinks for people and chatting with them. There are differences here and there but I won't compare it too much, though sometimes the comparisons are unavoidable.

So, for a game that is 90% writing, how is it? The answer is...pretty good. Sometimes the game can be a little on the nose with it's writing but that's not anything that really bugged me at all. It also tackled some decent topics, such as disapproving families, generational divides and fantasy racism (which is handled decently, tho analogues for real minorities in fantasy works are always a little awkward). The characters are fun and pretty good as well, tho you'll see only a couple faces the whole game. Which works out in favor of developing their stories more as you get to interact more than with larger casts. While there is no overarching narrative, each character story can wrap up in it's own way: good because you made the right drinks or bad because you didn't.

...which brings me to the negative I had about the game. The drink-making was fine for the most part, but I found myself messing up people's drinks because of either unclean instructions, getting the order of ingredients wrong (which it never explains to you matters) or because if I did get an order wrong it wasn't added to the drinks menu so I didn't know if I had made it and messed up before. As a result, while I understand they wanted to make the game a bit puzzling and so you don't succeed the first time you play the game (more on that in a sec) and see different story paths, it became frustrating because when you got an order wrong it felt like you didn't really have enough to figure it out. 																Ok, so after 3 hours of play, here's my take on this game...

TL;DR:
I think the combat mechanics are broken and don't work. As a neo-JRPG, combat is kind of core. If you don't like the combat, you won't like the game.

GRAPHICS: 8/10

In this game, the graphics are superb. I'm a sucker for cellshading and this game just renders the character's faces so beautifully. From the Character portraits in the menu to the painting-like overworld map, it is a sight to behold.

Music: 6/10

It's not bad, but it doesn't stand out that much. I did feel as inspired as with the visuals.

STORY: 4/10

Note: Devs have reworked on the story and characters since I wrote this review. Kept in spolers for archives.

So here's where it starts to smell. WARNING, SPOILERS AHEAD!! I will summarize the first 3 hours of game to give you an idea of how random and unengaging the story is. I've changed some names to make it a bit interesting, but doesn't change the story.

So you are are Finn (no funny name here, it's his real name), the classic-amnesiac slave-gladiator protagonist. most likely the 3rd prince of the Atlean Kingdom/empire. Your brothers tried to have you killed. You lost your memory in the process. I like at how they hint at you probably being quite an evil bastard yourself, back in the days. You are pushed in a gladiatorial tutori... AHEM.... arena. You get in a "fake" fight when you actually cannot really win, it's just 2 rounds and a cutscene of you about to get killed when your inner self/demon/power awakes and defeats your opponent. 

The you are introduced to ObiwanGeddobi, an old man/mage that rescues you, teaches you some more tutorials, asks you to help him find his dying daughter, and then dies (offscreen) while protecting you from baddies that look like ISIS members on crack. (second impossible fight, with 1 normal attack, one guy does 10x your max hp in damage) After his death, you fail to protect his corpse from carrion-eaters-harpy-thingies and he gets taken away onto the sunset. 

Now arrives mandatory YANDERE girl. After playing this dress is while and gold, no it is black and blue, for about 3 minutes, she agrees to help you find ObiwanGeddobi's daughter, but only if you help her find a big flying monster who's shadow you saw earlier. You prepare for a fight, but you end up digging up a lost ruin. "wadzifyak". After telling her that you've done your part and that time is of the essence because the girl is dying, you both enter the ruin. Inside you find Old Jesus that tells her that she is a Fatebound (roll credits) and that all the problems in the world right now are nothing compared to the invasion of the [enter random demon race here, I will call them fuzzy rabbits] that is to come. If the fuzzy rabbits are allowed into the world, they will destroy it. So he gives her (not you, because it's her responsability) the Main Fetch Quest to find the 4 ultimate weapons, the only weapons capable of defeating the fuzzy rabbits. Now that she has the quest is activated, she keeps her end of the bargain and leads you to 3rd party member. And right when you find her, YANDERE girl leaves.

So now you have found ObiwanGeddobi's daughter, Yuna, a healer/mage. She is dying but you give her the [enter random panacea herb here, I'll call it False Hope]. it's not enough to cure her but it will delay her death. She asks you to show you where her dad died. Upon arriving, you find the 3 ISIS crackers still there laughing it off. You fight. It's funny how now they seem to do some reasonable levels of damage. Of course, this time, you win, but for some reason, they still want some more, they insult you and Yuna. (in the story, some characters say that there is something weird making everyone corrupt and evil, for me, I just think it makes them stupid). So Yuna get angry and in a fit of rage, she disentegrate them. like, very easily. (she is definitely much stronger than her father). Now that the baddies are dead and she found her father's medallion, she dances him a soul-send-off, just like he name predicted.
And that's the end of my first play session.

COMBAT: 4/10

Enemies are shown on the map. They look like evil floating eyeballs covered in darkness. If they see you, they'll give chase. Run up for a face-to-face and you'll enter combat. Touch their butt and you'll ambush them, free turn for you. Let them touch your butt and they'll ambush you, free turn for them. Standard stuff.  Don't ever let them touch your but, you'll die.

So the combat plays just like a regular JRPG, except that each turn you give your commands to all party members, and then all characters and monster run up to their target and hit them, seemingly at the same time, but not really. There seems to be an initiative tracker to define turn order, but the way the animations are played makes it just seem random. With a lot of enemies, it looks like an orgy in the middle of the screen with damage counters poping up from time to time. With some other enemies, like the huge SandSquid-horses thingies, you can clearly see them rearing up to attack, and then waiting until you character's finished their attack pattern to sit on you with all their might...

you have goodish front-back row mechanic, melee chars need to be in front or they can't attack, and they can't attack back-row if there is a char in front. Same applies for enemies. So I guess that easier fights will feature melee creatures in the back that can't attack you at first, it limits how much damage you can take at the same time. Idealy, place archers and casters in the back row. Since all 3 of the first companions you find are mages and archers, your MC will always be in front defending, and the other in the back, casting.  Don't even try to cast if you're in the first row, be cause you'll get interrupted and loose your turn.

Some times, you'll encounter 2 caster enemies that on the first turn of combat will both cast a spell that hits everyone and does half you MC's hp in damage. 2 of this means one turn kill on your MC. Don't let the enemies touch your butt.

When you attack or defend, you get a quick time event. You get a ring with zones on it, then a clock hand races around the ring and you need to time a button press to get it right. Get it super right and you win a critical hit. I hate this system with all of my being. It's annoying, it's repetitive, it's random (both the target location, AND the button to press). Basically, it just gimps combat, and make it not fun. After looking at the option menu, I've discovered that you can remove the random of the quicktime event, but it gives you less XP. So you are telling me that it's basically hard mode? And it's on by default? I've also read some people say that it's comparable to Legend of Dragon. I'm sorry to say but it is not. in Legend of Dragoon, the quick time happens right after you select the attack option of one character (not after everyone's) and it's never random. In it's place, you get a rythm that you learn by doing over and over again, and you learn to never miss it. And over the course of the game, your character learns more powerful but complex attacks. And you become more powerful by learning the rythm of the attack. Here, it's one random button press that has no rythm and that may not appear when you expect it to because some enemy attacks might wreck the combat flow. I'll actually go and say that the whole quicktime event in Legrand Legacy breaks the flow of combat.

You have some spells that you can cast, but good luck, because spells are executed last and if you get hit first, there are some good chances you'll get interrupted, like against a boss who will target the caster systematically instead of hitting the now useless front-row defender that has no bonus against the boss but the caster does.

Oh, and don't even think of starting a boss fight without your limit break ready, you'll die.

I've got some more to say, I ran out of space...

Meanwhile, the Barista feels like an invisible deity that sometimes spouts wisdom at the characters.

Overall, Coffee Talk is a great time that I can recommend to VA-11-Hall-A fans or just people looking for a cozy little story they can get lost in.

																A frantic real-time game that has you throwing out cards fast to spawn units and cast spells. It reminds me a lot of a Warcraft three custom map. Necronator pulls heavily from Slay the Spire to inspire their mechanics.

To start you choose one of the two characters, a third is coming soon. They each have a unique playstyle and more decks that you can unlock while playing. I don't quite understand Mirabella's decks, they're incredibly slow. As you play and level up the characters you'll unlock upgraded versions of the cards to draft. It seems getting access to those upgraded cards is key to deep runs.

Then you go to a node based map that pushes you up to a powerful boss. The battle nodes on the map are what make the game unique! Your portal constantly generates mana to spend on cards. Along the path to destroying the castle, there are smaller castles you can defeat and haunt. If you take them over you'll gain more mana and they'll even attack enemies. In my experience, if you take a castle you've already won. The extra mana gives you so many more card options. Also, you can spam out cards so quickly it's usually enough to overwhelm anything.

There's some strategy though because in the later larger levels there are lanes. So you're able to adjust the path your units take to the main castle. It can get complicated with multiple crossroads. At first, it's important to head off enemies so they don't sneak by between playing unit cards. Once you get close enough to the enemy spawn it doesn't matter. Also, once you're already leading it's like a snowball rolling down a hill. You'll keep growing and be too strong for the enemy to contain. I like the mechanic and it makes the early game interesting. It's too bad it fades away.

You collect relics to make you more powerful. However enemies can have relics too and you must check them before starting a battle.Some enemy relics are at odds with your current deck. So my favorite deck, Fresh Meat, spawns a million minions. But the Militia Handbook relic will spawn three militia whenever the player plays a squad card. 																I already heard of other coffee-brewing games before, with VA-11 Hall-A being one of the most popular ones. However, I never got around playing any of those games before — Well until now. The title "Coffee Talk" already includes everything you have to know about the game: It's about coffee and maybe involves a lot of talking as well. That's quite accurate as all you do is serve coffee to your customers while listening to their stories.

Coffee and Talking
The player slips into the role of a barista in Coffee Talk who owns a café. However, it's no ordinary café as it's only open at night. The reason for that is simple: There are people who are craving coffee or just need a place to stay during unusual times. Although the business is, evidently, not profitable, as there are simply not enough customers during the night, the protagonist prefers to create a comfortable place nonetheless. The special thing here is that Coffee Talk takes place in a fantasy world with elves, orcs, mermaids, aliens, etc.

The Main Character
Well, Coffee Talk doesn't have a narrator per se, however, the main character surely does feel like a passive observer who only occasionally talks to the customers. Usually, I prefer more active protagonists so the reader can see them grow and can actually get to know them as this is critical for the character development. Luckily, the focus in Coffee Talk isn't the protagonist itself but the customers who visit the café so I found it just fitting that the main character doesn't interfere in the happenings a lot but still interacts with the people if he has to.

The reader doesn't get to know the protagonist at all, although they can freely choose a name for them. Everything else, however, such as gender, appearance, etc. stays mysterious throughout the playthrough. I guess that means that it's easy for the reader to imagine being the barista themselves.

What About The Other Characters?
The background story of the customers is getting revealed while the player serves them coffee. I found it so interesting that there are a few side-stories going on and looked forward to each new customer. You see, the same customers are visiting the café again so their story gets continued. I enjoyed that the reader gets to know the whole cast better but that's not everything, the characters are interacting with themselves a lot too. It was heart-warming to see them giving advice to each other and I sometimes just wanted to help them.

The thing I love here is that each of them has their own struggles that can be applied to the real-life as well. Although the theme varies from social problems to racism or anxiety, even game development gets thematized. I found each side-story interesting and whilst some characters come off as weird at first, I warmed up to all of them very quickly. In the end, I felt like they started off as strangers but became a small family that is tight-knitted thanks to the café they are all visiting.

Brewing Coffee
So, the most active part of the player is the process of brewing coffee for their customers. In total, the player has to select three ingredients to produce the coffee. A specific combination is needed for a special kind of coffee, although the customers sometimes just demand simpler versions such as hot or sweet cups. In this case, there is a bar available during the brewing where the player can see the stats for each ingredient. The recipe for each special cup has to be discovered, although the customers are giving the player hints at times.

Something that I found very tricky was the latte art for specific drinks. Luckily, it's not mandatory and doesn't make any impact on the game, yet it was difficult to create decent latte art. I used that feature around two times before giving up as it takes up a lot of time. Anyway, it was still interesting to add that feature so those who are very creative can let off their steam.

In addition to that, there is a "Free Brew" and "Challenge" mode available in Coffee Talk where the player can either discover new recipes or practice their brewing skills. The free brew mode is pretty simple and allows its player to take their time whilst the challenge one has a time limit so it's important to be fast.

Own Your Own In-Game Smartphone
So, there is a smartphone available in Coffee Talk that turned out to be quite useful. The usage of it is entirely optional, however, I loved the features it has to offer and ended up visiting it longer than I assumed I would. In total, it has four applications installed.

The first one is Tomodachill. Every person the player meets will show up in that application and it kind of reminds me of a reduced version of Facebook where the player can read more about the cast's interests. For unlocking more information, it's mandatory that the player gets closer to the character.

The Brewpad is probably the most useful application where the player can look up the recipe of all unlocked coffees. I found that was especially helpful in the free brew or challenge mode, especially as it's hard to memorize every recipe.

Let's move to the next one, The Evening Whisperss. As the name already hints at, there are short stories getting released each day that are written by a specific customer. Anyway, this was my favorite application as I ended up checking it out every in-game day. The stories are not related at all, yet, I feel like they are still lovely and I had a lot of joy going through each of them.

Lastly, there is the Shuffld application. This one allows the player to select another soundtrack to listen to, which is a quite nice touch I'd say, although I didn't use it at all.
Choices? And What About The Endings?
Coffee Talk doesn't implement choices, however, there are still multiple different endings available in this visual novel. So, the important question is: How is that possible? — Well it simply depends on what drinks the player serves their customers. In short: Getting them the right drinks does make a huge difference. Luckily, the fast forward feature gets unlocked when completing the game once so the player doesn't have to go through the same dialogue again and again. I found it was quite tricky to get everything right during my first playthrough, but luckily it gets easier once I got the gist of it.

Graphics and the Immersion
Graphics-wise, Coffee Talk is stunning. I always had a soft spot for pixelated styles and this visual novel didn't disappoint either. The thing I loved so much about it is that it's so detailed. For instance, there are windows available in the café where the player can see people passing by and rain falling down. These details made the whole game feel so lively, especially as the characters have multiple facial expressions. As a piece of side information, despite being a visual novel, this game does not contain any CGs besides a few ones at the beginning and end. Unfortunately, voice-acting is not present in Coffee Talk which would have greatly enhanced the immersion.

So, what do we have in the end?
Coffee Talk is such a lovely and relaxing game I ended up enjoying much more than I anticipated. I liked that this game didn't focus on one storyline but instead shows its reader multiple side-stories and a variety of characters who couldn't be more different. I got attached quickly to each of them and their stories. In addition to that, the process of brewing coffee managed to keep the game refreshing to me. That being said, I can highly recommend Coffee Talk to everyone who enjoys a cozy game with an excellent cast.
