																To sum the game up in a single sentence: A solid story for anyone who enjoys visual novel-like games, with writing that varies from wildly engaging to lackluster.

To put that in more detail:

Coffee Talk is a game about modern problems in an alternative, fantasy world. It speaks of the difficulties of communication, the woes of chasing your passion in a results-focused society, and the healing power of friendship (yes, seriously).

Allusions are made to the current political climate down here in the States, while Reddit-quality memes are referenced, and it all comes together in such a way that you may forget you're talking to a hipster elf instead of, well, that hipster from your intro to English lit class.

And that is both the biggest strength and weakness of Coffee Talk. Aliens, elves, succubi, vampires, and more all frequent your shop, and yet they're all so HUMAN. Outside of the opening cutscene and some light allusions to a certain event on the first few nights, Coffee Talk puts little effort into building its world. The game is so focused on tackling current issues that the story forgets to give its fantasy creatures any fantastical qualities, and this only becomes more notable as the tale drags on. The fantasy setting is clearly meant to be an allegory for our world and our issues, but I found myself wondering if the story could have been told more effectively if the cast was entirely human; the world is far too barren for the setting to have any real meaning on the plot.

Now, depending on the type of person you are, this may be a good thing. If you just want a game that lightly examines the U.S. and some of its culture issues while working under a lofi-beat-infused lens, then this game may be for you. But with that said, if you wanted a semi-goofy fantasy story with a setting that goes beyond pointy-eared boys and purple-skinned ladies, then you're likely heading towards a disappointment with Coffee Talk. All of these fantasy creatures are supposed act as an interesting framing device, but the world just won't let them branch out beyond their nature as allegorical tools.

The writing itself ebbs and flows in quality. On the whole, each character's arc is told with love and care; it's easy to find something to adore about each character even if they're not fully realized. The slice-of-life aspect of just sitting around and listing to these characters talk about their problems is so, so well done. 

However, there are many pacing and tonal issues. Simply put, Coffee Talk deftly handles its plot and characters until it decides that it no longer wants to do so. Many nights end abruptly, shoving you from one scene to the next right has things were just starting to get interesting. This happens far, far too often during the last third of the story. For a game that tries so hard to emulate VA-11 Hall-A, it's amazing that the devs chose not implement a "break" segment. Instead of creating an organic in-story stopping point for the player to save or quit, while also still allowing them the option to immediately continue with the night's issue, Coffee Talk instead chooses to just drop all of its momentum and shove the story right along to the next plot point. Far, far too often are we rushed from one scene to the next. Threads are left hanging every other night and, again, this only becomes more egregious towards the end.

The game also fails to maintain its tone. There are a few moments where characters lean on the 4th wall, or make poor attempts at humor to add lightness to the more serious moments. This doesn't happen often, but when it does it's a terrible mood killer. It feels as if the writers didn't fully trust their audience to be invested in the story, and that they are instead just trying to push you towards the finish line.

The gameplay itself is nothing special. Characters order, you click the ingredients to make the drink, and that's it. If you're following everyone's orders perfectly, then you barely even get any opportunities to draw that beautiful coffee art you see in the screenshots above! That "branching storyline" the game tries to sell you is mostly a lie. There are two, maybe three instances where the drink you serve a customer actually matters. You can screw up most orders for most of the game, and it really won't matter.

Even with all these negatives in mind, I CAUTIOUSLY recommend Coffee Talk. It's very, very flawed, and it could be SO much better, but the game still has its charms. If you can look past the problems listed above, you'll find an endearing cast and a lovely OST to enjoy.

												This game was so bad I just had to refund it, I'm sorry. There is a certain level of tolerance I can have for poor game design but, after experiencing the tutorial section, the standard of gameplay is simply too poor to warrant a full playthrough.

Let me list the ways:
1. The technical aspect of it is atrocious. Frequent slowdowns completely ruin any immersion, and the graphical quality does not warrant any slowdown from my setup. This is simply poorly optimized for PC.
2. The menus are inexcusably clunky. Why do I need to press up, then press B to select an option, then press A to exit? I can honestly not recall a game post-2000 that uses this kind of selection setup. 
3. It's not scary. Flat out. The jump scares are so flaccid and predictable that I felt like I was playing a parody of a horror game, rather than an actual one.
4. A severe lack of proper direction left me lost in a small area, which is quite the negative accomplishment. The lack of a map made things incredibly annoying, and having to do fetch quests in that area was simply a major pain in the ass.

A tutorial level is supposed to give the player a taste of what is to come for the rest of the game. Unfortunately, it tasted rotten. Perhaps I should have taken it as a sign when one of the professional review quote highlights on the store page, which are supposed to hype the player up enough to buy it, said:

“DreadOut 2 is a game made with much more passion and attention to detail than many other comparable titles and you can see that in every corner. In the end, DreadOut2’s problems are probably due to an insufficient budget.” - virtualseasia

In all: this game is certainly not worth it and should go back to early access status before trying to pass itself off as a complete release. I got this on sale and I honestly regret it. Bright side is: at least I got my money back.

																Its a decent game if you want to try something different.  I love the game play, and believe it has a lot of potential.  The developers seem to do a decent job listening to the community as well.  I would recommend playing it if you are fans of Roguelites, and want to experience one mixed with a RTS.  

With that being said there is a few negative things that really make it difficult to stay invested in the game after the 10 hour mark.  

• Survival Missions - These are just outright not fun.  Typically I would always have a set up that enables me to win (or lose) within the minute.  Sitting in the same match for three minutes even when you have full control of the battlefield is a waste of time, and makes me roll my eyes whenever I encounter one of these.  A possible solution would be to allow the enemy stronghold to be damaged (with a huge boost of HP) so for the runs where we are doing very well we still have a chance to get an earlier win than having to survive the whole three minutes, or just remove these altogether as they don't really require much change in strategy.

• Length of Runs - Each run can take awhile if you make it all the way to the 3rd boss.  Typically halfway through a run you already have established your deck/upgrades to the most optimal its going to get.  When you have 20 more minutes left in a run with a build that is completely capable of defeating any of the bosses, it becomes quite the chore to push through the last 5-10 regular battles leading up to the last boss. (when other games in the same genre feel satisfying to become OP, and defeat everything)

• Upgrades aren't Satisfying - A huge part of roguelites is to have different, and various ways to power up where after a unsuccessful run you just need to dive back in because you know things will be different the next time.  An issue with this game is that you will be likely seeing the same cards, and same types of upgrades (only three versions of an upgrade per card).  With such little sense of variety it can become very easy to feel a sense of repetitiveness that took its toll on me.  After I got my last achievement, I just didn't really want to play anymore.

With these things being said I still believe the game is good, and still worth giving a shot.  I love that you need to have map awareness, and plan ahead while also having the sense of urgency to act fast before you get overwhelmed.  The entire design of the game is really good, and the potential is limitless.  The Steam workshop support also always warrants praise from me.  Even if the modding community isn't very strong (yet) the fact mods are available/encouraged will be keeping me checking up on it occasionally to see if anything new is available to try.

I was able to get 100% of the achievements in less than 12 hours of game play which is insanely fast.  The hardest ones to get were the ones that required getting level 10 with each character as at that point I as going through the fatigue.  Of course this is subjective to change in the future after this review is officially posted.  If you are an achievement hunter then this won't be a stressful endeavor at all.

In conclusion, I recommend this game because it can be very engaging for 10-20 hours and adds a decent original change in the genre.  If you can get this from a bundle, or on sale then definitely do so.  Although if you are looking for something you can dump many many hours into without feeling bored then you may need to look elsewhere.   Updates/fixes are still being released periodically so I anticipate for it to be even better as time goes on.

Azure Saga: Pathfinder:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 

The mothership N.E.B.U.L.A is about to leave the planet Azure’s orbit. Based on the protocol, all vessels must return to N.E.B.U.L.A before the light speed jump is activated. This time around, one spacecraft has not complied with the procedure. The pilot is a young scientist by the name of Synch, who is accompanied by his faithful droid, Noide, and they are about to locate the last coordinates of the position in which Synch’s father was last seen. As they ignored the order to return to mothership, the governor deployed the black squadron to intercept them. And just when they were on the brink of finding the exact coordinates, they were shut down and crashed on the planet they know as Azure.  
 
Azure Saga: Pathfinder is a RPG/ strategy game with turn-based combat where you take control of Synch and his droid and discover the planet Azure and its inhabitants.

After the cut-scene introduction, your character Synch will realise that he has been unconscious for quite some time. The good news is that his droid, Noide, didn’t suffer any damage when they crashed. Their spaceship, however, sustained heavy damage and they need to find a way to repair it so they can find the place where Synch’s father was last seen.  This is where the story really begins and the gameplay is introduced. 

Basically, in each of the areas your characters explore, they’ll have a quest to complete, and as you progress through the game, they’ll be given side quests by talking to various characters who have an exclamation mark above their heads.  The map has from 14 to 25 rooms / tiles (this is the most I’ve seen so far) to explore per scenario. At first, you’ll have Synch and his droid in your party, but as you progress, additional characters will join your group.  One thing to remember is that you can only have 3 active characters at any given time, but you can swap characters anytime you want, including during battle. Getting back to the maps; they are 2.5D isometrics and you can move from one to the other by following the triple green arrows which are located at the extremities of each room / tile. Your party can move north, south, east and west, but you may not have all of these options available at the same time.  If there is an item within the room /tile surrounded by sparkles, this indicates that there are items you can collect. In most of your quests, you might need to find keys, or activate levers in order to open inaccessible rooms.  When you walk anywhere near a large blue diamond, your progress will be saved automatically. You can also use the diamond to teleport your party to other blue diamonds within the quest map. Your party will encounter fights every few rooms, which will keep you on your toes! 

Each time you enter a fight, you really don’t know what sort of opponent you will face. There are stacks of them (randomized in every fight) and if it is the first time your party faces an enemy, they’ll be able to call on VIGOR, the droid scanner, to give you important information on your new opponent, such as what it is immune to and what sort of attack to use in order to inflict maximum damage. In regards to your characters, they will have several attack options. The first one is to use the normal attack, which will not cost them mana, but will inflict less damage. The second is to use a skills move, but it will cost the character a certain number of mana points to produce the attack. If they don’t have enough mana, (represented by the blue gauge above your character’s head), well . . . your move will not happen.  The third attack is the united or combined attack, where three characters combine forces against one specific enemy. It can be a bit tricky when you face three high level opponents. The fourth one is the guard option, which when selected will try to block your enemy attacks. You can swap characters during battle, which is always handy, or just avoid the fight by escaping, if you can. There are plenty of other things to do in each turn, such as drinking potions (health or mana) or using items in your inventory. The health and mana gauges are located above each of your character’s pictures, and will decrease if they either receive damage (health) or use mana for a skill or unified attacks. The other gauge is under the picture and starts to fill up each time one of your attacks is successful. When it is entirely full, your character will be able to execute a fury move. Most fury moves are deadly attacks, with the exception of the priestess (so far), who can use the fury attack to heal your party. At the end of each fight, your party will receive coins, and every now and then, items too. The good news is that all your party will receive experience points, even the ones who weren’t fighting.

When finishing a quest, you will find yourself back at the ERE capital reporting to the king and his entourage. There you’ll be able to buy or sell items, such as potions, armour and many more. It’s always good to stock up on potions, especially the mana potions. 

Personally, I am still in the early stages of the game and at the time of writing this review I have played 8 of the main quests, which are straight forward.  I feel that the story is pretty good so far, as are the characters. In terms of the interface, it is easy to use.

Graphically the game looks great and runs well. The soundtrack and sound effects are really good too. In terms of the controls, you can use the keyboard or gamepad but the mouse is not supported, which is a shame. 

Positives:
~~~~~~~~ 

+	Nice graphics
+	Fun and easy to play
+	Good story and characters
+	Stacks of enemies, randomized in every fight
+	Good price point
+	Achievements and trading cards

Negatives:
~~~~~~~~ 

-	Mouse is not supported

A solid RPG game that will keep you entertained for many hours. Azure is a planet you must visit!

8/10

I wanted to like this game. I really did. Not only because management games are right up my alley, or because I just love Princess Maker style games, or because a dear friend gifted it to me. But because I DO love dark and twisted takes to those sim raising games.

A raising sim where you aren't raising a daughter but homunculi that are mere tools for a bigger end? It can't get much darker than that. You are basically playing as the very-very-very bad dad from Full Metal Alchemist that used his daughter in an experiment to keep his goverment money. But as much as I love those dark takes, I don't take well when people assume that my inteligence and capacity to differenciate reality vs fiction and good vs bad is null. Right as you start the game you will be greeted by a long text basically explaining why what you're about to play is so horrible and terrible and I'm not sure if it's just that the developers really think that the people who will buy this game are idiots, psychos or if they just want you to feel bad and guilty for playing it but it's certainly one of the two.

The gameplay itself isn't actually anything stellar, it's awfully easy to get hold of how it works and what needs to be done, and after that it's just a matter of repeating the routine over and over until you get with the correct composition for your beloved daughter's soul. Nothing else matters, and I don't mean it as a "Faust is just so focused on his goal that he ignores everything else", it's literally just that *nothing else matters* because there's basically nothing else. The game itself, despite the reminder of how horribly bad and cruel what you're going to enact when playing which appears EVERY HAPPY TIME you open the game, doesn't allow you for anything else but to follow the motions of creating homunculi, giving them humanity and then murder them. There was an ending added that consisted in Faust getting over his soulless daughter and deciding to keep the homunculi as his daughters and love them as they deserve, an ending that can be achieved with only one homunculi death because the game FORCES you to perform it. And yet... Despite the possibility of only one homunculi dying before getting that ending (and at a time no other homunculi are around) the ending plays itself with the daughters deciding they have had enough of your murderous and cruel ways (even if you have done NONE of that) and murder you in kind. Because you're a horrible monster that shall never be allowed forgiveness for playing this game. Or something.

The music is nothing to write home about, it's forgetable, so much that I actually don't really remember any of it. I assume there was some, otherwise the game would have felt even more of a drag to go through. The art style is unique but not that great either and it only adds to make the whole game feel like a bore. As for the story, well, the inconsistence I mentioned regarding that ending earlier it's not a thing that ending has alone. The whole story is just a mess and the SHOCKING PLOT TWIST of the true ending is just out of nowhere pointless-and-stupid-thing that makes you realize that the whole experience was, to put it simply, worthless.

This isn't a purchase worth the full price tag. Even a half price tag feels too pricey for what it ultimately offers. But if you want a game that claims to explore the depth of a father's grief, which by the way: it actually doesn't do it, and that either insults your intelligence or tries to guilt trip you for buying it... Make yourself at home, but there are games that do everything this game does much better and without insulting your intelligence.

																After 100%ing this game, I cannot recommend it. 

To start with what I liked about the game, the visuals are charming and many of the characters have their personalities written on their sleeves, the art team did a top notch job. Unfortunately, outside of its coats of paint the writing of this game is lackluster, and mediocre. 

Coffee Talk seems to have difficulty deciding what kind of story it wants to tell, and in doing so ends up having themes and stories told within it that conflict with each other. The game is set in a modernized fantasy world, and a driving theme of the narrative is that despite it's high fantasy setting, the world still contains real people with relatable problems. This is immediately undermined by the fact that all except for one of the stories has a picture perfect, "happily ever after" ending, and the game only just barely touches on the actual consequences of the one somber ending (the elf and the succubus) save for a single line of dialogue. In addition, many of the characters fail to have real personalities that hold up to scrutiny, As great as the art team was at showcasing their surface level traits to the world around them, the writing fails to give them depth, or intrigue. Ultimately any story told in this game comes off as shallow, and the characters don't end up feeling like real people, and many of them are unmemorable at best.

The shallow nature of the characters leads into the game's other major problem, the failure to take advantage of the setting. This game's entire plot could be rewritten to take place in our normal, mundane reality, and all except for 2 of the plotlines (the astronaut and the werewolf) would have their actual stories unchanged, the technical details might be different, but the scope of their problems and the solutions given would be almost exact. This is an especially grievous problem given the story repeatedly points out that it takes place in a fantasy world, and repeatedly attempts to draw contrast between a fairytale esque setting and the gritty, real life issues faced by people every day. Unfortunately, the game's focus on creating happy endings ends up making the fact that it's set in a fantasy world come off as self criticism, as if the writers understood that their characters ignore the reality of their situations and continuing to live their idyllic lives, knowing that everything will work itself out in the end.

Maybe if you're looking for something *very* lighthearted, and don't want a story that's going to present you with gritty realism and then make good on the promise that life can go poorly in their world, this game will appeal to you. But personally this game seems to skate around just about every part of its characters lives that I might find genuinely interesting, and fails to use it's setting in a way that feels satisfying or innovative.

																For me, this game deserves a mixed review.

Dreadout 2 is a third person horror adventure game taking place several months after the incident happened in its predecessor. As Linda once again, players need to battle against the rising dark force around the town, help Linda embrace her role as Keeper of The Dark, and finally tie up loose ends left behind the first installment. To be frank, I have a mixed feeling for Dreadout 2. On one hand I appreciate the developers went all out  implementing some new mechanic in order to make the second entry fresh and interesting, but on the other hand the execution needed some improvement. Compared to Dreadout, Dreadout 2 feels like a mishmash of ambition, trying to do everything and yet excell at none. Nonetheless, if you are new to the game or fans of the long-gone Fatal Frame franchise, Dreadout 2 is a decent game to pick up. I would still recommend it. I just feel like there are so many potential wasted or left behind in this game.

Things I Like About Dreadout 2:
1. Interesting Storyline
The story of Dreadout 2 feels like a novel, and I enjoy reading a rounded novel. Every instance gives a little insight of how the state of world become. From the beginning of small prank goes terribly wrong we learn that something has strengthened even the most harmless spirit to be able to possess living person; From the hospital incident we learn that the dark force can even make local legend come true and become one of Her servants; From the abandoned hotel incident the dark force is powerful enough even to reincarnate a person's fear, anger, and all sorts of negativity. Every event has a meaningful placement. Every placement opens up new clues and mysteries to the accident. Progressively, the truth envelopes, so does the horrible scheme.

2. Introduction Of New Mechanic
?New Combat. Dreadout is a great camera-focused horror game, and yet that is pretty much everything about it. Don not mistake this statement as complaint. The first game did some great jobs to diversify every ghost encounter. The game played just feel a bit repetitive or dare I say, not engaging enough. So here comes Dreadout 2, with newly implemented combat system. This mechanic makes the game much more fun and shakes off the stalemate of waiting-for-the-ghost-to-come situation. Plus, execute the first ghost feels awesome.
?Semi-Open World. Dreadout 2 presents a connected world for you to explore. You will no longer feel alone like the the first game. The town feels alive, with vendor selling various stuff, students giggling about the latest trend, and the hustle and bustle of traffic. This is a nice change of pace after forcing yourself to see the twisted and tormented spirits face to face. It even helps me understand how it isfeel like to live in Indonesia.
?Side Quests. An introduction of side stories is a happy surprise. Their existence not only help justifying the writhing dark force slowly growing stronger and what the influence may be, but also gives me, a foreigner, ideas about local legends and taboos, which interest me greatly. It is also nice to see Linda treat these occasional encounters as friendly as possible(should the players choose to). It really helps building her character as a keeper of darkness.

Things I Dislike About Dreadout 2
1. The "Linda-Hate" Trend Is Not Well-developed
Bully is a serious problem. In a story it could play a major role in a character's development, for better or worse. Dreadout 2 sets the stage, but doesn't seem to deal with the problem. In the beginning we learn that Linda suffers exclusion from peers. The Linda-Hate trend is the hot topic among fellow students. This is a good setup for Linda to be independent and iron-willed. It could even justify why Dark Linda is so strong. The oppressed emotions deep down her heart could be the major source. However, this idea is not developed in game. This is the only thing I don't like about the story. Dreadout 2 presents the problem, and the problem is never resolved or concluded for the rest of the game. A setting treated as a one-timed trick.

2. Poor Execution Of New Mechanic
?Combat Feels Clumsy. The new action section is weird. Every swing has a subjectively long  recovery time and you can't aim for different direction during your second swing. I know Linda is just a high school student. She wouldn't have the experience to master melee weapons such as kitchen knife and axe. Make sense in reality, yet this is a video game afterall. And shouldn't she at least be familiar with the weapons after two or three incidents?
?Empty World. Dreadout 2 branches out the map with several location to explore, creating a promising, connected world with sadly not much things to to do. You can only go through starting area of the chosen location. The rest you experience in the main story is locked up. NPC in such location doesn't even interact with you, serving more like background props. There is little incentive to go through any location. You really don't have anything to do beside porgress through the story.
?In Need Of More Side Quests. Even though only three are presented in the game, I like them all. Dreadout 2 should include more of these nice addition to the game, since it decides to add semi-open world. Several side quests can be used for more world-building, different side quests after each chapter and each area for reason to revisit, or even implement some kind of mini games for the faint of heart to have a nice change of pace.

3. The Questionable Final Boss Design
This section is dedicated to the second final boss. Blorong is the evil deity behind everything that happened around Linda. As a result she should be hard and challenging. How should we do so? Making her agile? Making her attack range long? Having a fixed number of minions besides her? How about two thin strings constantly interrupt Linda's movement? This! This is the most annoying thing about the boss fight. When you think you have the opportunity to retaliate, one of those stings will stab Linda's shoulder, forcing her to flinch and lose that opportunity. They do not stop even if she distances herself away from the boss. They just keep stabbing and giving me a hard time to recover. I really don't get the reason behind such decision. It's not like Linda can stunlock the boss to death. Blorong herself is quite resilient, and minions around her already make the fight challenging but still doable.

4. Default Brightness Setting Is Way Too Dark.

5. Linda Why Did You Cut Off Your Pony Tail?? You Looked Great With It!

																I've now played the game enough to get a feel for it. Overall it has been a positive experience. I was looking for a classic turn-based style RPG and that's exactly what I got. (To be updated upon completion but here's my impressions thus far)

Battle System / Mechanics:
The battle system features a turn-based element similar to FFVIII or Lost Odyssey's timing mechanic such that you have to time a button press to do full damage for every attack. It's difficult at first but once you get 20 luck for each character and some practice it becomes a lot easier.  There are several elements of the battle system which I find refreshing in fact. The guard mechanics for each character gives a specific bonus which is VERYeeee useful. Unlike other RPGs, I found myself guarding strategically during difficult fights to survive. Another change to a common feature is spellcasting. There is no MP, instead spells known as grimoire, have casting times and a chance to be interrupted while casting. That means no casting healing spells outside of combat so items will become your best friend.

Story/World:
I won't go into too much details to avoid spoilers, plus I'm less than halfway through, but the story is par for the course. Ragband group of adventurers must band together to save the world. I'm playing after the rewrite so I can't speak for the original dialogue but the current dialogue is well-written. The world building elements are also captivating. I found myself thinking about the impact of story elements on the world of Legrand as a whole including topics such as oppression of the poor and genocide. Some elements of the story may seem a little bit cliche like the romance elements but they still have a chance to redeem themselves. Also there's a world map you can walk around on. ^-^

Characters:
The main characters all have unique physical and personality traits to them. I've just received my final party member and I can tell that each one of them has motivations which influence how they act. Some of the characters also have hidden pasts which could come up in the future and shake things up.

Graphics:
So the graphics. Having grown-up playing PS1 and PS2 rpgs, I can say that the graphics are definitely nostalgic. The 2D backgrounds are certainly detailed and I like the use of Live-2D over the usual static character portraits. That being said, the animation is very janky and lifeless at times. In my head, I just imagine this game coming out 15 years ago and I'm able to get past the PS2-level graphics.

Other:
Difficulty: This game is quite challenging and I find myself having to grind and really practice my strategy to win. Some fights would be impossible without using your Arcana (limit-break) so the game expects you to save it for bosses. That said I appreciate a good challenge these days.

Inventory: You can only hold a limited 350 items. While it adds an element of realism, I find myself getting over-encumbered fairly quick if I don't deposit all of my items in storage before starting a new area. Personally, I could do without it for quality of life.

Weapon Upgrading: You cannot easily equip different weapons. Instead you can only change weapons when you forge a new weapon at a town from what I've seen. This kinda sucks because some weapons give different bonuses like more HP and defense as well as magic vs physcial attack which could prove useful depending on the enemies you are facing.

Thanks for reading!

																This game is an almagamation of a number of features from older JRPGs and a heavily flawed ode to them.

Pros:
- Combat (think simplified Judgement Ring from Shadow of Hearts). Adds a bit of skill to the combat.
- Army battles (grid based simplified Fire Emblem). Helps break up the monotony of random battles and long text heavy chapters.
- Art. Environment and character designs are solid.

Cons:
- Inventory/Crafting/Equipment system. Equipment (weapons only) can only be changed in towns and at blacksmiths. Even going back to an older weapon requires you to have both money and materials necessary to reforge said older weapon. Most items are only available via crafting at an alchemist in town. All of this is fine, but you are only allowed to craft using materials in your inventory. Inventory also comes with a weight/encumbrance feature that forces you to stash materials in storage or be forced to slowly walk through towns and dungeons. You constantly have to check the recipe to pull out the required materials before you can craft anything.
- Plot progression. JRPGs are linear, good ones create the illusion that you control the pace of the story by allowing your to explore towns and map at your leisure, advancing the plot as you interact with NPCs, etc. In this game, the woes populace of every town are forced upon you as soon as you enter them. So are the solutions. Even new party members feel forced into your party (one of them mugs you in the beginning of the chapter only to miraculously save you in the boss fight later. Why, cause said character felt like it). I know this game is called 'Fateboud' but this is overkill.
- Writing. It is either bland or uncomically bad. Up until chapter 4, every character reads exactly the same, and in a text heavy game like this one, that's unforgivable. Attempts at humor feel forced and are cliche and predictable. Chapter 4 is where the writing improves dramatically, but then in Chapter 5, it takes a nosedive. The '3 virgins' conversation is especially cringeworthy and is where I have stopped playing.
- Rock, Paper, Scissors fights. Remember in Suikoden those drama filled one-on-ones you would occassionally have with major characters? This game has them too, except it's with you against a bunch of bland grunts over and over again. How do you go from wiping out mobs of them in random encounters to being forced into a life-and-death struggles against singular foes mere moments later? No skill whatsoever is required to win or lose these too numerous occurances.

Since this is a VN ( Visual Novel), Writing and visuals are #1 with the barista minigame as a fun distraction and helps add to the story if you're enjoying it. 

The Writing:

The writing is pretty much what you would expect from a indie title about a coffee shop in Seattle, all the characters basically have societal issues that are 1:1 with our own except for the Werewolf so the use of monsters instead of other human races wasn't really needed, or really used to it's full potential. Wasn't blown off my feet but it was acceptable and wasn't a problem, if you're politically progressive you'll definitely vibe with the characters.

Audio & Visuals:

The visual execution on this is FANTASTIC. Really did a great job on this one, they nailed the vibe of a modern coffee shop alongside a well drawn cast of characters and fantastic background ambiance. The music eventually became a bit of a snore fest as it seemed to repeat the same few tracks and sound too samey after a few hours ( I played the entire game in 1 session), but considering the selection of tracks on offer it seems to be more user error than the game.  


Barista "Minigame": 

I liked the barista minigame,  it's a fun way of spicing up a visual novel that only adds to the story and doesn't penalize you if you don't know the recipes or remember what someone likes. I had the cheat sheet pulled up for most of the game, and other than forgetting the *spoiler alert* It didn't to affect the story all that much other than you potentially losing some more backstory on the characters in one of the apps on your phone. 


Conclusion:

While the game's story may not be winning a Pulitzer prize for originality, Coffee Talk perfectly nails the environment and vibe of a coffee shop in Seattle and does it beautifully. I hope to see more games like this in the genre that can make Visual Novels a bit more stimulating, but relaxing; just like a Masala Chai.  8/10 Would (and will) buy again :)

																As someone who loves VA-11 HALL-A and then seeing Coffee Talk I definitely wanted to see what it had to offer with the similar genre. The game is most definitely a delight for me.
The pixel art in CT is beautifully detailed and pleasent for the eyes.
The designed background excellently displays the calm, comfortable and secluded atmosphere of coffee shops I definitely routine. I love the touches of having the stories take place at midnight and you can see the pixel animation of rain pouring as you see people of many forms walk pass the coffee shop.
The characters by default are the best of the game. Since the main premise of the game is to listen to the characters tell their stories and not only were their stories engaging and fascinating they felt like stories coming from real people. Majority of the characters are non-human races but their identities and tales feel so human wether they're talking about prejudice, careers, communities, relationships, overcoming their personal struggles and so on. If I didn't see myself in their stories I knew someone with a similar experience. Their pixel designs are really really good and I love the subtle animations they execute such as change in expressions, drinking their coffee and checking their phones ( I personally love that older customers are using flip phones instead smartphones I know a lot of elders like that)
I also have to praise the developers on how well they handled the length of a one day segment in the coffee shop and how dialogue is well edited. One day's worth of events and conversations never felt boring because the day and conversations never dragged or padded out, the script knew where to stop and proceed to next day. I don't have a habit for noticing such things but here I did notice and the scripts are perfectly handled in my opinion as I still remember the conversations and took some values from them.
The soundtrack in conducted by one person (around 20 pieces very impressive) they're great to listen to and they complement the atmosphere perfectly. Sometimes  I pause the game just listen while I stare at the beautiful pixel exterior.
The coffee making process is fun especially in the endless mode and the varieties of beverages are impressive.
The only thing I don't like about game is the main character the barista. He's not horribly written just the typical faceless visual novel main character who mostly listens to the characters on screens with almost no value to the story and I'm not a fan of those. Fortunately the developers knew not to waste unnecessary time or writing on him since he's basically just supposed to be our first person perspective and make the coffee so they kept his dialogue minimal and added the green haired girl Freya to more than make up for it as the mediator.
I definitely recommend Coffee Talk for fans of Cyberpunk Bartender and anyone who loves hearing life stories in engaging ways.

																I would give this a neutral to slightly positive review. Usually a good concept and poor execution leaves me frustrated, but the concept, along with the excellent art style and variety of homunculi, was solid enough to hold the whole game together. I found this game extremely fascinating, but not quite fun to play. It feels as if a few tweaks it would be greatly improved. I think as an art piece it's truly interesting, damaged only by the ending, which ignores the homunculi and stray from the essential themes of humanity, sacrifice, and obsession. I would definitely recommend this to true fans and developers of indie games because it's an example of bringing to live an excellent and difficult concept through interactive media.
The art and presentation is beautiful, and I loved the many 'daughters' you could create. I loved the main characters, his obsession, and the lengths he is willing to go to save his corpse daughter. I do wish the homunculi letters could flesh out more interesting and unique personalities and relationships with 'father' based on affection. Maybe I am cold, but there were only a few cases where I felt sorry to kill my homunculi, and a little more pathos would have been appreciated. I disliked that we are told outright how the character feels about killing them, as it takes away our own response to murdering sentient beings.  I didn't feel much of a connection with the townsfolk, or the ramifications of earning their trust or distrust.
The gameplay itself is somewhat grindy. The most fun activity by far is creating new homunculi.  The attachment issues could be greatly improved by adding more to the interactions with the homunculi (perhaps by allowing more personal activities with them per week, and gaining more affection through playing with and learning about them than through gifts.) And maybe an ending or two involving the homunculi, like having them rise up against Father, or something equally terrifying.

																I wanted to like this game so badly, it had such a strong start and some good ideas, but by the end it had just done so much to make me hate it.

For one, the combat has two sections: taking photos of ghosts, and melee combat to zombies. Each with their own issues:

Taking photos only does damage to ghosts if your camera is static-y while you're looking at the ghost, which means that even if you have the ghost in your reticule, if there's no static, you'll 'miss'. This is an issue because there's a bit of a cooldown to taking another photo, and in multiple boss fights this means you get hit. A few boss fights see you getting stun locked because you miss a shot despite DIRECTLY taking a photo of the ghost. Teeth grindingly frustrating. 

Melee combat's issue is that it's lacking a dodge button, which feels like it should've been there, considering most fights have you getting hit or grabbed no matter what (including the ridiculous final boss fight). Feels floaty and unsatisfying.

Otherwise, there are a fair few bugs and smaller, weird game design choices. Combat is bad, but a few encounters had me stunlocked to death with no way out - when you get hit the game takes control away from you, it feels awful. 
We have a world map area selection option, despite the game being linear. Considering how the first area is a bit open, I imagine the idea was for the game to be more freeroam. There's an option for messages and phone calls, but it was never used in my playthroughs (I'm not sure if there's a side quest or something that uses it?). 

The story is bad. It sets itself up nicely, then suddenly feels rushed and unfinished, and then it just... Ends. Something about the pacing of the entire game feels off, and the ending is unsatisfying - makes me think there's dlc or more games to keep it going somehow. But 3ish hours to complete isn't great. 

Lots of good ideas here but implemented all so poorly that I can't look past it. I wanted to be scared but honestly I spent more time being frustrated (that ??????? tiger boss, I swear). Give it a miss, maybe something to keep an eye on on the future if it ever gets very heavily patched.

																As soon as i saw the title to this game, I had a good feeling. Then after watching the trailer i knew i was going to love it, and I did.

This is simply a huge zen experience, Soothing background music, nice stories with a mixture of relatable and oddball characters, and a no pressure game mechanic.

I'm a big fan of Sukeban Games' Va-11 Hall-A, and this matches a lot of the gameplay and art style while swapping cyberpunk for fantasy. While some people may see similarity like that as boring, it shows me that the situation and style works for this kind of narrative game: one where many stories are told and they touch each other ever so slightly.

The differences are mainly that the drinks system has it's own complexity in Coffee Talk and it's a LOT easier to screw up. You're given very little basic info in your recipe guide at the start and add to this as you discover named drinks. Adding to this lack of outright information, the order of ingredients seems to matter so swapping the additions may produce different effects on the drink. The factor the drinks has on the story also seems to be rather binary: right or wrong, and if it isn't binary (as is my impression) anything to this effect is rather subtle and isn't explicitly mentioned. (This is all in contrast to Va-11 Hall-A's system where you're given all-bar-one recipes off the bat, ingredient order doesn't matter as it's pure ratios, and the story outcome is based a on a mixture of if the drink is wrong, satisfactory, correct or special, plus the accumulated alcohol value) So I'd argue that if a Coffee Talk sequel is on the cards, i hope that element is given a bit of TLC to eliminate some bugbears and give the player more power over the story.

As a minor side-feature, you can do latte art. While I'm no artist, and i found the controls a bit fiddly, i do like the attention to including this feature, even if it's only a bit of vanity as it's rarely asked for by the characters.

As for the endless/challenge mode, this is where zen goes out the window in Coffee Talk. Your recipe info (or lack thereof as the case may be) carries over and you're given orders quickfire against the clock trying to earn more time. This is where the recipe collecting falls flat in my opinion, it's a nice idea if the story was longer and there was a bit more nuance to knowing the drinks on a second play through and unlocking other routes with them, but you shouldn't be asked for a drink by name with no hints if you've never made it and have no info.

I could talk about the story, but i'm going to say very little other than expand on what I've said before, based on the fact that's what you buy this for: the story, and if i said any much more i feel that would negate some of the discovery. The little i will say it that the setting is "fantasy injected into modern life" and it does a good job with the mix of character races, weaving some of their unique traits into the story, while keeping the feeling that if all were human, they'd have a place in real-life society.

If you like short stories, narrative in general, or just want something to zen out to, get this game. It's not perfect, but the bits it trips up on don't detract from the parts you're honestly buying this game for.

One of my all time favorite games is Va-11 Hall-A and ever since, I’ve been on the lookout for similar games ever since to scratch that itch it left behind. The closest I’ve gotten was playing The Red Strings Club which does have you literally pouring drinks to bring out certain emotions in your customers, but it turned out to be disappointing (for me at least). When I heard about Coffee Talk though, I knew I was going to pick this one up and play it as soon as I could. My decision was hammered home even more after I played the demo. Well, now that Coffee Talk is released how does it fare?

Taking place in Seattle in an alternate 2020, you find yourself in a world that hosts not only humans but fantasy creatures like mermaids and elves. Though, that doesn’t mean this world doesn’t have it’s own set of problems. That is where you come in as the owner, and only employee, of a small coffee shop named Coffee Talk. What sets yours out from all the others is that yours is the only one that is open only at night. Ready for anyone to come in looking for a hot drink and an ear to air out all their frustrations.

Coffee Talk’s cast of characters are wonderful as each bring in their own unique personality to the table and stories on what’s currently happening in their lives. Each one manages to interesting to where most players will want to hear more about them and hope that they’ll come in before you close up. You’ll start out with Freya, a regular that always comes in to write and is aspiring to have a book published. It’s not long before you meet up with an elf and succubus couple that’s struggling with their families not approving their relationship and what the future holds if they never do; a cop that’s totally not taking too many breaks to have a cup of your coffee; a vampire model that gives insight on and to whoever happens to be there; a werewolf that’s trying to find a drink that will calm him down during his Fury; and more. You also have some other world building elements through daily newspapers (headlines only sadly), Tomodachill profiles that opens up more information as you get closer to the characters, and you’re even able to read some of Freya’s short stories to give you a taste on how she writes.

Brewing up drinks for your customers is pretty simple. At first you’ll only have a couple ingredients, but you’ll slowly get more as inventory comes in. You’ll pick a base, a primary ingredient, and finally a secondary ingredient. While you’ll brew the usual drinks like espressos, lattes, and flavored milk, there are also special named drinks you can discover and customers will occasionally request. However, you won’t have the full list, only having the basics already in your Brewpad, as you’re meant to discover them yourself. As some customers will request named drinks, with some giving hints and others not, it also means you most likely won’t be able to give everyone correct drinks. Luckily, Coffee Talk doesn’t change anything other than them saying it’s not what they ordered apart from two instances. These two instances are telegraphed so it’s not hidden away if you’re worried about that.

For lattes, Coffee Talk also lets you create your own latte art if you wanted to. I personally found it hard to make anything, well, pleasing. Basically the long you hold own, the more milk will be poured and it’ll be pushed down. If you don’t like it when you try it out, you can completely ignore it.

Coffee Talk also features an Endless mode with two different choices. First, you have Free Brew which lets you make anything. This is mainly used to let you figure out all named drink combinations as you won’t be able to make all of them in your first playthrough or be able to figure it out if you’re not given any hints. Then there’s Challenge Mode. Challenge Mode, well, challenges you to make as many correct drinks as you can for your customer before the time runs out. Each correct drink adds on more time so you can survive longer. It starts out pretty easy with them just saying what ingredients they want outright. It slowly brings up the difficulty as it brings your base to the end of their request and occasionally requesting a named drink (that you hopefully discovered before now). Lastly, it gets more vague on what ingredients they want, but more specific on how they want sweet, warm, cool, or bitter they want their drink to be. This is where it gets challenging as it first starts with only requesting one aspect to be a certain way to all of them. Though, this part is a bit confusing at first before you figure out what the customer actually means. Asking for a drink that’s not bitter and extra sweet is obvious, but what about less and just regular sweet. Especially when they just plainly say “I want my drink to be bitter” and they hate it when you just load it up. Well, you might not have noticed, but the coffee maker actually tells you what constitutes as a drink having a low or high amount in each. 1-3 bars is less, 4-5 is just right, and 6+ is extra. When the game asks for a normal amount of one of them, it will only accept 4-5 as anything more counts as it being too much.

When you think of a game centering around being a barista, I would be surprised if the first thing on your mind wasn’t a cozy coffee shop where you can go and study or write. Coffee Talk certainly doesn’t disappoint if you’re expecting a cozy atmosphere. The coffee shop just shouts cozy vibes with how it’s decorated, the characters are wonderfully designed and brings in a pop of vividity, the soundtrack is relaxing and I could easily see them being in a “relaxing cafe music for studying” playlist, and the rain certainly brings in another addition for those that find rain relaxing.

This game definitely reminds me of a 10 hour rainy mood loop of Beneath the Mask that I listen to sometimes while I write so I’m not writing in complete silence. Combining a relaxing soundtrack with the sound of rain pouring down outside and the image of you just sitting in a coffee shop watching people walk and drive by the window.

One thing I do wish was that Coffee Shop was a bit longer. Not because the price doesn’t fit, which I do think it does, but it felt like there could have been more interactions between the characters. While these things didn’t bother me much, others might be disappointed that giving wrong drink orders doesn’t really affect anything outside two separate instances and it doesn’t show the complexity of brewing coffee. The latter is a shame as I would have been interested in learning about it, especially since I even looked up how baristas make latte art in an effort to understand how the latte art minigame worked.

VerdictWhile Coffee Talk might not completely scratch that itch that Va-11 Hall-A left in many of it’s players, it will satisfy those that have been looking for similar games. While it can disappoint in some areas, it gives players a wonderful cast of characters, a cozy atmosphere to relax to, two endings, and a challenge mode for those who are looking for a challenge.

Coffee Talk is a visual novel, made by a game studio based in Indonesia, known as Toge Productions. It's their first game and they've definitely hit a home-run in their first try. 

The game revolves around you being a coffee shop owner and your job is to provide wonderful, lip-smacking beverages to your customers, while they tell you their life stories. Each customer has their own set of personal problems that they'd like to share with you and while doing so, they also raise concerns regarding life in a game industry or other international issues (such as the recent pandemic). The writing is indeed excellent and is very easy-to-follow. 

Talking about gameplay, there's only one job and that's to deliver beverages. However, there are multiple varieties that you can serve - from green tea brewed with honey to cappuccinos with beautiful latte arts. Since gameplay is fairly limited, the main focus in on the story and writing. Not to mention, the soundtrack is fantastic. It's soothing and helps you concentrate when leading lines of texts. 

Overall, Coffee Talk was indeed a breath of fresh air - a breakout from the world of indies that are filled with rogue-lites and metroidvanias. Not that I have anything against those genres, it’s that they have been utilised so many times that it becomes difficult to re-invent innovate and be unique.

																So, it has been a few months since I finished Nusakana. This is probably the first game to which I can't give an unbiased review, but I will try.

TLDR: Nusakana is the most character-driven life sim I have ever played. For those interested in the genre, I can't recommend it enough, but you will have to put in an investment.

Nusakana has many English/grammar errors, usually not enough to make sentences hard to understand, but enough that you sometimes have to guess the level of emotion with which something was said. It has several technical faults and a few broken collisions, and the combat, fishing and harvesting are generally uninteresting. It is also at the top of my 'list of favorite games', surpassing the others I had considered nearly-perfect by such a wide margin that I can't use a number system to score it. 
As a general rule, I have avoided life sim games because the gameplay is uninteresting, and the characters are seldom 'real' enough to hold my interest. I'm not sure what made me pick up Nusakana, except I had the feeling there was heart to it. My expectations coming into it were that I would find it relaxing and hopefully the characters would feel real enough that I would enjoy it. Instead I found myself busily scrambling around the island with new friends, trying frantically to keep pace with all the various story-related quests that kept showing up. All of these quests feel integrated into Nusakana's world, instead of being merely RPG-style fetch quests with no purpose behind them or story-reward for completing them. After a few months the flood of things to do slowed down and I was able to find the relaxing pace I had been expecting, but there were still very few days without some special event to make it a unique day in my mind.

Character interaction is the big draw here, though. While many of the characters seemed to start as clichés (perhaps because I’ve seen all the clichés so many times), by the end of the game they formed the best supporting cast I've ever seen - and I've played Chrono Trigger, Fire Emblem (all of them, both good and cringe-y), Kingdom Hearts and Katawa Shoujo. You won't get as much interaction from any individual as you might in, say, a branching visual novel - think 2,000 words per person as opposed to 30,000 per person - and the interactions won't be as explosive, either. Think spending a day picking peaches as opposed to discovering your modified microwave is a time machine. But the characters start feeling more real as the game goes on, and the world feels more real as your interactions with it change. This is the only game I've played where I can say I was genuinely interested in every one of the 30+ characters by the end of it.

I will note that I had to give it a decent amount of time before it started to mean anything to me. My general thoughts while playing went like this:
0->25 hours: Hmm, this is OK. Better than I was expecting, anyway.
25->45 hours: I wonder if places like this still exist.
45->60 hours: I think I'd like to live here. 
60->90 hours: It's weird to say that a game can affect you as a person because of how cringy that can sound, but this game did exactly that.

In closing:
--Technical score: 7/10. A good effort and no significant bugs, but lots of grammar issues and a few graphical ones as well.
--Story score: 9/10. Actually quite good, even if it gets confusing at the end. Everything gets explained, but you may need to hear it more than once. Things I had ignored because I thought it was hand-wavy game logic turned out to actually be key points.
--Gameplay score: 8/10. If you're looking for something relaxing, this works well. And if you're a completionist, be warned that I had to use about six pages of notebook paper for all the lists I created of things to do next, in what order, and how to go about it. You will enjoy it more if you play it without a guide, which isn't hard because no guide currently exists. =)

--My personal score: 13/10, and I actually mean that. I only had two perfect games before (neither of which are on Steam), so I don't use the word lightly, but 'perfect' games just can't compete with this.

																It is difficult to review Coffee Talk without comparing it to VA-11 Hall-A. Both games have the same core gameplay: they are visual novels, but instead of choosing from dialogue options, you make (or don't make) the drinks ordered by the clientele, and events play out differently depending on those choices.

Coffee Talk keeps things relatively light (although it does touch on mature subjects). Rather than delving into the deeper philosophical concerns of speculative fiction, it presents some basic modern-day problems - dressed up in a light urban fantasy setting - without going too dark nor into especial detail. The result is a cozy, friendly experience that wraps up neatly (with a little twist at the end) and doesn't overstay its welcome, but doesn't leave a strong impression, either.

And that is where the two games diverge sharply: in both tone and complexity. If you want a deep, dystopian cyberpunk world filled with bleakness and intrigue, with several branches to discover and storylines to pursue, definitely play VA-11 Hall-A. But if you want something relaxing, more relatable to the present day, and significantly shorter and more straightforward, then Coffee Talk is your ticket.

With so many monsters and traps here and there, the mini bosses and the boss is crazy as well, yet the recovery items are rare, and you'll reset the game play if you die. I think the devs should put difficulty options before the game starts so a loser like me can win too.

 ART: 9.5/10 Yes, maybe you are fed up with pixel art since almost all indie games use this style of art nowadays, but this one is different. The color palette is pretty vibrant and successfully brings the hellish atmosphere to us. I like how the artist gives crimson glows here and there, and some flaming winds which make the atmosphere looks so hot. The animations look fluid as well, so natural.

 UI: 7/10 Pretty neat, but feels standard. I don't think I need to give more comments about it.

 MUSIC: 8/10The composer's decision to make the BGM a rock music with electric guitar is brilliant. It suits the game play very well. One more thing I like about the BGMs are that they are looping but not boring, at least for your first 1 hour of playtime. 

 SFX: 8/10 The sfx gives us a feeling of early 90's arcade games. Arok (the playable character) shouts manly every time he attacks. There is also that one guy who shouts every time you make combos and enter the store.

 CONCEPT: 7/10 The premise of a guy trying to escape from hell is not a new thing. This game needs more explanation about who Arok is, why he is prisoned in the hell, and why he must escape it. It's the devs homework to add the lore into the game.

 OVERALL RATE: 7.8/10

																Know the painting "Nighthawk" by Edward Hopper? You are the barman/barista, you serve drinks to a few night wanderers and listen to them as they vent their life's small and big issues. 

I have just finished the story mode and I loved this game. I started with the demo, went on with purchasing the full game (you have to start anew), and went on completing it.

I'm a big fan of Terry Pratchett, who loved to write about real-world issues using a fantasy world.
I'm also  a big fan of a webcomic where a number of protagonists are barista in a so-called "Coffee of Doom". For some reason, my barista was called Hannelore.
If the devs of Coffee Talk had managed to fit in a library somewhere, or an orangutan, I would be starting a cult.

The only thing I would complain about is the drawing of a motif in the cream on top of a drink. I'm sure it's working, but I couldn't manage to make nice pictures.

Two things which, depending on taste, may be seen as negative: 
One, the story mode is a visual novel more than anything else, the only decisions you have to make are about the drink-making and it is very light (this part, at least, is definitively neither a barista tycoon game nor a time-managing game - although the challenge mode may be precisely the latter), and the customers tell you the recipe most of the time. I'll have to go through the story again to see if giving customers the wrong drink may change the direction of the story. All I can tell is that, at one point, you have better remember the favorite drink of one protagonist.
(EDIT: I fininshed the game a second time. Serving the 'perfect drinks', or not, does change the many possible endings)
Two, the stories/backstories are very close echoes of real-world issues and recent scandals - notably on racial/immigration issues, or about US healthcare access. If you want evasion, that may not be the game you want. Try the demo, it should tell you enough.

But as you can guess, as for myself, I didn't see these points as negative. There is an author tract, but it is stated right there in the game description, and it was part of the appeal for me.

The art and the dialogues were mostly OK, to my taste. I loved the music. I especially enjoyed the discussions between the two protagonists who worked in the videogame industry. A few situations or dialogues may feel cliché, but I was good with it. Your mileage may vary.
Chekhov would be proud. During the 'start of the day' loading screen, you can see the moon rising, and going through its cycle from new moon to next new moon as days (or rather nights) pass. Yes, it has an importance, story-wise.
Because I'm an old guy, I think I recognized the inspiration for some of the 'photos', like the girls' band or the frontpage of the newspaper, notably the one about immigrants from Atlantis and how some cop is treating unarmed, sitting people.
Oh, and be sure to wait for the end of the credits, for an extra scene (not sure if you get it if you skip it). I doubt that the devs had that in mind, but it reminded me of an episode from the old black&white Twilight Zone TV series. And I learned though this scene that, if you see plotholes/discrepencies during the story (which I totally missed), eh, maybe these are actually clues...

So you can pry this game from my dead, cold fingers.

The first 3-4 hours really kinda lame, and then the pace picked up after at least, you get the to one of the "Arena City" that i forgot its name, since it kinda escalated to a more heavier story.

For me, there are 2 annoying parts that need to be fixed:

Doesn't feels natural, and there are a lot of awkward moments that just doesn't click to me. For example? When they decided to talk about virginity, in one of the scene. Like, what the hell?

																A good continuation to the DreadOut series of games, where it expands some of the world Linda (our heroine) lives in (you get to explore her downtown and school, pretty cool) and how the ghost presence is ruining her everyday life by turning her classmates against her and subjecting her to frequent hallucinations.

 Linda doesn't move at the speed of molasses anymore either and sometimes even has access to actual weapons, making this the most Silent Hill entry yet. I would say these are generally improvements as a whole. However, D2 also fails to address some lingering gameplay issues that existed in previous DreadOuts, such as bosses being mostly cheese. While they seem to deal less upfront damage this time around, there's extremely little tactical play in the fights. Bosses frequently move very fast and can enter solid objects most of the time (being ghosts), leaving you really no clear way to determine where these warping lunging pains in the butt come from. You just kind of run around and hope something misses so Linda can regenerate, but this is problematic given the extremely tight hallway nature of everything. Why is everything so cramped?? There's also the occasional lack of clarity in trying to figure out what you're supposed to go/do next. While the game has a notes section for guidance, it updates only occasionally. 

Combat, when you get an actual weapon, is pretty good all considering. The stabbing and hacking animations feel pretty solid. Sometimes you'll have access to a flash feature on your phone, which can stun said monsters too. Handy! But other times, Linda just doesn't know or remember how to do it, which feels unlikely. There is stealth this time, but it's very crude at best. It basically consists of walking slowly. However, it doesn't seem very solid. Trying to sneak by certain blind ghosts with stealth, as directed, doesn't really work. They just know you're there anyway. You can't just stand still because they'll keep swinging at you until you're far away. Honestly, it was always better just to run. Stealth definitely needs to be tuned up. I would also like to see a dodge button, considering how random and warp speed fast enemies are.


Currently very early past release at the time of this review, there are some bugs. While I haven't run into many, they can be pretty severe. As such, an obstacle enemy in the third act with an instant kill move did not move/despawn from his position, making getting to a certain required alleyway impossible. But on loading to the most recent save point at that scene, he's suddenly not there anymore. Well alright then!

While I gave a reluctant thumbs down to the first DreadOut (the infamous Scissor Ghost encounter is the definition of the poor boss gameplay in this series), the series has been getting better with Keepers of the Dark and now D2, if just gradually. Graphics are a bit nicer, vehicles have more design than just being boxy mini-trucks, and the NPCs, while, not necessarily very revealing in their dialogue, do help paint a more living world. I love learning about the Indonesian mythology and getting a vibe of the culture of a land far from where I live.

Despite some old drawbacks and new ones, I would recommend DreadOut 2 and I hope the series continues. With Silent Hill gone, this is the next best thing, frankly. Like the others in the series, it just needs polish.

																You know that Youtube stream with the lofi hip hop and the anime girl doing her homework? Coffee Talk is basically that, with a little more interaction.

If you're looking for a quiet way to pass a few hours, Coffee Talk has got you covered. It's a pleasant little story, that, while a little quirky in places, is nonetheless an enjoyable time. The story basically tells itself, with little interactions in the form of coffee making to help move things along. Don't go into it expecting branching storylines, big explosive moments or action scenes. This is, first and foremost, a story about a coffee shop and the people who go there.

Which brings me to a few critiques. While the world is interesting, a lot of it feels like window dressing; a quirk to make the game stand out. There's really only one character who needs to be non-human, and while you get little pieces of world-building, none of it feels relevant to the stories told on screen. It takes nothing away from the game, but I feel it doesn't add anything either. I would have enjoyed the story if it had been set in regular Seattle just as much as this alternate one.

I was also left feeling a little left out by the end of the game. Interactions, even including coffee making, are few and far between. This fits in well with the role of a barista, I suppose, but as a player it left me a little wanting as I watched lovable characters converse more with each other than they did with me. On a personal note, I was disappointed at the lack of romance for the player, but considering the shortness of the game, perhaps that is for the best.

But I would still recommend this, especially if you're looking for something peaceful to do to pass the time. The characters are enjoyable, the soundtrack is relaxing, and I sincerely hope something more comes from this world in the future.

= Your typical RPGMaker game
= Standard battle system
= UI design is good, but the icon layout did not feel intuitive at first
= Full controller support, but with minimal guidance for keyboard users

In-depth review
Story
The game tells a story about political intrigue. Basically, there was an evil plot devised by someone in a certain kingdom, and it’s up to the main character (who is the princess) to stop them. To start, the princess was tasked to hunt the leader of a rebellious faction. And then the adventure began… That may look like your standard JRPG story, but it is actually deeper than that. I will say no further though, to prevent any kind of spoilers.

The plot is nice and well thought out, though the only and the most lacking of all would be the writing. Some grammatical errors also persist on the release version. This might be due to the lack of a good editor fluent in English on the developer side. However, the mistakes are mostly minor, so I think it will not leave a major impact to the story. 
In the pre-release version, there were some rushed scenes which will leave you, as the player, speechless. I have not checked whether this is still true in the release version though, but I will leave this here nonetheless.

Gameplay
Like many RPGMaker games out there, you will play a turn-based RPG (but with more tactical options). The action order is shown though, so you can plan more thoroughly than many other RPGMaker games. 
There are also 3 types of attack, Normal Attack which recovers 10 TP, Magic Attack which requires MP to cast but does not recover TP, and Special Attack which uses TP. There are also 2 types of healing items. One can be used inside combat, and the other is non-combat exclusive. 

Lastly, the game has a hidden attribute weakness/strength system which is kinda different from other RPG games. For instance, you may think that Fire is weak to Water, but in this game this is not the case. Fire is both strong and weak to ice but neutral to Water. So if you cast a fire spell on an ice enemy, it will deal a strong damage, and if you cast an ice spell on a fire enemy it will also deal a strong damage. However you will deal normal damage to water, and minimal damage to fire enemies. In short, Fire >><< Ice, Fire ==== Water, Fire …. Fire (hopefully this is understandable lol).

Those 3 types of attacks, 2 types of items, and attribute weakness/strength system need to be utilized wisely to move on, since TP is limited to 100 for each character and they do not have much MP to cast spells anytime. However, if you are a veteran to turn-based RPGs I’m sure you’ll know all about those intuitively.

On the matter of difficulty, if you have played similar turn-based RPG before, Normal difficulty is the good place to start. You can even go to Hard mode instead if you prefer more challenge. On the pre-release version even the Hard mode was so easy that I’ve beaten the final boss in less than a minute, but thankfully the developer addressed the issue and rebalanced the game.

But if you just wanna enjoy the story, normal or lower is recommended.

Graphics
Well, some tilesets and NPC sprites are the ones you can see in every RPGMaker game, but let’s forget about that, and talk about the original ones.

For the character design, I think it’s decent. They use anime-style character graphics, so for those turned off by anime, this game might not be for you. However, they are unlike those overly exaggerated anime characters using, like, absurd huge weapons, cute colorful costumes, cringe dialogues, etc. They all seemed… normal to me, which is a good thing.

The UI graphics is also good enough. Pretty simple, but still good. It reminds me of Tales of Berseria UI graphics, though…. The only downside was that the way icons are laid out on the menu felt so confusing at first. Another thing I like was that there’s

There are also some CG Arts to collect throughout the game. Some of them are good, while some others are not so. 
There is also another matter about the graphics, but I will say it on the following section.

Sound & Music
I think the strongest aspect of the game is the soundtrack that I’ve never even once get bored of them. The battle themes are so immersive, especially the boss themes. They might not be at Nihon Falcom’s or Nier’s soundtrack level, but at least they are immersive and very enjoyable. The only thing that I don’t like was the music that played on sad scenes, it felt so out of place to me. 

I also like the opening and ending themes, in which the singer was fleurishana. If you’re not an Indonesian, you may not heard of her though. Too bad the opening movie was low in frame rate and (perhaps) in not so good resolution though.

Controls
I have played the game both using a Logitech F710 Wireless Controller and a Keyboard, and I have not found any issues. There are different kinds of issue, though: Even if you are using a Keyboard, the interface is still showing Xbox controller input buttons. Also, there are some functions which are not explicitly stated IIRC. That is, using LB/RB, PgUp/PgDn or Q/E for cycling through characters on a menu, pressing ? button for skipping a turn in battle, and ? button for an extra option (Retreat). 

Others
The game is created by an Indonesian developer, so expect a lot of Indonesian cultural references being laid out here and there. Just like those Japanese games which add a lot of Japanese cultural references. The references are mostly about Indonesian foods, others are Indonesian jokes. If you are familiar with them, you will like those immediately, but if you don’t, you will not get them though.

Overall
When I was playing the pre-release version, I guessed that the price would be around $10. But to my surprise, it is actually half of that. The game has a good amount of content, despite being an RPGMaker game, so I think the game deserves more than $5. The game has a good story, gameplay,  and music, after all. But I guess it’s a win-win both for the devs and the players, so eh, why not. For the price of a burger which you will consume in less than 10 minutes, you will get 10 hours amount of gameplay! It’s a steal, if I may say so myself.

The game indeed has a lot of flaws, and many of them are not stated in my review. But judging by the game, it seems the dev will be developing another, or maybe some more games. I’m sure the future games will be much better, so I’m looking forward to it. The devs also seems to be highly responsive of feedbacks and bug reports so that’s a huge positive in my book.

With all those, I’ll give an overall score of 6 out of 10 for this game.
