This is, if not the weirdest game on Steam, then certainly in the running. 

Go to Indonesia, unravel an ancient mystery, learn Silat, and date fish. All in a nostalgic pastel color pallette with soothing music playing in the background.

Nusakana is like the gonzo lovechild of Harvest Moon and Legend of the River King, and despite English not being its original language, it is clearly a labor of love. In fact, the production values are so high that I think it would have been a cult classic if it had released back in the days of the SNES. As is, it commando-crawls at top speed out of steam's RPG Maker ghetto, punching komodo dragons in the face the whole way.

If you're willing to play something a bit different, then there's a ton of content in here. Day/night cycle, days of the week, quest boards and faction loyalty, RPG combat, fishing, crafting, language-learning, and dating, and a plotline that runs deeper than I would have expected. Somehow, rather than turning into an unharmonious kludge, all these elements work together, producing a play experience that is both relaxing and satisfying.

If you liked Harvest Moon, I'd say this is a solid $15 game. If you like to explore weird avenues of game design, or just the weirder stuff steam has to offer, I'd impulse-buy this on 50% sale.

If nothing I've said above even remotely appeals, then steer clear. This strangeness is probably not for you.

								A neat little game. You are a villain and your job is to defeat the heroes. You have a deck of cards, each with a point cost. You have a 'nexus' point, that produces 'mana' to spend on cards. This rate can be increased by capturing points on the route to the enemy 'nexus'. These are protected by them firing arrows (your own Nexus does AoE fireballs). You can spend 'mana' on buffs, instant attacks or units. Units are needed to capture the various places so are key. The enemy also spawns various units which will attack your Nexus. After battle, you move onto another place on the path to the final battle, this can be Market (Buy new cards), another battle (you gain card and souls, which are used to buy other cards), a campsite, where you can heal your Nexus HP (any damage taken is not automatically healed) or upgrade a card and finally a random event (which is positive or negative). 

The game itself is fun, neato graphics that should be viable on many systems. Odd bit of humour here and there.

Negatives? Very little content makes the price very steep. There is a single playable commander and a single 'map' (though the maps are random, by this I mean with a single hero to fight throughout). So, give it a few months if you're short on cash. I've played over 2hrs and have done the maps a few times (I restarted due to an update) so I am around Lv.4 or so as a commander. Not sure what benefit this level brings outside of a new starting deck(?), but perhaps there will be a sort of RPG mechanic added at another date.

So, overall? If you've got the money to spare and like a bit of fun during a lunchbreak, I'd recommend it. If you're looking for a game to spend hours on and not run out of content, then I wouldn't. I am, myself, looking forward to more content.

																This coffee shop has a lot of stories to tell
Introduction??Coffee Talk is the very first visual novel I've ever played and boy! oh boy! I am blown away. I didn't expect a straightforward "reading exercise" could manage to create such a credible setting along with charismatic characters. The simplicity of the Coffee Talk is elegant.


A place that is only open when the sun is sleepingCoffee Talk is a game about, well, coffee and talking. This visual novel takes place in the fantasy urbs of an alternative present-day Seattle. A time when the war between races is but a footnote in history. When humans, elves, orcs, and vampires learned to look past their differences and coexist BUT radicals and racists still draw breath.

Coffee Talk displays some cruelties of modern life and how people are drowned in their work. It makes use of our real-life situations like racism, shootouts, gun control, parties that goes awry for young folks, and with the most noticeable one being an epidemic to further aid the credibility of its world.

You're the owner of the said café, opening your place up only after midnight that attracts a rather eclectic bunch. You're an affable barista shtick; Attentive and thoughtful listener who comforts the customers by serving them warm drinks. Not having a specific background on your character immensely helped the narrative to direct its focus on the customers.


	
	
		Typical life problems like this are often told around the Coffee Talk 
		Community Created Artwork for Steam Artwork
		By: Amirite
		
			Which adds an extra layer of believability to their well-developed characters and background stories		
	

Your customers are patrons of the night who find solace in the corner of your café. Each having his/her own story arc that might conclude with a little secret if you serve them the drink they need, not want. There's only a handful of Characters but they are varied and developed wonderfully. They usually converse with each other for a long time. Their little stories are either fascinating or plain sad to hear, but in no way they become tedious for later playthroughs.


You know, I'm something of a latte artist myselfFrom what I've gathered (considering this is my first entry to the genre), visual novels offer some level of interactive gameplay along with the reading part. But still, don't come looking for extensive interactions from Coffee Talk because it falls behind the genre's standards. The dialogues are periodically broken up by a coffee brewing mini-game.


	
	
		Coffee brewing mini-game is simply mixing only a few ingredients 
		Community Created Artwork for Steam Artwork
		By: Amirite
		
			Yet I found it delightful experimenting with recipes. Not to mention the shenanigans you can do with latte art. You either end up trashing the drink or making a special one		
	

The brewing process is as simple as it gets. Drinks need a base ingredient of things like coffee, green tea, tea, and chocolate powder. Two other ingredients can be used to add flavors. Ginger, Mint, Lemon, honey, and cinnamon are ready on the shelves to be mixed into a special drink. My goodness gracious, here comes the milk. My new hobby and obsession. Adding milk to drinks allows you to do latte arts, to bring out that sleeping artist inside or just goof around with funny drawings.


A warm and cozy coffee houseVisuals
The representation of a cozy and friendly café through pixels is done delicately. The silhouettes of moving people and cars outside the café make the rainy nights of the city more lively. There aren't many animations for characters, but I'm grateful for their unadorned beauty. Their expressions and emotions are excellently depicted through only one frame of a picture which only forms a more believable and vibrant character out of their 2D nature.

Sounds
The moment the main menu music started playing, I knew it's gonna be my new jam. Chillest lo-fi beats composed by Indonesian composer Andrew Jeremy. The soundtrack is slightly chip tuned and perfectly captures the vibes of a pixelated coffee house where you need relaxing tunes to spend your time.


	
	
		Smartphones. Inseparable part of our lives. 
		Community Created Artwork for Steam Artwork
		By: Amirite
		
			Read the news on the Evening Whispers app. Follow your customers on their social media. Skip to the next track if it's not to your liking. Or write down your super-secret recipes for later use.		
	


??TECHNICAL??
Specs: GTX1050 2GB - Athlon II X4 645 - 8GB DDR3 RAM
The game runs using about 40% of VRAM at 1050p 60hz.

??BUGS & ISSUES??
    Not a single one
Verdict??Coffee Talk is the perfect game to unwind after a long day of work. Press the auto-play button and pour yourself a cup of warm drink. Sit back, relax, and enjoy memorable characters in a mellow fantasized story inspired by the typical real-life problems. The game might a bit short which offers 5-7 hours of story. But there's definitely some replay value there if you're going to finish each character's story arc. Also, Challenge and Endless modes are there for those who love to make coffee mindlessly. Whether a 20-30% sale or full price, this experience is deemed worthy of the price tag.

																Legrand Legacy is a bit of a homage to The Legend of Dragoon and other PS1/PSX era JRPGs. The combat is turn-based and feels very much like The Legend of Dragoon with its QTE-style timed attacks and defends. The dialogue is mostly silent with a few sound effects spread around very sparingly for coughs and sword clashes and things like that. The dialogue system hails back to games like Kartia with its currently speaking characters vaguely animated in a 2D sort of way. (This feature looks a lot like it utilized Spine or Spriter, but it looks great IMHO.) The levels all look and feel handpainted, which is odd when the characters don't really match that style, but I forgive that based on the fact that Final Fantasy VII had the same problem and still looked great to me.

The overall feel of the game is that it's a decade late to the 3D turn-based RPG craze. What I mean is that it doesn't offer a lot of gameplay elements or polish that would warrant buying it over an older title. If you're looking to satisfy that RPG itch and just played the classics already, then sure, pick this up. It's enjoyable. However, if you haven't played many of the classic PS1 era RPGs, I recommend saving Legrand Legacy for after those.

The older games in the genre seem to have some major advantages. For example, Legrand Legacy has timed attacks to get "perfect", "good" or "poor" status for the attacks, but you only ever do one button press for that; The Legend of Dragoon has the same type of system but makes you do the timed attack button presses more often and even has you use those timed button presses to counter counters from the enemies. Legrand Legacy isn't boring, mind you. It offers some very challenging boss fights. I simply wish it could have some tiny improvements to make it more dynamic and feel more alive.

I remind myself that a small, independent studio made Legrand Legacy. It's a good game on its own, but keeping in mind that it's from a fairly small development team, I'm very impressed with it. These devs previously made Lost Castle, which is fairly stated, a different type of game, so Legrand Legacy feels very fresh from them rather than a rehash of a genre. I hope they'll consider continuing to make different types of games in the future and trying new things.

In the end, it comes down to personal taste and budget. "Is Legrand Legacy worth $25 to me?" you ask yourself as you continue to wave your mouse cursor over that "add to cart" button. I personally think it's a good game, and while $25 is a bit steep, the devs are good at what they do. You'd be supporting the right kind of people if you bought Legrand Legacy. It's a good game, not an amazing game, just good. It's priced accordingly. If you like JRPGs but want something a little less anime-ish and more grand fantasy, Legrand Legacy is the right game for you!

																The scope of this game's series expanded, while nearly everything else degraded. The first game wasn't a masterpiece, but it was very enjoyable and had some incredibly memorable and wacky moments. Keepers of the Dark was a fantastic improvement to DreadOut 1 and also had a handful of entertaining fights. Now, we're stuck with a buggy mess of a sequel that remains a mystery because the plot barely exists and nothing makes sense whatsoever. 

Here's a short list of pros and cons, instead of me rambling too much at the start-

Pros:
1. Gameplay has evolved and gotten better in some aspects
2. Some bosses have unique and fun designs
3. Music is still fairly good like the first two games. 
4. Some areas are detailed very well.

Cons:
1. Bugs. My game crashed after the final cutscene. Everything loads in incredibly slowly.
2. Combat. Prepare to be stunlocked half the time. The flashlight helps counteract it, but it's not enough. 
3. Buggy AI. I had to chase a boss for over twenty minutes because it flew across the map and never came back.
4. Plot. You'll never know what you're doing, nor why. The first DreadOut was very concise and at least had a more understandable story. This derails everything and goes all over the place for no reason. 
5. NPC's. Some are alright, some are bad. Some clip through walls, some clip through the floor, some are floating, etc. 
6. Bosses. Some of them have pretty decent designs and attacks, but then some have only two moves or spawn enemies that stunlock you unless you stunlock them first in a looping flashlight stun while stabbing them. 


I'm really shocked. I thought this would be more enjoyable or even janky and fun, but it was painful almost all the way through. Keepers of the Dark was promising and good, but I don't get how this is the final product. It ends abruptly, there's no conclusion, and it just frustrates me to no end. Are they planning on selling DLC just to wrap it up correctly, or are we going to have to wait another few years for a real conclusion? 

Either way, I think that this series is a good one. I just wish this game wasn't so disappointing, broken, repetitive, and lackluster. I do hope they'll make more or at least patch out the bugs I ran into so it's a better experience for everyone.

Another game in a long line of rogue lite games that function similarly to Slay the Spire while trying to provide their own spin on the card based rogue lite subgenres. That's not to say it's bad, just that if you're tired of playing games like this then you might not enjoy another one.

What this game does different is that it's a tower defense game where you play as the enemies assaulting the towers. You generate mana and it pays the cost of your card and plays in real time. You use your cards to summon monsters and they march down their paths to go attack the enemy strongholds. Each fight lasts about 2-3 minutes with a run lasting just under an hour. There is some slight variation in the fights, some you win by defeating the main enemy keep, others you survive til time runs out, or fight a big boss who wins if they reach your tower. 

After a fight you pick from one of many paths and choose where you'd like to go. Engage in more assaults, engage in an elite assault for a passive boosting relic, go to a shop to buy or remove cards, visit a camp to upgrade a camp or restore your tower's health. There is some strategy involved but for the most part I just summoned whatever I could afford and did fine. There are multiple commanders for your team that have a different starting relic, passives, and cards that all strive for a different kind of build.

It's a neat game but some tremendous camera issues and a bug with spell targeting make it a little annoying. The art style is pretty cute though, a mix of pixel and anime-ish art. I really like the chubat. Personally, I'm not big on it but I think that there is a small community out there somewhere that would enjoy this. But I don't see why someone would choose this over any of the other numerous card based rogue lite games out there especially ones within the same price point. 

TL;DR I recommend it if you wait for a bigger sale or if you think your current rogue lite of choice isn't cute enough or want something realtime.

																[Review : She and the Light Bearer]>>>SPOILER ALERT, kinda<<<


A heartwarming fairytale
8.5/10


Finally.
It's been 3 years since my first encounter with She project and i always wait for this miracle to happen. And god do i love this game.

This might be the longest review i've ever written

Thanks to Mojiken Studio and Miss Brigitta Rena for creating such amazing fairytale
And thanks to Toge Productions for the publishing this awesome project.


A bit of a history.
So about 3 years ago in mid 2016 is when i first acknowledge about Itch.io. In one of recommendation section i saw one of Mojiken Studio's game, A Space for The Unbound (if i recall yes, that's the game i saw) and played it. I start browsing their library and one of their project caught my eyes, She Who Once Was Lost.
It's a simple crossing-road game with beautiful scene and story by Brigitta Rena, although it's just a Pre-Alpha of Project She. At that point i fell in love with the project and always waiting for it to rise. At first i know that the project won't be finished anytime soon because well there aren't many hype, and of course it'll took time as it's a full hand-drawn game. But i'm starting to hype since i discover She and The Light Bearer FB Page and DAMN THE HYPE IS REAL. I feel soooo much joy and excitement just of that, and knowing they team up with Toge Production to publish the game, i know it'll be awesome. And it did.



-About the game-

She and The Light Bearer is a simple story-driven visual-novel point-and-click puzzle game, which actually feels like a storybook. In She and The Light Bearer, you play as Firefly, who is a Light Bearer (duh..), wandering through forest to seek Mother. In your journey you face few obstacle, meet new friends and stuff to uncover your duty as The Light Bearer. It's not a hard game and pretty sure you can finish it in 2-3 hrs of gameplay. Tho it's a simple game, the visual art and background music is what makes this game amazing.
.
As usual i'm going to review base on 4 pillar of game development, Gameplay, Story, Graphic, and Music. Even though i love this project so much, i'll stay honest to review the game as is. And i'm also comparing it base on She Who Once Was Lost because there are so much things i love and hate about how they change the project.
And i'll try my best not to spoil the story.



-Gameplay-

It needs freedom
6/10

The gameplay is 180 degree turn from the original She project. The previous one is not a storytelling game but a crossing-road game. Of course this one is better, it got interactive way of telling how firefly going through the forest to find mother instead of avoiding weird creatures passing between tree trunks to light up objects.

I know gameplay is not the main dish of the game. It's just a simple interactive visual novel with puzzle and find-the-object kind of gameplay. But still, i think they could do more to make the game more exciting. Like, maybe instead of getting an indicator of where to click in the find-the-object sequence, they simply let player click wherever without any indicator but with some movement of the places we can click. It'll be more interesting and much more challenging. Or maybe not giving any clue of where the poles are. Or not having more dialogue options. I'm not saying the one we have now is bad, it's a cool one honestly, but i think we could get more.



-Story-

Go Deeper please.
8/10

Playing the previous game kinda ruin the surprise of knowing about what our objectives are in this game, isn't it?

The main focus is clear here, they tell us about how we should protect nature and how there's hope in every one of us. Also pretty sure the sole game's reason of existence is because miss Brigitta Rena really, REALLY loves nature. I love how they keep the four core value of the project and the representation of those core just like the previous one, but i think they forgot what backs those core values. Yes i remember when you died in the previous game there's this kind of sentence : "Know your enemy" and the creature's value on the side of that, like 'Ignorance' (sorry i only remember that one). Too bad they didn't put those simple things in the game. I mean, yeah i know i'm looking for mother but isn't it'll be more awesome if they explain about our obstacles. They give and told us about what we should have and understand, but why they told us about what we shouln't have?

But still, the story in this game is awesome. the poem is great, the conversation feels natural and cheerful (most of the time). And i like how things get more serious without losing the humble feeling of the game. I also like how the more i play the game, the more i relate to firefly. And i love how everything is okay in half of the storyline and suddenly everything is messed up. But in the end everything is resolved and there's this joyful feeling when you complete the game.



-Graphic-

Holy sht that is wonderful.
10/10

The art is the reason why this game is so unique. I'm pretty sure almost all of the asset are hand drawn and that is the reason why i buy this game in the first place. 
I love how they represent everything so complex yet feel so simple and natural. I love how the cute the characters are and how they stands out but still blends with the environtment. I love how everything is in motion, telling us even a simple humble forest have a dynamic life in it without us knowing. I love how they use different color palette to make everything having different emotions in them, and how everything feels and is what it should be. I love how they put some big trees on the side to cover the view to make it looks like we're in the narrow part of the forest. I love all those cute humble characters and how they behave and mostly i like how everything is in harmony. It always feels heartwarming to see.
There's this kind of comfort, this feeling of relax and made us feels like home in first few chapter but then we felt so much sorrow in the corrupted part. There is this kind of joy everytime the character act and reacts which always made me giggle a bit. There's this feeling of understanding about how and why they made this game after completing the game. And i could guarantee you guys, $10 is nothing compared to this masterpiece. it simply deserve more.

Also i love how they keep the bulb. lol


-Music-

Perfect resonance of nature
10/10

This is one of the unique things in the game. The music in this game is simply amazing. It's smooth and relaxing yet uplifting. The sound effects of nature simply made it deeper and complex. It feels like everytime i hear the music i feel a humble breeze and relax. and in some part it feels cleansing and holy. I know this time it's not as slow and relaxing as the previous game's Rikala Semana, but that is of course with reason, and i think it's a good move. I saw the video about how they create the music few months ago and damn those are amazing way to create music. The music is so complex and natural, so satisfying to the point where i stop playing just to listen the music for a while with full volume on speaker. Even i can't describe how every unique instrument in every instance of the bgm is well made to make us drunk in harmony, sunk in melody, and enjoy it dearly. It feels like nature. It feels like home.

----------

There's so much feeling i can't describe about this game, but it's okay, i'll leave it as is so you guys could enjoy it like i did. There're some bugs and stuffs that kinda disturbing but it's still okay i guess (i'm not in the mood to explain bugs this time). It's not the best game out there, but it'll still be the one i always adore and honor. It's a long waiting. But every second of the wait worth it. I'm pretty sure there'll be no other game exceed this one. At least, no other game will find it's place in my heart like this one does.
It's a harmony and a melody. And i'm glad i finally complete it.

Thanks for creating such masterpiece.

																So I just finished the game. As most of the comments say this game makes for around 10 hours of content, which is quite decent for a RPG Maker game. Aside, there's a lot of positive and negative aspects to talk about so I'll divide them into Pros and Cons below:

* Pros: 
- Impressive visuals for a RPG Maker game. Sprites aside, I found the main menu, character portraits, and especially the combat GUI very visually appealing. The artwork is amazing, both the character design, the monster design and the backgrounds. 
- The idea of inserting "Visual novel-like" cutscenes in place of plain text made the story more inmersive.
- The music is great too, giving the game BGMs appropiate for each scenes, and the opening and endings in particular struck with me. 
- The story, while nothing spectacular in my opinion (which granted, may be a bit inflated...) is interesting for avoiding the typical Chosen Hero fare of RPG Maker titles.
- The difficulty is balanced enough. The option of multiple difficulty is greatly appreciated, and while it's true the game isn't that much harder even on the highest difficulty it still posesses a degree of strategy during battles given the enemies' elemental resistances and weaknesses, plus some of the bosses' special attacks.

* Cons: Again, putting aside the stock engine sprites... 
- The english translation is terrible, there's no other way to put it -- the english is very basic, immersion-breaking but at the very least the story is understandable, however even then its ridden with typos. 
- The slog of obligatory battles between Chapters III and VIII were tedious and annoying, especially since you're not allowed to do anything else until it's finished. 
- While the story was charming enough, the romances leave a lot to be desired, not a single one of them feels natural at all. 
- And this is more of a personal gripe than anything, but I don't understand why any dev would consider it a good idea to add collectables in a game where it's entirely possible to miss them permanently, especially if you need them to unlock bonus content. What's the point then?

In general, this game is worth the 5$ price tag, even if for the experience alone. It's fun, it looks cool, and it's accessible for all players. Aside from the clunky english translation, the annoying Ch. III to VIII slog, and the missable content -- which admittedly are mostly beginner dev's problems and can be learned from -- this game is worth the price.

and now onto the short review


TL;DR Review


//intro//

Hey what is up my name is MF Kraven and I'm here to bring you another less than 10 mins review, today I will be looking at When the Past Was Around. WtPWA is a point & click adventure puzzle game with a haunting yet beautiful theme of grief. It's about remembering, forgetting, love, sorrow and everything that may lie in it. Is When the Past Around the next worthy tearjerker or should you forget about the game completely?
Lets find out!


//Graphics, Sound & Artstyle//

I wanna start off by saying that everything that the artists and composers put forth on When the Past Was Around are absolute geniuses. All emotions evoked from me as I experienced the game. The artstyle paints a picture more beautiful than Studio Ghibli films, the score elevates the art to a level of serenity & sorrow. 


//Gameplay//

Like any other point & click puzzle game, the actual gameplay doesn't stand out. Many have compared the prologue to a Rusty Lake-esque game, to a degree I agree. However the stylized simplistic way of where everything is positioned wont have rookies of the genre looking up what to do next rather, everything makes sense with the exception of one or two puzzles. I really appreciate having on the top right corner a button to press to highlight what may or may not be an interactable item or action.


//Price//

7.99 USD

//How many hours estimated//

I was stuck in two puzzles that really didn't make a lot of sense to me, with that & grabbing some popcorn, it took me about almost 3 hours to beat the game.



//Final Thoughts//

When the Past Was Around is a gorgeous game with an eclectic artstyle. I evoked emotions in me and had me on the verge of tears in some scenes. I had fallen ill a few years ago & some of the imagery took me back to a battle I couldve easily lost to my illness. Without spoiling anything..... the ending was initially inconclusive to me, but that is only due to the fact that the game is not voice acted; this is where my first negative note comes from. The game would serve better as a film rather than a game, don't get me wrong, I really liked the experience however- with half of an understanding at what's happening, a little dialouge would go a long way. Only other complaint I have is two of the puzzles in the game had me scratching my head wondering what I was supposed to do. Having 90% of the achievements, I obviously passed the game but it was through deductive reasoning but I just know there was a method to this madness, I would just like to understand HOW. In spite of everything just mentioned though, the game remains a treasure. The story is one that almost hit too close to home. It's art, only through interpretation can it be genuinely enjoyed. Is it perfect? No. Will you feel a lump in your throat as you see Eda cling to the very existence of her beloved Owl? In my experience, yes. It's an experience for connoisseurs of romance novels to embrace, a tale for the widows of the world to live through. Have I made my point? 

For the asking price of 7.99; I find that it's more than reasonable for the experience you are getting. 

Buy it Now!

Posted: 26 August, 2020
																It's always commendable when a developer decides to create a game that revolves around folklore from their own culture. Home Sweet Home did an outstanding job bringing a chilling tale centered around Thai mythology to life. Paper Dolls was an incredible homage to terror from Chinese legends. Now Pulang: Insanity promises to do the same, it's a psychological horror game that is steeped in Indonesian culture and superstition. It isn't necessarily a first for the genre (DreadOut, Pamali), but it definitely is an under-explored mythos in the world of horror.

The biggest element that seems to be make-or-break for most people regarding this title and its 'mixed' rating on Steam is the story. As aforementioned, it's a psychological tale, and as usual with all stories of the type the narrative can be pretty confusing if you're not fully invested in the experience. You play a man named Rudy, who lives in a lavish mansion with his wife and daughter. The mansion seems to have problems of its own, as you come to find out all of the maids have quit, and his young daughter is acting weird. Before acquiring all of his luxuries, Rudy lived an unemployed life, drowning in debt and poverty, until one day he performed the Pesugihan ritual; a black magic spell where the caster becomes instantly rich beyond their wildest dreams, but they must keep performing offerings to satisfy the Toyol (an undead infant that is conjured within the ritual). Of these offerings, a minimum of three human sacrifices are needed.

The story evolves from there, and although it takes the long way around, it gradually unravels the closer you get to the end of the game. Eventually, everything is spelled out during the final sequence to clear up any confusion that may come along with its convoluted telling. That said, the plot is told in such a way that it keeps your mind focused on the game, and it keeps you pondering exactly what happened between Rudy and his family. The voice acting is actually pretty good, the translation is very well done, and there is enough turn-taking between cutscenes and note pick ups to keep even the most nit-picky horror fanatic satiated at how the tale is conveyed.

As for gameplay, Pulang: Insanity is your typical horror walking simulator, complete with key and object finding; at least that's how it presents itself during the first hour of its campaign. It has a deeply immersive atmosphere that hearkens back to the Silent Hill franchise, an inspiration that can even be seen during its main menu sequence. The environments are teeming with fog and rain effects, and the graphics look really superb for a low budget indie title. The sound effects really suck the player into the midst of it all, and the droning ambient soundtrack is the cherry on the cake that tops off what would be an overall complete package of mesmerizing terror. That is, if the game didn't suddenly change direction half-way through. It's at the midway point that you'll discover that there are multiple one-hit kill enemies, and that their AI is a frustrating implementation that completely tears apart all of the deeply engaging content that the developer strived to create up to this point.

There are only a few different "enemies", and from what I could tell by the patch notes the problem that I'm going to talk about has only been an issue since May 2020, when there was a patch to make the "enemy AI more aggressive". Essentially, you'll come upon a few areas where there are some floating monsters who follow you around. That's about all they do, if you run into them you die, but with the developer's update they follow you so fast that you can barely escape them. It also doesn't matter if you turn off your light source, crouch, or try to hide; they don't need to see you to follow you. In fact, when you load into an area that has one of these foes, they'll completely make a B-line straight for you from their spawn location, and since they're ghosts they'll just clip through all other objects and houses. There's an invisible string tethering you to them, and the most irritating thing is that you'll end up running straight into them every single time. The worst is a bird-like creature much later in the game that is so fast you cannot outrun it once you ever see it, and you can't miss it. This is where I quit and just watched a walkthrough instead, where someone who played this title back at release didn't have these issues.

Another problem that does need addressing, albeit to a lesser extent, is the optimization. Running this game on an i7-6700k/GTX 1080 at a resolution of 1080p, I was unable to find any setting where I pulled a stable 60 FPS. For context, though a bit dated, my rig can still run every modern AAA title at 60+ FPS effortlessly. At worst, the frames fell to 40 FPS, and this mostly seems to happen both outside during the rain, and with the flashlight on. The problem becomes less prominent further into the game when you have to use the lantern, and when the areas are more closed in. 

Pulang: Insanity really his the nail on the head in almost every single way. The manner in which it tells its story, which utilizes a great variety of both cutscenes and notes, is very close to an AAA grade title. Though some may argue that the plot is overly complex, it's all explained in the end and if you really follow the lore and the notes, it's easy enough to at least keep a thumb on what's happening and what may have potentially gone down. Additionally, the game houses some of the most immersive atmosphere and ambience that you'll have the pleasure of coming across in a small indie release, and the developer was able to successfully recreate that Silent Hill feeling in a lot of different ways. It's too bad that a game that has so much going for it has to get a refund and a non-recommendation due to something as simple as incredibly frustrating AI that borderline breaks the entire game. If this can be fixed, I'll turn my negative review into a positive one, and implement a higher rating.

																If there’s one thing I love apart from strategy games, it’s story-based games driven on by the crippling boredom/excitement of employment. And Coffee Talk fits into this genre very well. The characters are all written to be believable and the chemistry between them and their different relationships are perfectly mirrored by the dialogue. You, as a player, actually end up feeling emotions and connections to these characters through your dialogue as the barista, something most story driven games should always aim for. The world building is also very competent, with an interesting premises of different fantasy races living among each other in a society not much different to ours. The overarching story of the world is written in a way that is both interesting and influential to our characters’ stories, while also not going into so much detail that it draws attention off the main characters’ arcs.
The gameplay is relaxing, if not a bit disappointing. While I do love the casual point and click mechanics used to create drinks to give to customers, the fact that it’s really the only real input the player has in the story sort of takes away the influence our character has, and basically ends up making the game a novella with the occasional break for the player to make coffee (or tea). While it is a nice idea to make the drink that you give the customer the only way for your character to interact with the story, it makes the story very binary in the fact that you have the choice to either do the order right or wrong. If you get every order correct on your first run (which may be helped by grinding challenge or free brew mode to unlock coffee recipes) you effectively get through 90% of the story within your first run.
This, sadly, does mean that the replay value is very low. You have to play the game a second time to get the best ending and a secret achievement, but after that there’s nothing that really changes in the story. Even then, only the second run, the dialogue only changes notably on 4 of the days. Thankfully, if you were grinding for achievement on the second run, like I was, the fast-forward button becomes a godsend. I think it was a very smart idea to only allow the player to use it after they’ve completed the game at least once, so they can’t skip the story, and that, on your second run, it is unavailable to use during any new dialogue. It’s useful if you want to skip over the parts of the story and dialogue you already remember.
Apart form the nit-picking, though, the game is, overall, pretty good. The gallery and comic sections in the extra menu were extremely interesting to browse, and the addition of the challenge mode was a good call, at least in my opinion.
If you like heavily story-based games, don’t mind not having that much of an input in the narrative, and enjoy stories loosely based on realistic scenarios, I’d highly recommend this game. It’s a good 3-4 hours of calm story telling.

																 Overview 
Horror is hands-down the bumpiest ride of any genre in gaming. Some titles are amazing, others are a complete waste of time, and you often don’t know which is which until you’ve gotten your hands on them. Pulang: Insanity is, unfortunately, one of those disappointments as a strong introduction quickly gives way to a lackluster experience that will likely leave you thinking more on its wasted potential than on its accomplishments.

 More Tease Than Terror 
The story of Pulang: Insanity is a promising one, looking at it on the drawing board at least, but its major flaws make it far less enjoyable than it could’ve been. I spent much of the game only vaguely knowing what was happening, in a disaster way as opposed to an arty one, and pushing forward anyway. Luckily, the linearity of the experience made it so that I never actually got stuck at any point due to this and progression kept at a steady pace throughout, but this made it more of a horror-themed walking simulator than a horror adventure. Once you throw on a healthy dose of key hunting (sometimes actual keys, other times items like valve handles) and you’ll spend a lot of your time seeking out items that will open up the next area for you to explore. Rinse and repeat.

The horror atmosphere is decent but it struggles as it competes with the disjointed narrative. The setting itself is creepy enough though you’ll often be distracted from it by sudden, seemingly random cutscenes that tell fragments of a story at a time, often involving the main character knowing something that we don’t and only some of that ever being explained. Add a dash of animations that glitch fairly often and an English translation that’s botched enough to require the reading of lore documents several times to get all the details, and you’re guaranteed an experience that feels increasingly like a bargain bin experience the longer you play.

 Wait, What Am I Playing? 
The further you get into Pulang: Insanity, the more it seems to lose sight of itself. This isn’t just the vague and confusing story, this includes the gameplay mechanics as well. Hunting for progression items is a chore and the icing on the cake is that there’s no easy way to use these items. You have to open a full-screen inventory, often having to select the inventory tab instead of the one for documents, and there’s absolutely nothing resembling a quick-select menu. Considering the Pulang is really more of a walking simulator than anything else, I don’t understand why it doesn’t simply use the correct progression object when you click on what it’s supposed to be used on. Your flashlight does act oddly when you get near an object that you can interact with, though I’m not sure if I consider this a good thing or not. If you’re here for a walking simulator it’s a nice benefit; if you’re here for a challenge or any kind of a thought-provoking experience, it’s probably something that you would’ve liked to figure out on your own.

 Verdict 
Pulang: Insanity isn’t the worst game you’ll ever play but there are certainly superior horror titles out there that are more aware of what they are and do it better. I didn’t experience any game-breaking bugs which made me happy but the actual game itself couldn’t live up to the hype that its own intro built up for it. Its story is interesting enough, if you can piece it together, but could’ve been executed in a far more orderly and clear way**. If you’re looking for a good horror walking simulator, this title may not have the depth of story and atmosphere that you prefer. If you’re looking for a good survival or puzzle horror, there likely isn’t enough actual game here for you. Either way, Pulang: Insanity may not be the title that some of us had hoped that it would be, but there’s enough inspiration here that OZYSOFT might be able to pull off a very solid horror game in the future if they can take their vision and create something that flows more efficiently.

It was certainly not a bad system and it's exactly what I'd expect from an indie team. But it could use some improvements in a future release.

The world was interesting. It's nice to see a JRPG that isn't afraid to dive into topics like slavery and having important character actually die throughout the story. I will say this though, Finias has to be the worst designed zone in the game. I'm assuming English wasn't the developers native language and some of it just accounts to a rough translation and cultural differences.

It was also great to see a handdrawn 2D world map with 3D sprites on it again. Really brought back that nostalgic feeling.

Overall I'd definitely recommend this game to JRPG fans. It's not perfect by any means, but it's a very solid $20 indie game and exactly the type of thing I'd love to see more of in the future by this team and others. The AAA gaming industry is a joke and indie devs are the real kings now.

This is roughly a point and click adventure which includes a dark story, symbolism, time management all in one for a plot where a single father is trying to revive his only hope in the world: his daughter. He is an alchemist and he was banished to the forgotten parts of the city where the people who did not belong lived. There many many things happened and he lost his daughter and he uses the forbidden arts to revive her. 

The gameplay is all about that mouse: clicking and clicking. You have to earn money using limited resources which you summon homonculi of different emotions. It's your job to choose jobs for the homonculi depending on those emotions. You must also preserve your daughters body until the soul ritual is complete. You must birth, raise, and then ultimately kill the homonculi in order to find the right combination that fits your daughter. The excess body parts of the homonculi can be sold for extra cash. You need to have good relationships with your susbstitute daughters so you can do that by giving them gifts and playing with them. The shop in the game have neat little items that can make you progress things faster too. SO all in short: the story of this game can make you very uncomfortable especially since the homonculi are your substitute daughters and you actually DO have good relationships with them before either kiling or selling them. 

The villagers of the town have their own cryptic feats and pasts as well and you will learn their stories on your journey. 																Words are the principle way in which humans communicate. We loved them so much, we gather them into languages with grammars and syntax so we can put them together to express the all but simple thoughts in our minds. We can not imagine a world without words, and yet how often do they fail us. "It's something I just can't put into words." Sometimes words are not enough to say what we want to say. Sometimes you need to communicate without them.

This is the form of communication that When The Past Was Around chooses to utilize. It tells a story without words. Music, images, actions and reactions. Anything that can perk your senses and move your attention, but isn't a word, is utilized by the game to slowly unravel a mysterious and emotional plot. Along the way there will be puzzles to solve and things to remember, and even a few fun secrets. When you finish the game, not a single word will have been spoken, and yet you'll feel like so much was said. You'll feel emotions in your heart that were placed their directly by the creators, but that you didn't actually interpret through language.

It's an amazing sensation and will hopefully open your mind to a bigger world as we continue to explore the very limits of the medium of interactive entertainment. 

Because of this I highly recommend you go in as blind as possible and try to solve every puzzle without looking them up. It will be quite difficult at first, perhaps even frustrating. The very tool we use everyday in our speech is being robbed from us and taken away, of course it's going to feel foreign. But there will be a moment it begins to click, and suddenly your conscious mind will begin to fade and you'll start thinking in concepts rather than vocabulary. You'll see what's going on and understand it, but not need to say it.

The story will end. You'll cry. And then you'll say, with words once again, "Wow, that was a good point-n-click game."

Posted: April 4, 2020
																I'm on the latté art screen, waiting for my last achievement, so I think that it's the perfect time to write about my experience with Coffee Talk. It's a concise, small gem in the field of interactive visual novels not unlike VA-11 HALL-A. I can see so many similarities that I want to compare in the review, but I think it's just better to stick to calling it "coffee-themed VA-11 HALL-A with a more modern touch."

I think that the story was like a nice small shortcake. It's really not a lot of food and it's not a complex meal, but it's a nice experience with a cup of tea or coffee in the evening. The plot is only like a wave on the beach just slightly washing your feet. I personally feel that character dynamics could have been pushed further, but they have done well with the time constraint that the game has.

In terms of graphics, I think that it's very well done. The characters feel animated and active, rather than just sticking to a static sprite that changes moods every so often. The UI design is wonderful and simplistic, and the backgrounds set a solid foundation for the worldbuilding to occur on. If only there was more worldbuilding, that is.

Worldbuilding is something I'd say is necessary in these "service novels" as I like to call them. The immersion is expanded upon by magnitudes. In VA-11 you could browse danger/u/, read Kira Miki's blog, and more. The most worldbuilding we get in Coffee Talk is through natural dialogue and the little segment of news you get at the start of a day. In-dialogue worldbuilding is done very well, however outside of it, there is very little to supplement our knowledge of this fantasy-like place. 

In terms of mechanics, I think that Coffee Talk has wonderful ways to depict a drink's properties with 4 bars of different qualities, as well as providing you with very good feedback in regards to drink design. Most of the drinks in the earlier part of the game are things you can figure out by yourself within the given 5 tries, and you only need to dig deeper into the dialogue transcript. I only have a small issue in regards to the order of ingredients in drinks. Often times, your solution for a drink may be right under your nose - you only need to swap primary and secondary ingredients. This can, and has lead to frustration before. 

As a tiny side note from a barista: I think that the latté art mechanic is super interesting, albeit it could use more work. I quite enjoyed playing around with it!

TL;DR with VA-11 HALL-A comparisons:
The game is a very short experience (5 hours max) that conveys aesthetics and story in the same way that VA-11 did without heavy worldbuilding, with less immersion and more focus on in-the-moment situations, rather than overarching plots.

																While my experience with this game started off rough, by the end of this game I was really in to the story and looking forward to what would come next. I found all of the main characters interesting, and many of the plot twists managed to keep the plot going and retain my interest. The plot starts off a bit too proper-noun heavy, somewhat feeling like Final Fantasy 13, and the first several hours were a bit confusing in not really understanding what was going on, but the game manages to come back to many of the early events and really flesh them out in a satisfying way. By the end of the game, the characters are really relatable and likeable.

My experience with this game is probably somewhat unique in that the development team released a major story re-write and mechanics update when I was about halfway through the game. I can't comment on the story re-write (which was meant to fix some things about the likeability of some characters) for the first half, however there was definitely a noticable improvement with the characters in the second half. Most of my complaints had to do with the battle mechanics (and reason for using CheatEngine to bypass them), and the mechanic changes in the patch significantly improved the game. Specifically a difficulty selection was added and the player now has the option to disable battle QTEs, which are used for pretty much every action otherwise.

Likely taking a cue from the Suikoden series, Legrand Legacy includes 4 separate battle systems. The standard turn based battle system will be the most battles you encounter. During the main game you will also encounter some 1 on 1 fencing battle segments much like found in Suikoden titles. And you will also encounter several tactical skirmishes mostly in the 2nd half, which I personally felt were a bit too difficult (though I'm not a fan of tactical battles generally). There is also an optional mini game that includes a real time battle combat.

For an indie game, I found the graphics were quite impressive even if not perfect, being about PS2 era. The handful of FMV were really well done, and the character models and backgrounds are pretty good (as long as you play on high settings). I found that many of the character movements seemed stiff, such as during some story battle/cutscenes in the Arena, and some various points where there is some odd pathing, but nothing that can't be looked past understanding that this was a smaller indie team.

While I found the first few hours a slog, and had serious doubts about the game when I played the tutorial- I'm glad I stuck through it. By the end I was really interested and found I really enjoyed this game. I can only imagine that I would have had a better experience had I started off with the v2 patch instead of only playing the second half with it.

For full disclosure, I was a Kickstarter backer.

																My Lovely Daughter is a tricky game to give a simple review to but for the sake of those considering whether or not purchasing it, this is what I think:

This is a game for managing small tasks and routine if you break it down to its most basic level. If you are the kind of person that enjoys games like that, you will easily find yourself having a good time with it. The kinds of games that feel a little bit like work, but in a way that is very laidback. It can be very grindy, but if you find your pace with it you can easily get everything you want from it.

The meat on top of those gameplay bones are the aesthetic and the framing. It is not as story-deep as I would like. That element is there but it leaves quite a bit to be desired? The daughters are really the spotlight of this game. If you like monster girls, there are a lot of them, you get little letters from them throughout the game informing more about how they perceive the world and their personalities. The wiggle room of  how much you'll grow to love and empathize with them varies from person to person, so I suggest seeing maybe a bit of playthrough of this game first and if it interests you, you probably have something to gain from playing this. The art is simple but pleasant enough, not what I would call eye candy but it makes the game stand out a little bit more.

The way it handles its themes though I'm quite mixed about. I'd say this is a game I feel a little uncomfortable thinking about, but not playing. Its intent to be offputting is very clear, and I don't feel any maliciousness coming from it, but you will stop caring that you are killing innocent girls, just from a play perspective. It's repetitive enough that it won't impact you after a certain point if it impacts you at all. As someone who was a victim of child abuse, this kind of dark content can be a form of catharsis, but it varies from victim to victim and I would find it completely understandable if this game came across as rather tactless to some. There isn't all that much to meaningfully spoil but the game doesn't make playing from Faust's perspective something that has weight. It proposes itself as a game about family and 'how far you'll go for it' which implies a sense of foreboding guilt? But I assure you that you'll never really be able to put yourself into Faust's shoes outside of the actual gameplay. 

If you're looking for an in-depth look or for it to have something insightful to say about child abuse, this is not the game you're looking for. If you want a game with elements of child abuse presented in a way that is sympathetic to victims while also not really giving them any way out of the cycle of suffering they're trapped in, this game is it. Maybe if you have not been exposed to these scenarios before, it might be a different perspective into the world that you're not used to, and I don't think that's without value, but it doesn't exactly handle them in ways I find extremely helpful for strangers to the subject either. You know. Child Abuse Bad. That's not exactly a very revealing statement. There is more to the text that you can gleam from if you spend a lot of time with it, but it's not something that comes with the experience itself.

In the end, the game only managed to snap me out of numb grind once or twice while reading letters and I felt something for a second and then promptly clicked "Kill her", because I "had" to. That's how games are. But I feel it could've been more meaningful and heavier than that. If it's not your type of game then you'll really won't have fun playing it either, nor is it fun to watch. 																 It's an okayish game that had a lot of potential. 
Let me clarify something first: I liked the game, but certain aspects of it that I will describe below made my experience with it a mere "...eh...". Since Steam doesn't have a middle ground on the recomendation buttons, just a Yes or No, I have to go with No.
I will now tell you what I went through and therefore what you will probably feel like while playing, just to give my insight on the matter. I will try to be vague enough to not spoil anything.


 The game 

Maybe you are here reading the reviews on this game because you got attracted to it's theme, just like me. A dark game where you have to sacrifice homunculi to get your daughter back. Sounds awesome! Will you get in a dilemma of killing them or not for the sake of a loved one? What would the implications of that be in the main character during the ending?
Let's play it!

Then you find out that you can't. 
Seriously. 
If you wanna progress through the game, you have to kill them. Sure, you can just not kill a single one and get one of the endings, but then the game would either be over really soon or you would get stuck in an eternity of repetitive tasks.
Just like that, the game became a bit uninteresting for me. But hey, maybe I'm being too judgemental right off the bat. Let's play it more so I can get a better idea.


 The gameplay/story 

In the beggining you will be put through the tutorial and the basics of the game. They are intuitive and relatively easy to understand, so no worries there. 
You will also be introduced to our main character. Like or dislike him, his story and pursue for his daughter's life is going to be somewhat cativating, which makes the thrive for the development of the plot to be bigger every week. You may find him to be a bit gullible, but you will want to find out the outcome of everything anyway.

However, later you will realize that the gameplay is minimal and extremely repetitive. There is so little you can actually do that sometimes it might feel like a chore. It also is pretty much linear, which kinda dulls the story a little bit. Also, since there is no way to progress unless you kill the homunculi, you will probably just get apathetic and simply stop caring about them.
But even though with all these frustrations, you still wanna see how the story develops and how everything ends. 


 The endings 

The true ending will  surely  make you go wait, what???
 I personally think it was a bit crappy. Maybe the road that I had to go through to get such and ending intensified that feeling, but I can safely say it could be a lot better.

There are other "game overs" endings in the game, but I heavily discourage for you to go for it in your first playthrough, because they actualy delete your save file (Like, really? If you get a "game over" screen, kiss goodbye to all your progress). If you want to go for them first, check a guide and do them in a separate playthrough/save file.

When I finally finished the game and got the true ending, I immediately loaded it again and went for the most obvious bad ending possible in an attempt to complete my diary. Even thought I sucessfully got it and made progress in it's completion, going for another load just to find my saved games to be blank really discouraged me. Nope, not going through those repetitive mechanics again.


 The veredict 

Even though the plot is interesting to an extension and the theme is pretty awesome, the repetitive, linear and annoying gameplay, allied with the somewhat lack of actual content and a pretty meh ending made the game bland. 
In the end, what could be a very freaking awesome game became an average experience.

My final rating would be 5.5/10.

I can only hope that Toge productions will take this as a learning experience and step it up for their next game. I absolutely love their previous work and will surely still follow it.

																TLDR: .Played for 1 hour. Heavily influenced by what seems to be FFVIII, but seems lacking. Graphics aren't polished in some areas. Combat could use a small rework. Dialogue is a little stale. Overall, still a somewhat enjoyable game. 7/10



What to say...

FIRST IMPRESSIONS:
A jrpg that seems to be influenced by FFVIII...kinda heavily. 1 hour into the game, and I'd say the similarities are pretty close when it comes to objectives, specifically the first BIG boss fight. I wont say anymore as for spoilers but if you've played FFVIII then I will say this...FIRE. Also the main character has some lovely scars on his face, wonder what other main characters have scars on their face............Anyway moving on.

STORY:
For starters. I have only finished the 1st chapter of the game. That being said, I'm not going to be too critical on the story. However, from what I have experienced so far, i do have a slight issue: the dialogue. The interactions between characters just seems extremely stale and unnatural. The actual quest story in itself is an honorable one, but because of the dialogue you cant really get invested.

GRAPHICS:
The game is an indie game, so I don't expect much out of the graphics. However, some of the backgrounds are just plain blurry and pixelated. I understand the aesthetic of painted surroundings and all, but sometimes it seems that the graphics were made too small so they just enlarged them to fit the screen. To be quite frank, I think FFVIII (the original) has better graphics. Once again I understand that this is an indie game, but its also from 2018. If I had to put a positive spin on it, it definitely screams early 2000s in both in game graphics and in pre-rendered cutscenes. Right at the beginning of the game, before you start your journey, there is a small in-game cutscene that looks atrocious. All the fighting animations are pretty standard: not great, but not terrible either. Character design is pretty alright, they of course suffer from this style of jrpg specifically when walking around a town/ or not in a fight. Blocky and not all that enticing. For Dialogue scenes, it kinda is 2.5D...ya know: Pictures that would look plenty fine if they were still but for some reason they twist the picture and move parts of it to give it "life". Honestly, I prefer Different stills to show reactions than the method used in the game. I would even rather have simple text boxes, but that is just a personal preference.

GAMEPLAY:
As soon as you load up the game they recommend you to use a game pad, but its completely possible to play with Keyboard and mouse. It's not like playing with controller is any better for the game play either... I mean yeah, walking around some of the levels would be slight easier to do, but it doesn't make the game any harder with KBM. The reason I would recommend a controller is because all of the instructions for combat are controller based. It will tell you directions keys that you will need to press at a specific time to land a better hit/block. This can get confusing if you're using WASD for movement. Fighting is pretty standard for a jrpg. Turn based, somethings do more damage against other things , so on and so forth. There is an "interactive" key to the combat and sadly...it's required that you do well on them, because if you do poorly, it will kinda ruin your day. Most jrpgs give you an option to either sit back and let your characters do the work and then if you feel like it you  do "quick-time-esque" things while your character attacks to do bonus damage. In this game, if you decide to sit back and not interact in the battle your characters will do ????? for damage. This concept, to me, makes combat feel like a chore instead of a fun battle. Engaging in combat is pretty meh. Instead of random encounters, there are ghosts on the battlefield that you can some times sneak around, but for the most part, if you see 4 ghosts you will have 4 battles, and that doesn't mean 4 enemies either. from what I have seen so far in chapter 1. enemy groups will be anywhere from 1-3 enemies.

OVERALL:
I want to love this game. I want to get sucked into the story. But so far, it kinda falls flat. It's not a bad game. and the 1 hour that have played so far was still kinda enjoyable even while everything feels a little off. I will continue to play this game, and hopefully, find it more enjoyable than what it is currently. If I were to fix anything, I would take away the requirement to constantly interact with every single attack that every single character makes. Before an attack sequence simply press button "whatever" and that will allow you to either make the attack stronger or weaker. I'm not quite sure I could be comfortable paying $20 for this game. Game feels like I bought it from a resale store on a whim. I could see myself paying anywhere from $5-$10. Anymore than that feels weird.

RATING:
7/10

																I played two hours, and got a refund.  This is a "tentative" no.  Here's why.

The gameplay.  For me, this is usually the most important point about a game.  The initial strategy and tactics seems sound.  You put a character up front and usually block while your back row pegs the enemy down.  Fair enough.  But the QTE system isn't engaging.  I usually enjoy QTE systems, but the good one's have variety.  It doesn't matter what ability your do or use, its the same QTE EVERY TIME.  Shadow hearts at least mixed it up per character.  If you're going to keep it the same, its just a redundant button push.

Overworld hit detection.  The game allows you to get the jump on the enemy, and they can get the jump on you.  This is all by hitting the back of the enemy.   The problem is, the hit detection isn't very good sometimes.  You'll THINK you hit their back, but you actually walked through them and they got the jump on you.  Not good.

Poor game design.  Game started off decently until you get to the temple.  At this point, I'm just grinding through the same mobs.  I liked the shortcuts back to the healing area, but JUST grinding mobs gets old.  Then, later you find what appears to be a secret room.  The game has already shown you there are shortcuts back, and it implies there's going to be one more before the boss.  So you take the secret room and BAM, unavoidable boss fight you weren't prepared for.  

Each of these things aren't big on their own, but the combination of these things lends the game to feeling unpolished, and at most a C to B effort.  Honestly, they might want to get rid of advertising how great their game was in some competitions, because it got my expectations up higher than the game deserved.  Still, art is great, story seemed average RPGish, and I'm sure the tactical combat would get more complex as you received more characters. 																 In A Nutshell Azure Saga Pathfinder (ASP from now), is a rather classic JRPG with some unique mechanics and an interesting setting. In this game you will live the adventures of Synch and Noide, a human and an android, crash-landed into an alien world, where they will forge improbable alliances to get their spaceship back together and return to their mothership, or at least try!

The gameplay follows the classic JRPG model, with a global map where all discovered locations are displayed, locations divided in sections (squares, in this case), containing items, chests, secrets, fishing spots, and quest-giving NPCs. Some parts of locations will not be accessible at first, but only later as parts of various quests. Many locations will be mandatory for the main storyline, but some are optional and will lead to secret bosses and quests. 

In ASP, you will find a less in-depth customization of character than many other JRPGs, as the only equipment that can be changed are two pieces of armor, and two attachable jewels, categorized clearly in items more oriented for support, mage, tank, so your choices in what to equip to who will be pretty clear to make. Jewels can activate additional armor proprieties if they are the correct type. There also are no level-up choices, attributes or anything like that, completely automatic in that sense.

Combat is turn-based, all the allies will act in the same turn, and then all the enemies. There is a system of weaknesses / resistances of certain enemy types to certain ability types, or damage types, basic statuses such as stun, poison, silence, taunt and so on. There also is a system called Fury, charging a special attack bar the more damage your characters sustain, to then unleash a powerful attack with unique effects. One of the unique mechanics consists in the Unity attacks special moves that can be discovered by attacking in the same turn with a precise order of character skills. There are 50 combinations to be discovered, each with unique effects and powers. 

Overall, i found ASP a decent JRPG, that could use improvements especially in quality of life, the story is pretty cliche and you will get a hint of what really happened from the beginning, but that doesn't mean it's bad at all. Quests are often fetch or kill quests without particular interest, and frankly they are rarely worth doing, plus, a special mention must be done to the last level, which i a total game design DISASTER and results in a very annoying and frustrating experience. So much that it prevented me from finishing it, in fact.

 Gameplay Analysis 

 General Gameplay 
Gameplay is mainly divided into exploration and combat. Exploration is done in real-time in an isometric map, and features some puzzles to solve from time to time, fetching keys and elements to progress in levels, getting quests and rewards from NPCs, and loot from chests. Fishing is also a thing and is a nice simple mini-game to pass some time and get some Fish as consumable, to use in battle.

An arena is also unlocked at a certain point, featuring challenging encounters and unique rewards for those who are brave enough. Some additional progression elements are uncovered later on, such as Tattoos, used to specialize further your team members, and also Gem Fusion, to fuse gems of the same type and rank in more powerful versions. Crafting is also a thing, usable at crafting benches found in various levels, but it is not very useful to be honest.

To buy all these things you will need money, dropped from monsters, or gained from chests or quests sometimes. In the game's first half money will be an issue, but then later it won't.


 Story 
The story is a bit predictable, but good enough to keep you entertained. It is not particularly over the top, or well written, but not bad either. Average.

 Combat System 
Combat is turn-based like in most JRPGs, the only unique mechanics being the Fury System and the Unity Attack mechanic. Enemies will have weaknesses to specific abilities and types of damage, as will your characters. Classes are clearly divided into DPS, support, tank and so on, with abilities to match these roles. enemies willa swell have Fury abilities (but not United) and unleash them when the time comes, often only bosses have them though.

A better explanation of vulnerabilities, status duration, and effects would be good, as often it is not exactly clear what is weak to which attacks, and why. Other than this, a pretty solid classic JRPG combat system, even if quite simplistic if compared to other titles.

 Content & Pricing 
Priced at 13€, and lasting a good 25-30 hours if you are aiming to complete every optional boss, secret quest etc, i'd say this game has a good content price ratio. A good deal.

 Balancing & Challenge 
Some bosses can literally stun-lock / silence-lock entire parties without specific items / builds, making such battles very cheesy. Luckily most of these are optional ones. Nothing apart from this.



 Technical Analysis 

 Graphics 
Well done 2D hand-drawn style, animations and effects. Artistically, ASP has a very good eye-candy for an indie title and hits the mark in depicting the world it is set into.

 Sound 
Average soundtracks and effects, without particular praise.

 Performance & Stability 
Nothing to report. Solid.

 AI 
Enemy AI will generally be tied to their specific class: support units will heal and buff, DPS will attack viciously, tanks will do their job, stunning and crippling enemies. Overall a good AI for a JRPG.

 Quality of Life 
There are many problems here. Quest items are not displayed on the map even if you visited the room they are located in, so if a player misses them, he will spend hours roaming maps to try and find some key or bauble to open a door. Arena battles do not heal party if victorious. Players cannot certainly escape a battle if they wish to do so, but it's chance based. Levels with much weaker monsters will still trigger encounters and make players lose a lot of time for no reason. Quest items cannot be picked up if the quest for them has not been taken, forcing players to huge backtracking. 

 Bugs / Issues 
The issues mentioned above make the last game level a very frustrating and not fun experience, I personally spent 5 hours roaming that single dungeon in search of a quest item, but since it was not displayed, i gave up, and spent tons of resources in the process because of unskippable encounters all the time. A very sour drink in an otherwise pleasant experience. This was the only MAJOR issue with the game.


 Conclusion & Rating Azure Saga Pathfinder is a decent JRPG, with problems in quality of life that impair it a bit, and a complete disaster in level design regarding the last stage. Still, i suggest it to JRPG fans as it is pretty good overall, but mind my words, you will get angry at the last stage!

 RATING: 6.5 / 10

																Note: I previously published the review below on my personal blog, but the sentiments still stand.

It’s taken more than a few demos and blind playthroughs on stream for me to get to this point, but I am extremely honored to finally review this game that has come from a Toge Productions, an indie game studio based in sunny Indonesia. I was lucky enough to be gifted an early access key on release, but I took my time playing the game because I almost didn’t want it to end.

I know some people are going to think of VA-11 Hall-A, where you play as a bartender in a cyberpunk setting. An admission here is that I have never played VA-11 Hall-A, so you will get a raw, unadulterated perspective from me here. Nothing against comparing both of these games with each other, but I’m not really in the position to do so.

Anyway, onto the coffee and the talk! And that is precisely what this game is about. One of the few times a game title actually corresponds to what you actually do. You play as a self-named barista, serving hot beverages – coffee, tea and chocolate concoctions while listening to the problems of the people. Except, wait. These aren’t your average customers. In an alternate universe, set in this year, you are surrounded by other species like vampires, werewolves and orcs.

What really stands out from the game as a true juxtaposition are the extremely human interactions, dialogue and relatable characters who aren’t human. The dialogue is really well written, with words sculpted carefully by Fahmitsu. He manages to create a well-balanced blend of pop culture references, humor and interesting scenarios without sounding forced. Not an easy feat in the world of game writing, let alone writing itself.

The graphical style is pixel art, commonly seen as an ‘ugly’ art-form. Here, it fits in as beautiful and aesthetically charming. There is just something that feels so cozy and familiar about all of this, alongside the music. The soundtrack is simply wonderful, filled with chill beats and that lo-fi feel. It really sets the mood for all the interactions in-game. In fact, it’s so good I regularly listen to the playlist outside of the game which can be found on Spotify and Youtube all thanks to the composer, Andrew Jeremy.

After playing through all the modes available – firstly the main story mode, with interludes of challenge and endless and I must say that story mode is where things shine. Of course I enjoyed creating my own ‘latte art’ without all the spills. What more could you want?

In short, this game feels like home. Uncomfortable, awkward dialogue and situations which ask for you to be creative, just like real life. This game is for those who like visual novels and story-driven games, point-and-click adventures and when you just want to curl up and relax on a rainy day or a late night, without grinding for levels.

So why not pull up a chair, grind some coffee beans instead and try the free demo? And if you like what you try, then I’m sure the full game is just your cup of tea.
