Coffe Talk may not seem like a whole lot on the surface, especially compared to VA-11 Hall-A(Valhalla), but if you take the time to get to know this relaxing yet event-filled tale, you'll find yourself immersed in a beautiful tale of unlikely souls coming together, their lives enriched by more than just the beverages they drink.

Fun fact: I've never actually been in a coffee shop before, at least not something official, like a Starbucks. The closest thing I'd say I came to one was a little social hall at NWMSU, but it never carried that kind of vibe. It's never really bothered me that I've yet to go to one; I'm not the kind of person to seek out a barista joint just to mingle. Hell, I've officially quit caffeine(bad for my health, I've abused it over the years). That being said, when I first heard about this game on Steam, I was immediately drawn to it; I'd played VA-11 Hall-A before, a bartending simulator, and despite the fact that I despise bars IRL, I absolutely LOVED that game, so I knew I'd be in for a treat with this one.

Now, I didn't expect Coffee Talk to be perfect. It isn't, but for a bartending simulator(may as well call it one, since it carries such vibes even though you never sell alcohol in it), It's pretty darn close.
Picture this: It's 2020, in Seattle(no, I'm not joking, that's the setting), except the world is a bit different in that there aren't just humans, but also fantasy races-elves, dwarves, orcs, succubi...even werewolves and vampires! The game blends these races together in a world similar to our own, where, instead of waging war on each other, these races(species?) are finding their own ways in life. Of course, life is never easy, and there are a few stressful things going on in the world, as the occasional news headlines will tell you, but there is a place one can relax-Coffee Talk, the local coffee shop open at...nighttime. It's safe to say this isn't your ordinary world, and it certainly isn't your average Starbucks, but all of this only makes the game world much more intriguing. After watching the well-made opening cinematic, I knew I was going to have fun with this one.

Story-wise, this game is a collection of smaller plotlines that interweave with each other in a clever fashion, and at certain points some characters will pop in to update their tales, then jump back out for a bit. The one  plot that is always there is that of a young, green-haired woman named Freya who is slowly but surely working on her first big novel. Even though she already provides numerous short stories to the game's newspaper, The Evening Whispers, she's ultimately hoping to get a book made of stories inspired by the many events and tales she hears in the coffee shop itself. While she doesn't get particularly invested in the other stories, I still love Freya nonetheless; she's very entertaining, she makes me laugh a lot, and the fact that she's going for a story based on the in-game coffee shop, a story about only humans no less, gives this game a bit of clever self-awareness you don't see in many others.

Another thing I love is that you, the player, get sort of a character as well! When you enter a name you choose for the save file, that name is used for the barista(formless and genderless), who interacts with the characters on his/her own perogative. Not only that, but if you play the game enough, you'll find an interesting secret about said barista, too.

Other stories in the game include Baileys the elf and Lua the succubus, a young couple in love, despite their relationship looked down upon by their families; Rachel, a nekomimi pop star looking to get her solo music career going, despite being at odds with her father Hendry, who is opposed to the idea; Jorji, a human cop that mainly gives advice to Rachel, as he is a father of three, though he has light banter with other characters; the odd yet shippable couple of Hyde and Gala, the former a vampire that seems to have an eye for the kinkier side of life, and the latter a werewolf who is not only looking for a way to control his transformation, but is also a war veteran with PTSD issues; Aqua the shy mermaid and Myrtle the stoic half-orc, a pair of ladies that come together to work on an indie project for a gaming convention; and Neil, the astronaut, or at least he looks like an astronaut, but is actually on a mission to breed with people on Earth for a special reason I'll not spoil here. As you can see, most of the characters are paired and, as such, don't always stand out as much on their own, but all the stories in this game were enjoyable in some way. Everyone gets a decent amount of screen time, and their unique personalities and looks help them add something special to the game as a whole. It does kind of stink that some characters get more time than others, but they are all memorable and loveable nonetheless.

As far as actual gameplay goes, all you really do is serve coffee when a character asks you to. They'll usually give you the ingredients necessary(although a few brew recipes are given at the start, with more added as you discover them; can you collect them all!?), but sometimes you'll have to experiment, which adds a fun bit of mystery to the game. It can be a bit frustrating when you don't get all the ingredients, and thus you may screw up an order here or there, as I did, but you aren't really penalized at all for a mistake(at least from what I can tell), so you can rest easy that you'll still have fun, mistakes and all.

Aesthetics are where the game really shines. There's no voice acting, which is fine by me, but the whole game looks positively stunning. The shop itself gives off a relaxing, calm vibe, even as you watch silhouettes walk/run back and forth in the outdoor background, a rainy nighttime city street. Each character is colorful and vibrant, eye catching, and they all have varying expressions and, as such, visibly react to certain dialogue.

On top of that, the music...just, THE MUSIC! It is 98% easygoing and relaxing(there's one or two instances where it actually picks up a bit, mainly for story purposes, but it still works), and it really fits the mood of a coffee shop very well. I've played a lot of games, and many of those titles have very good music, but I've never had the enjoyment of basking in a title where the music fits so perfectly. It's even fun to listen to OUTSIDE of the game, so feel free to look it up on youtube the next time you need to study or relax.

The only area this game really lacks in is replayability, which largely depends on whether or not you're fine with the endless mode, where you, erm, "endlessly" serve customers coffee. The main story does have a bit of replay as well; in addition to simply trying to get every single coffee order correct, beating the game once will clue you in on four different days where you're guaranteed new dialogue, which will ultimately, yet subtly, reveal the barista's true nature. Endless mode is a cool way to rack up some achievements, but I don't typically worry about achievements too much, and even then the repetitiveness of it all may not fit well with some people.

Ultimately, I'm so glad I picked up this little gem. It isn't every day I see slice-of-life storytelling in a game outside of a visual novel, but Coffee Talk definitely gets the job done. It's not quite as engaging or memorable as VA-11 Hall-A, but it still managed to keep me sucked in with its characters, stories, visuals, music, and atmosphere. This title is a must for anyone who enjoys more story-based games, or simply likes the idea of a title themed around serving coffee(and that's considering the headache it must be to be a REAL LIFE barista in our current situation). So if you're looking for a more relaxing title, give Coffee Talk a taste. It's not quite a masterpiece, but it's definitely theraputic.

																Indie Treat Raises Reviewer Affection Slightly
My ratings:
ThemeArt/GraphicsMusicGameplay8576
Overall: 7

Thematically, the game is very good, and hits a target not oft aimed at. It definitely accomplishes the task that makes this type of game enticing, which is giving you an overarching 'good' reason to perform dark and evil deeds. It tells a classic tale of hubris and consequences that is mostly lacking from the video game medium owing to its desire to constantly 'reward' players, and for that alone, if nothing else, I value this game highly. That's not to say the rest of the game is bad, however, it does sport the usual shortcomings of what it is, a budget indie title.

Theme: While the theme itself is a major draw, the game's writing suffers from a lot of hokey metafictional artefacts and, frankly, a plain and simple dearth of writing. What is there is fair-to-good and conveys the theme and its story well, but for a thematic game like this, writing is the color by which the painting that cannot be seen is created, and there needed to be more than the three colors actually used in the game's art. The stories of the townsfolk are about as long as a standard RPG dialog and, frankly, are quite mundane and irrelevant outside of the theme itself. Something like 60%+ of the writing is 'discoverable', which means that tedium further creeps its way in when one wishes to experience everything the game has to offer...more on that in my gameplay discussion.

Art: A word on the art and graphics of this game: The art is definitely not bad or awful by any stretch of the imagination, and to some degree I understand the decisions that were made, however its in a style that I'm afraid must be considered cliche and unoriginal at this point in our cultural development. The artwork itself is used exceedingly sparingly when one considers that this is a game that is all about theme. Animations are 2-4 still frames, 90% of actions are accompanied by still images. The aesthetic is dark, but cartoony and not at all threatening. There are varied attempts to make the whole game more creepy, but it's more clumsy 'boogie-woogie'ism than anything.

Music: The music, again, is thematically good, but not especially memorable. It accompanies the scenes well, but there's precious little of it also.

Gameplay: The gameplay is interesting at first, the discovery of the varied homunculi is fairly fun, and there's a lot of theme development happening during the gameplay. Sadly, the gameplay rapidly devolves into tedium; there are effectively only 26 possible homunculi (25+1 failed result type which appears to vary slightly by how it's made, but is mostly useless and doesn't matter) and the work stage of the game is boring and easily deconstructed into a whack-a-mole design. If this game were really any longer (it's a rather short game), this would be a major sticking point, as the novelty wears off rapidly. The game's end goal is known from the outset, and there's really only two layers of actual gameplay (if you don't count whack-a-mole, which I do not). The overall goal is reached through guessing-and-checking input stat values, not the best design choice.

Overall, I say the game is worth a go, but you do have to like the theme. I hope this game is the jumping off point for bigger and better things from this developer.

I've also encountered a few bugs - such as the game crashing, or character sprites disappearing, or quest triggers not working quite right. For the price, there's an almost absurd amount of replayabilty, and given all the effort the devs have put in I would have happily paid a bit more.

Rising Hell combines a bit of action / combo based combat with a rogue-lite formula that you are used to. Each subsequent playthrough will most likely give you currency to unlock new weapons and a new character as well as sharpening your skills for the next run. The combat is fast and tactile, with your moves comboing nicely from one enemy to the next. Often you have to use enemies to gain extra height as you are attacking / killing them and that can be a really neat way to progress through these stages.

At the top of each spire you'll be able to choose two locations to go to next, and let me just say, don't take the Slaughtering Spire. Just.... never ever ever go into the slaughtering spire. It's full of sadness and sawblades that chase you like the lava levels from old Nintendo games. 

You'll be able to buy upgrades to your character as you climb higher and higher as long as you are diligent about killing all of the enemies that you find along the way as well as picking up some free upgrades in the form of "Artifacts" that make your primary attack different. I am partial to the Shock Claw as hits will start zapping EVERYTHING on the screen at once for high damage. Those are always nice.

tl;dr - A neat new take on an old genre that has enough action and platforming to keep you coming back for more. Definitely a fun game from start to finish. My only grip is that unlocks can take quite some time, but if you're in it for the long haul it's no problem.

Posted: 22 September, 2020

																Some stories require a million words; others can be told without a single letter.
Looking for an emotional rollercoaster and do not want to read lots of text? Then When The Past Was Around is a game for you – it masterfully presents its message through just pictures and music while touching your very soul with its wordless beauty. If anybody ever tells you that games are not work of art, show them this title. 


	
	
		Finding a memory 
		A Screenshot of When The Past Was Around
		By: futaba-tian
		
					
	


Pros:Absolutely gorgeous artwork – each and every detail is masterfully painted with pastel colors by gentle strokes of a brush. Each picture is unique and special. Both characters are lovable from the very moment you see them. And all backgrounds are both lively and lonely, but always vivid;

Music – oh, this music! Even though there are not that many tracks and all of them follow the same tune (which is the main thread that connects all scenes), these sounds are very important for the plot and enhance it to an absolutely new level. Sweet, sad, enchanting, bitter, tragic and happy – just one tune can be all of these;

Characters – even the ones in the background are carefully drawn to look special and to support the main characters. And what about these two? Eda and the Owl became my friends while I was playing the game, and I worried about them as if there were real people. The authors created a miracle and made both of these characters believable and realistic while still keeping the mystery during the whole story;

Story – as I have mentioned above, there is a grand mystery that keeps you engaged until the very end. Who is this Owl? How is Eda connected to him? What happened before we came to this world and what will it bring? The story has several important philosophical and psychological points, so do not take it lightly;

Puzzles and interactive features – I should say, there is a really good variety of both. There was literally everything a point-and-click title could have: looking for objects, matching them with other things, moving pieces to the right place, rotating pictures, building or ruining stuff, you name it. The best part is that you can click on a lot of objects in the background and interact with them – some will just produce a sound, while others can be opened, removed or even broken. 
Cons:Some puzzles were a bit too difficult; one in particular burnt my brain and made me struggle with it for over an hour (I will tell more about it a bit later);

Quite short – just about 3 hours;

If you quit the scene, you will have to start from the very beginning of it and not where you stopped before.
 
 Currently, there are two bugs accroding to the user feedback: 1) sometimes you cannot change screen resolution properly in the settings. There is a guide that helps to solve this problem: 
	
	
		Resolution fix 
		A Guide for When The Past Was Around
		By: Zyryanoff
		
			Few players have reported that after interacting with options, like switching the game language, their resolution stucked at some uncomfortable value and can't be changed forcing them to play with compressed screen.		
	
 2) the screen can expand randomly in different chapters and lock you from moving anywhere. I had this problem too at one point, but did not even know it was a bug before I saw other people complaining about it. This issue can be solved by restarting the chapter.

	
	
		Music and Nature 
		A Screenshot of When The Past Was Around
		By: futaba-tian
		
					
	


Some random thoughts
To begin with, I cannot but complement the developers that created this little gem. It is just SO beautiful in every aspect! The artwork is magnificent, and it was obvious just from the screenshots. In the game itself, all pictures look even better. I love this kind of art style – with lots of neat details, calm colors and a bit fairy-tale-like. 

Music is also enchanting, and all UI features have their own violin sounds. As I have already mentioned above, there is one tune that is the main connecting point for all parts of the story, and trust me, it will touch your heart the very moment you hear it.

What else…ah, right! The point-and-click parts. It is definitely not a hidden-objects game, even though yes, you will need to search for some items. And yes, you do have an inventory. But still, there are no outlines of the objects that you need to find, nor any words that tell you what you need. So, compared to classical examples of the genre – such as many games by bigfish or Artifex Mundi, - I would say that Then When The Past Was Around is definitely a point-and-click title. This part aside, there are enough interactive features to keep you entertained through the whole story.

Speaking of the puzzles, all of them are really interesting, even though several still confused me. My main advice here is to look for clues. Some are well-hidden and require major brain work, while others are in the open sight or will come in later. So try to be as be attentive as possible, it is worth it.

Oh, by the way, as a good example of why rushing through this game is a bad idea, let me tell you the epic tale of my grandiose stupidity. There was a puzzle with numbers that you need to find somewhere. I immediately noticed several leads and started cracking them. Combination after combination, I began doubting both myself and the game: is it broken? Is there some kind of glitch? Why is not it working?! An hour later, I gave up and brought my mother into the fight. We both searched for clues, tried mixing numbers and just everything possible, but once again nothing worked. ‘OK’, I said and started bugging two of my close friends. They also decided to join my epic battle with the puzzle and offered their own suggestions. 

An hour and a half have passed…I was almost ready to just close the game and leave it before I decided to throw my laptop out of the window. And then, finally, it hit me! The solution was in front of me the whole damn time – and I just decided to overlook it. It was so simple, and yet I spent 90 minutes chasing an absolutely different thing. Well, my friends and mum definitely had a good laugh at my expense when I told them what I was doing wrong. And so did I, to be honest, because my mistake was hilarious. So, boys, girls and young individuals, do not repeat my mistake! 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2236051827

Would I recommend the game?
In the end, the only thing I can say is do not think twice: buy this masterpiece right away. And then spend a bit more money and purchase the artbook and the soundtrack too. When The Past Was Around is worth every coin and minute you spend on it, and its touching story will leave you craving for more. The best part is that it is both inspiring and mysterious until the very end - it leaves some unanswered questions, but does not feel unfinished; instead, this game lets your imagination run free. And it is amazing.

For starters, there are a decent number of relics (items that effect everything, usually based on some criteria) that give you some strong boosts if you have fielded less than 6 units. Then half the game is spent playing against enemies who get to make a card in your hand useless every few seconds if you have less than 10 (will be lowing to 6 according to the roadmap) units on the field. Do you want to try and field a small but strong elite army if the relics line up right? Good luck when you have to wait for mana to regen and by that point there is a solid chance that your card gets 'silenced'. Silenced isnt just some minor condition that can be fixed, its a card in your hand that now CANT DO ANYTHING. The only way to get rid of it is to redraw your hand, which can cost from free (if you wait long enough and are playing the toy maker) to 40 mana (of which you only get 100 from the base hero). 

Then there are all the enemy relics that trigger when you either play a spell or a utility. It is usually some small thing that can be mitigated (like spawning a few units from places on the map that can be defeated), but then in the third area any time you play a spell you are either getting a card silenced, or a random card (quite possibly the card that you are waiting for the right time/mana to play) gets discarded. This might not be so bad if the spells/utilities didnt also appear to be a valid deck strategy until you come to this section. There are a decent number of spells/utilities that boost your units in hand and or on the field.

At first I thought that seeing the enemy relics was kinda cool because they could vary up the games between boss battles, then I quickly realized that they only came in two flavors. 

1. meaningless relics that are just there because your 2 floors in and the basic enemy units really dont have enough hp/armor/attack to threaten your units without +150% attack/armor/hp. 
Just make their base HP/Armor/Attack high enough so that the base units (which change every floor, and so their base attributes should be based on that) that your facing are correct for that area. Then add those into the random pool of things that can change. +25% attack means FAR more when its rare and its not boosting a unit whos base attack seems to be close to 1.

2. Relics that are meant to punish a specific play style. 
Already touched on this, but when an entire floor seems to get a silence when spell cards are played, or discard when utilities are played, or silence a card if you dont spam cheap units to get above the arbitrary number of units. Really punishes decks that are made around that style of play. Make those RARE modifiers and unchain them from those floors so that yes, you can get a game where every other card gets silenced because your deck is mostly spells, but it wont happen so often that it feels like your being punished because your not playing the game how it was intended but you werent told about.

I cant really recommend this game because it appears to have been designed for a very specific play style and punishes any other style of play.

																This game is visual novel meets "Cook, Serve, Delicious-lite". 

You are a coffee shop owner, striving to make your customers happy, and improve their lives, one warm drink at a time. Get their orders right, to help them get a good ending. And in the process, you just might find out more about yourself.

Story
Surprisingly compelling, though some characters are definitely get far more interesting story lines and more satisfactory "good" endings than others. Even if you have a perfect playthrough, there is some content that you won't see on an initial play. But, you can easily skip through already seen text to catch the missed bits on a second round. 

The game has some well done fourth-wall-breaking moments.

Music & Sound Effects 
The lo-fi music is really relaxing to play to, making an already casual, chill game even moreso. 

In terms of sound effects, there really wasn't much in the way of variety; mostly drinking sounds and the bell at the door to indicate people coming and going. Phones occasionally "buzz" (which will also vibrate your controller if you have that enabled).

Game play
Most of the game is, like a visual novel, a lot of reading of text. The real "play" comes into whether you get the drinks right. For some, they'll give you the full ingredient list. For others, you need to intuit what to do. Note: The order that you add the ingredients in can have an impact on the outcome.  The Free play mode is good for trying to play test and figure out mixes. Other than that, you get 5 chances to make a drink before having to hand over what you've made. Once you've discovered a recipe, it goes into your notebook (which carries over if you start a new game on the same save). 

Overall
I definitely recommend Coffee Talk to people who enjoy casual visual novels that don't necessarily have a dating sim component.

Posted: March 23, 2020
																Please note this is an early review, I will add more detail as I play more hours. Also, I was a Kickstarter backer of this game. 

 1. Why I bought this game 
 1.1 The Combat Ring 
I saw this game as a spiritual successor of Shadow Hearts, which I played I, II and III, a turn-based rpg. Shadow Hearts was the first game I ever saw a ring being displayed at the moment of attacking, where you have to press the correct button of a spinning ring in your controller at the right time. 

This transfers the rng of critical hits to you, the player, rather than to dice rolls. Hit 3 pie slices in size of the ring for a good hit, a much smaller portion for the critical hit, or miss it for a poor hit. The idea also applies to defense, where a "critical defense" makes you immune. If you dislike this, the game lets you disable it too, but I'd say you're missing part of the fun. 

 1.2 The storyline (No Spoilers) 
Shadow Hearts also had an unconventional take to storyline and characters' background and motivations. You never know what to expect. The theme was also overall darker and more gruesome. Not your cheesy fantasy average game. At least in the first 3 hours of Legrand Legacy, you will also get to experience that. There will be blood and death. 

 2. Combat and Other Misc Features 
On Kickstarter, the devs behind Semisoft made it clear they wanted to bring into a game mechanics they appreciated in another game. From this standpoint, I can think of no other company to compare than Tokyo RPG Factory, the folks behind "I am Setsuna", "Lost Sphear", and "Oninaki". Lost Sphear, in particular often being referred to like a game where "tried too many mechanics, but ended up superficially handling all of them". Likewise, the map exploration of both I am Setsuna and Lost Sphear is a clear love letter to Chrono Trigger. 

When you approach Legrand Legacy, you have to keep in mind Semisoft had a similar vision. They wanted to borrow aspects of previous games much like Tokyo RPG Factory and try to bring them together. 

 2.1 Graphics     PS2 Era Style
    Unique: Character dialogue has "live" features. Eyes, face, facing direction all are live as the dialogue unfolds. 
    Painted background map (make sure to set settings too high quality or it will look horrifying!)
 2.2 Combat     Combat Ring from Shadow Hearts
    Elemental Weaknesses (FF, etc), Physical Weakness, Type of Enemy Weakness 
    Grid Positioning in Combat (Just Front and Back ). +dmg, +defense, need to kill front enemies first if not ranged.
    Map Hazard (reminds me of FF8 Ifrit Lair)
 2.3 Soundtrack      So far so good, but they went the extra mile to even get a song from the same singer of Nier Automata (see a trailer here on Steam of characters artwork). 
In addition to that, the game explains the lore as you go. You would hope this to be granted, but consider games like Final Fantasy 13 and it's a constant need to data log and you will see what I mean.

Again, this is a first-hour impression of the game. I Will update after a few more hours in.

 3. Not so Great Stuff 
     The font for debuffs/buffs is awful. It's small, blends with the background and nearly impossible to see. Thankfully you can inspect the mob in every turn to see if the debuff applied or not.
    You can't buy gear. You must use materials that drop from mobs. What's worse is that there is no log that tracks who drops what. You have to do it yourself based on the loot of each encounter. You can also craft items at a cheaper price with loot, but the game also let's you buy them (two different NPCs). However, same "who drops what" problem. 
    Currency can only be obtained by selling loot. That is fine, save the fact you really are gambling on what you sell: You don't know if the item won't be needed later, forcing you to grind for an item you have to manually keep tabs on who dropped it. 
    The "limit break" is really broken. Normal attack: 3% damage. Limit break: 48% damage of mini boss. Add to the fact you can store it from other fights until the boss and blast everything in one go, and you can cheese quite a bit the fights.

																Nusakana is an entirely non-linear and pretty much open world RPG with an insanely good bossa nova-ish soundtrack, made completely with custom assets and with tons of content & replay value, all in an extremely ambitious RPG Maker project that looks nothing like you'd expect out of a RPG Maker game. In this game, our silent protagonist finds himself in the exotic island of Nusakana for a year long vacation, where he connects with the peculiar culture of its inhabitants, encounters all kinds of bizarre creatures and beings and discovers the mysteries of the island with the help of a load of different cute fish girls.

Gameplay: Nusakana can be very unforgiving and slow paced at first, at least on the classic difficulty (aka the "way the game is meant to be experienced" difficulty). The game is built almost completely around time management, and its importance is made very obvious at the very beginning of the game where you must decide on whether you want to explore the island (which is overwhelming enough at first and then becomes even larger once new time-gated areas open up), take part in time-consuming events scattered around or build up money to keep yourself supplied with items and stronger equipment (the weapon system where you have unique skills for the different weapon categories is really cool in particular) through hunting, fishing and gathering quests. The enemies in the harder but more rewarding hunting quests can be brutal, and as such, require preparation (you'll definitely want to find some partners as soon as possible) and also some consideration as you'll end up losing time and/or resources as you search for the right creature only to end up being vastly underpowered. The turn-based combat system is very quick and fun to go through, especially once you get two or three partners with all sorts of unique abilities, passive or active, to make combat even more varied.  The animated portraits of your character and your primary party member during battles is a really nice touch too and makes them a bit more lively and fun to look at (just look at the way Kat sits on your head or Mica stands on your shoulders!). The protagonist doesn't start with any skills until relatively later on, and as such, combat isn't very engaging at the start especially due to the aforementioned difficulty. There's also a fishing mini-game that is integral for certain quests and events, but you can ignore it elsewhere if you don't find it fun, like me.

Eventually the time management becomes less harsh once you find optional skills for your partners that lets them control weather (allowing you to take on weather-specific events freely and with ease, unlike a certain quest early on involving a thunderstorm) and you won't need to take on hunting quests after amassing enough money, letting you enjoy a bit more freedom. About the time limit of one year of in-game time, you don't have to worry about it at all, as you have tons of time to relax and enjoy the game as much as you want. For reference, I finished the game with three or so months of in-game time after 70 hours of gameplay, and it will surely take you way more than that in multiple playthroughs to see all content and/or get all achievements.

Story/writing: Being a completely non-linear game, the story also follows the same kind of logic and is mostly left for the player to piece together except for the final stretch/climax. While it all seems simple at first, the stakes are significantly raised later on as the mysteries surrounding the island are uncovered and everything goes into a much deeper direction than you'd expect. Character-wise, the writing for the 19 or so potential party members (or more appropriately, friends) is spectacular. No matter how generic and archetypal they might seem initially, it's impossible to not like any of them once you get to know them better through their events or quests. Some of their interactions with the protagonist feel very personal too and after enough time spent together you can even pick your favorite girl to marry, each one with their unique epilogue scenes. The different characters all have optional events you can find where they interact with each other in all manners of ways, giving some extra depth to them.

Music: Combining jazz and bossa nova, the soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal and of extremely high quality, solidifying the tropical and exotic feel the game wants to convey.

Technicalities: There are some technical negatives to be found, some of them existing only thanks to the RPG Maker engine itself as far as I know. Summing them up: The game's native resolution is too low, forcing huge letterboxes on all sides in fullscreen; Similarly, screenshots taken are of very low quality and resolution and the game might crash when taking a screenshot in fullscreen; There are more typos than you'd expect and some weirdly flowing dialog at times (some of it is endearing though) but I feel like most of them got fixed throughout the years as past reviews make it seem like they were much worse. All in all, I'd say none of those issues are serious or *too* annoying, and it's worth sitting through them even if it takes some patience. I also want to point out that an issue that caused tons of lag in certain areas like the sea fishing zones seemingly got fixed since the last time I played, which is really nice.

In conclusion, Nusakana is a stellar experience and a true hidden gem that deserves love from anyone who enjoys unique (J)RPGs, interesting settings or cute girls in spades or any possible combination of those. Definitely get it, even if not on sale, as this game is absolutely worth your time and money. If you can get past the initial slow and harsh pace, this game will become an experience that will stick with you.

																LEGRAND LEGACY: Tales of the Fatebounds is a wasted potential, but overall still comes out as decent and enjoyable experience made by developers who listen to the community.

RATING:  6/10. 
I'll start off with what I dislike:
 Sub-par narrative. - WARNING spoiler potential 
The game started off nicely. Party members were interesting with their own distinct personalities, backgrounds, and personal issues. Along the way, they found themselves in disagreements, having trust issues, while they needed to face trials to test their "worth". With this scenario, you would expect each character to have a personal development throughout the game, right? BUT THE GAME SAYS HELL NO. You are going to see this pattern very often: At first, let's be friends! -> A moment later, ??? you I don't trust you! -> And then a moment later, I'm sorry I didn't mean to hurt your feelings, my bad -> aaand a moment later, ??? you all I'm done with this ????!. Some party member have either bipolar disorder, or they are just a bunch of idiots who do not learn from their mistakes.
Bad ending - non spoiler
After the narrative and some characters tortured me for hours, the ending finally executed me and my controller. It tried to be that "philosophical" bittersweet ending with "deep meaning", but it just didn't deliver nor it was rewarding. It left me with this kind of "Uh, what? Seriously? That's it?" feeling. 
Horrible level design - non spoiler
The most noticable flaw and it can totally ruin your experience. There is no random battle. You need to engage your enemy from behind to ambush them and receive a free turn, OR accidentally get ambushed by enemies thanks to: awkward camera angle, small collider/enemy hit detection, quick-sudden enemy movement, and your slower movement. Good luck fighting enemies in this game while getting ambushed. More often than not, you can expect yourself to reload your save file after that fight. 
Unintuitive inventory & storage UI - non spoiler
Inventory system automatically "expands" when you have so many types of items. You can either scroll up or scroll down on that 1 big page to access different parts of your inventory. The issue is, when your bag is filled with tons of different items, and you transfer 1 page worth of those items to storage, somehow the system does not automatically scroll up to show me the "next page" of items I am supposed to see. 
Poor animation quality - non spoiler
This may not detract the experience for other players as much as it did to mine, so players may ignore this part if they want. I am aware this is an indie title made with tight budget, but I still want to give my criticisms as my support for the devs for their next project. In short, animations are floaty, characters have poor posing, with lack of understanding how a body moves in general.      
Poor graphics quality - non spoiler
Same as above. May not detract the experience for other players but it does bother me. Graphics has lack of cohesion. This means character models do not blend with background, UI doesn't blend with background, and characters' shadows are poor. Maybe it's a good idea to add some post-processing? Or if the game already has it, then please improve it. This is a quick tweak that should make the graphics overall look better significantly. 
What I like:
Tactical, intense, challenging turn-based combat
Combat involves QTE where you are required to press certain button at the right time in order to get good or perfect results. This system makes me truly focused on each fight and prevents me to mash the attack button. But what makes the combat feels tactical and challenging is the combination of brutal enemy design, different types of attacks (impact, slash, pierce, elemental attacks, and debuff magic that works against boss!), item management (each character is only allowed to carry 4 different items during combat), as well as both of your positioning and enemy positioning. 
Tons of side contents
Tactical tabletop combat, fencing/1v1 dueling, archery mini game, gladiatorial mini game, fishing mini game, shopping mini game. These features are not available since the beginning, however. So go find out yourself. 
Good soundtrack

																This is more of a first impressions than an actual review.

So.
2+ hours in so far, and I have to say that I'm enjoying myself MUCH more than the first few hours of the first game. The slightly bigger budget the devs must have gotten definitely shows in a lot of areas.

First couple things I noticed right off the bat are the obviously improved character models for (most) characters. The main character looks great, although she must have started wearing a bra since the events of the first game as the jiggle physics have either been removed or forgotten (they will be missed lol).

NPC models on the other hand... Hoo boy.. They run the gamut from actually really good, to "how did they manage to port PS1 models into UE4??"

The animations are a mixed bag. Walking around looks and feels MUCH better than the first, but cutscene and in-game animations definitely look rough, and have an almost amateur SFM look to them. Very obviously hand-made, but they do the job as well as they can, and you kinda stop noticing after a while.

The environments are definitely a step up from the first. The original game had a very "Inspired by Fatal Frame" feel, while this one has a more "We REALLY enjoyed the first Evil Within" style. Not that either of those are a bad thing at all mind you.

The one place the low indie budget definitely shows is in the voice acting (or should I say; lack thereof). Most of the character interactions are done with subtitles while making "oohs" and "ahs" and strange grunts in the background. But then there's a few fully voiced characters intermingled, and some characters speak without making ANY noises.. and.. it's just a bit messy in my opinion.

Gameplay is both improved, and also feels like a step back in some ways. The series continues it's tradition of simultaneously giving you a lot, but also next to no information of what to do or where to go at any given time. I get it, this is a survival horror game and shouldn't hold your hand. BUT, I also shouldn't have to resort to looking through the control mapping menu to figure out how to do basic things. There's no feedback when it comes to performing certain actions, and sometimes the game doesn't even register a camera attack when it very obviously should have landed etc. Enemies that you need to photograph can stun lock you if you're not careful. Physical enemies you need to melee can not only do the same, but can also get stuck inside your character, or trap you against a wall while you watch helplessly as Linda dies yet again due to circumstances outside your control.

The "open world" hub area seems nice on paper, but in game it seems superfluous and unnecessarily large, with really nothing to do or see in it. I don't want to jump to any conclusions since I haven't beaten the game yet, so I won't hold it against the game as a negative right now.

There's a myriad of technical issues and questionable design choices on display, such as enemies getting stuck trying to open doors (same with the player character now that I think about it). Absolutely ridiculous "blocked" paths usually with a small plank of wood and a tipped over chair keeping you out of a certain area. No visual indicator in the first person camera mode as to where a ghost in in relation to the player, something Fatal Frame solved a decade ago. The "sprint" is a joke, and amounts to about 1 1/2 seconds of a minor speed boost. I could go on, but I won't.

It may seem like I really dislike this game, but that couldn't be further from the truth. I've been loving the atmosphere and most of the gameplay so far. This is more constructive criticism, than me trying to sh*t on the devs. I know they had a small budget and team to work with, and what they've managed to release is very impressive so far.

Hopefully with some patches and a bit of elbow grease, this game will be up there in the ranks of hidden gems/cult classic horror games. I wish the devs all the best, and really hope they turn a profit so we can maybe one day see a Dreadout 3, or something else from this team.

																A surprisingly good game.

While this may seem like your typical RPG Maker title it has so much polish done you barley notice it.  As the store description says you play as a 'tourist' on a tropical like island.  The game is a mix of JRPG and sim dating, in a sort of modern themed setting.

People that have played a JRPG before will feel at home.  Enemy's can be seen on the 'world map' and can be evaded by redirecting your character.  Battles are fought in a traditional turn base system.  You are only allowed to field 1 additional companion in battle but you can have up to 2 extra for support.

The artwork is simple, but nice and consistent.  The battlers for the player and companions are actually animated which shows a real commitment to break out of the RPG Maker mold.  The developers definitely put a fair amount of their own artwork into this game which gives it a unique feel.

Music is another selling point for this game.  It has an indie folk feeling to it which meshes well with the setting and narrative.

The gameplay is a mixed bag and kind of where things go a bit off the rails.  I'll break this down into a few bullet points:

-Survival mechanics: while not bad in it of itself it kind of feels out of place for a game that is focused on relaxation in its theme.

-Time constraints: the game has a time limit and managing time can be very brutal for a new player that doesn't know the lay of the land.  The mechanics that progress time can be aggravating depending where you have to travel.

-Severe punishment for loosing a battle:  again, not a bad mechanic in itself but conflicts with the laid back nature this game is trying to convey

-Factions and bounty system:  there are multiple factions in this game and completing RNG quest can give you money and reputation.  The main issue with this system is it's very RNG based and you will often be presented with a quest that will want you to access an area that is way beyond your character level.  Also if the quest is late, you are docked payment.  As I said previously, this conflicts with the laid back nature the theme is trying to convey.

None of these mechanics are bad, they just don't feel like they belong in a game with this kind theme.  So if you intend to chill on a peaceful tropical island while fishing and chasing fish themed wifus, this game is not going to let you do that.....  Unless you play on easy mode.

The relationship mechanics are kind of straight forward, having gifting and talking to gain points with X per day limits.  You can also gain or loose relationship points with active party members depending if you release or keep the fish you catch.

I kind of have mixed feeling about how relationships are handled in this game.  Like in many sim date type games you are only allowed to 'marry' one at the end.  For some game types, like simulation this isn't that big of a deal as gamplay is varied enough, has sufficient story derivatives  and is generally geared to multiple play-throughs to warrant spending the time to unlock most/all endings.  I really like Nusakana but I don't think I have the gusto to do a 3ed play-through.  This is one of those stories that I feel would really benefit from a harem ending or at lest make the ending modular to include the routs you unlocked.

The fishing mini game is kind of clunky and un-intuitive, but is sort of a given considering the engine they are using.

The story is nice and very 'folk tale' leaning in its overall theme.  Some of the NPC's talk in an intentional engrish fashion to sell the point that you are on a foreign island.  However the engrish is unintentional at times as the developers are not native English speakers.  This can lead to confusion on what to do next as the editing isn't all that great.

So is this game worth it?  YES!  Despite its rough edges this game is filled with charm and is well worth it!

																Nusakana is a prime example of the perfect utilization of RPGMaker. Although it’s definitely not your atypical RPG it’s a refreshing take on the genre that offers a lot to those who give it an opportunity.  The game incorporates the traditional components of a JRPG in RPGMaker style but it also features critical components of an adventure and romance game as well. Some have already compared it to Pokemon meets Harvest Moon and in many ways I would have to agree that that is probably the best way to describe the game. I thought that Studio Namaapa really worked hard to make a cohesive art and audio style befitting of the game. My favorite aspect of the game was the level of freedom that it offers. Too many RPGMaker games feel locked in – the game designer expects you to do certain things in a certain order and don’t offer much leeway. Instead, Nusakana allows you to explore, adventure and hunt at your leisure. Thankfully the world is of a significant size giving you a lot of areas to explore.

If there were flaws in the game it’s that the English translation isn’t the highest quality. Those of you playing from countries where English is a second language will not have an issue playing but it could have been worked on and perfected a lot more than what it is. It’s also arguable that although the developers did a great job in creating an open world in a RPGMaker game that perhaps a better level of concentration in developing the story would have been wise. Don’t get me wrong I enjoyed the open nature of the game immensely but it felt that the main story was missing a lot of what was perhaps initially intended.

In all, I understand the negative reviews on Steam although I myself would place myself into the significantly higher percentage of people who enjoyed the game. Nusakana can be recommended for those who enjoy rock solid RPGMaker games and JRPGs. There’s more than enough content in the game to be discovered for it to be a good purchase.

Besides sound effects, it has also licensed two soundtracks by “fleurishana” which really add to the personality of the game. It also includes beautiful collectable artwork by various artists as an additional perk in the story.


Conclusion
Insurgence Chains of Renegade definitely gets the thumbs up from me. It is not the most complex game you will find, it is a simple and classic RPG. Platonic has stuck to the basics and done it right. It will be enjoyable for anyone needing a nostalgic RPG experience.

Rising Hell is a vertical Rogue-like platformer, where players control an unstoppable force ready to slain all sorts of demons into pixelated blood!

Gameplay is the high focus of Rising Helll, delivering an arcadish spirit where your fortune balances between your own skill and items that are randomly placed. Players ascend vertically defeating several types of enemies, which, the higher one goes, the difficulty they’ll become. Foes drop items such as vitality and special weapons, but sometimes relics too. These artifacts allow players to purchase new skills.

At each round, it’s possible to use one special skill, and they very from improved running and jumping, or to extend your base damage. Unfortunately, it’s only possible to take one special ability and I personally felt three of them would be a much better choice. After a while skills become really good and it’s a shame only one at a time can be selected.

At every New Game the dungeon-like climbing starts over, but midway through the challenge there are vendors who are ready to sell some temporary boosts, or even sacrifice a percentage of your life for new weapons. It’s a nice change, but after awhile the offers become repetitive.

Not only there are creatures waiting to devour you, but traps and obstacles may end up with your efforts. Some levels even offer a Bonus Location, these are perfect to farm orbs or at least increase the chances of finding a special weapon. Bosses provide a fantastic challenge with well done attack patterns, and at the same time, perfect to overpass them at a much higher level.

Although the game advertises multiple unlockable characters, at this current moment, only two are available. The gameplay is pretty fluid, with the protagonist using his hand as main weapon. The most noticeable feature is the ability to attack an enemy and leash on it. This opens the possibility to climb your way by just going from one target to another.

The visual hell portrayed in the game varies from what location you choose to go. Different areas change in color and level structure, but in the end they change more mechanically than in its pixel design. The color contrast within the deep caverns, mixed with the bright flames of the demonic beings for sure grants some amazing views! Rising Hell level design will clearly please those who decide to climb patiently and take one enemy at a time.

Those who are ambitious enough to conquer Hell, there’s two modes for it: Campaign and Challenge, each with goals and rewards. If aiming for the maximum, it’s recommended to choose a soundtrack of your taste. Not that the present music is bad, but will eventually become repetitive.

Overall Rising Hell is a great bet for a different platform, setting the challenge vertically, but still offering solid content and plenty of in-game hours. Definitely recommended for those of you who enjoy the concept.

Gameplay-wise, the game is very similar to Clash Royale in the sense that you'll be playing your cards in real-time as the mana bar below is constantly being refilled. Your opponent will do the same. Units will automatically follow the path, much like a creep does in a MOBA, but in this game, you'll get to switch the signposts to direct your units onto the path you want. There are also more "structures" you can and should destroy (usually) along each path as opposed to having only the final castle at the end of the path like in Clash Royale. In some ways, these structures are like the towers in a MOBA game but if you do manage to destroy them, you'll get a nice mana regen boost.

For me, the game is very addictive and fun at the beginning, though I guess some people might feel like the game's too easy at that point. I've managed to get to Sector 3 on my first run, which is a personal best. I only lost Sector 3 mainly because my deck is spell-heavy and I was severely penalized for that. 

However, after that first run, my character leveled up to level 4, and unlocked a deck and some new cards which I don't get access to from the get-go. This is where the balancing of the game became an issue. The AI has some insane relics that gave them massive boosts while I'm still playing like I'm in level 1. I felt that I was severely handicapped and I wouldn't be wrong. 

Pros+ Really challenging, yet addictive and fun, gameplay after your first defeat. Before, my character is still level 1 and the battles seem rather easy... not that I'm complaining :P
+ Short sessions per sector - around the same amount of time needed to finish a MOBA match.
+ 3 unique characters with very different playstyles and decks
+ Nice progression system where you'll get to unlock (and only unlock) more powerful cards or new starter decks the more your hero levels up. 
+ Mobile-like graphics that look good here. I actually quite like the card art and the game map as well! 
+ Some randomization which makes every playthrough with the same character slightly different. 

Cons/Feedback- Glitches - enemies getting stuck; cards that don't do as stated (the archers; I had both versions - an upgraded one with longer range and one with normal range. I sent them out at almost the same time, but they both stood in the same position when they fire projectiles at the enemy)
- The game seems to push you towards building a well-rounded deck. Lean towards any one side and the game will penalize you heavily, eventually. 
- Leveling up a character seems to penalize the player somehow. Enemies end up starting off with much stronger units and insane buffs while I don't.
- Balancing is a major issue here. I've encountered games where the AI has insane relics that basically forced me to play my deck the way it's NOT supposed to be played, while I can do NOTHING to hamstring my opponent.
- Game froze for a bit in my third stream. I thought the game crashed.
- The game isn't in early access but it has many issues that are often associated with a game being in early access. To put it simply, Necronator: Dead Wrong isn't ready for release.

OverallAt the moment, I would not recommend buying Necronator: Dead Wrong unless it is on a steep discount. The game still needs a lot of work and it just feels like the game was forced out of the womb before it's ready. However, if you've seen the gameplay in action and loved every moment of it, then I would definitely recommend wishlisting it and checking in now and then. There's something really special here and the game does have lots of potential; it's just that the game is marred by, mainly, balancing issues and glitches, which I hope would be fixed some time soon.

								A rough diamond; vibrant beauty hidden beneath an unpolished edge.

If I had to describe Necronator: Dead Wrong (at it's current day two stage) with a single sentence, that would be it.

The game has a certain alluring charm to it. The artstyle and graphic design (somehow they found beauty in conflicting elements), for one. Or the innovative mixture of reverse-tower-defence and card games. It is also, at it's very core, just fun. It has the "thing" all the flash games you might have played as a kid had. And I mean that in the good way. It's a simple "pick it up and have fun" game.

However, as of now it's really... Small? It needs to grow and evolve.

Current typical early access problems:

- Balancing. Second deck sucks.
- Just not enough content. Needs more units, more spells, more everything. But speaking off, I really like the dynamic upgrade system. It's a smart and elegant bandaid, the randomness and variety makes it feel like there are more cards that there actually are.
- The UI is suffering from the typical "early development rough edges". Why oh why is there no button to re-orient the in-combat map? Why do I have to *drag* around *RIGHT* click to rotate? That feels like something a mobile game would have, just give me a button pretty please, I like buttons.
- There are many minor bugs. Some cards just stop working after getting upgraded. Sometimes things happen and you just don't know why
- There is no way to display unit information once they are in the fray, besides their tiny healthbars. It'd be nice to be able to mouse over units and get a nice "tactical" info popup.

However, I believe these problems will be handled competently. I can't state this enough, but Necronator is clearly a labor of love. And that is exactly what I like in Indie games.

I love Princess Maker games, and I really wished that the series hadn't gone dead! I can't believe it's not a daughter raising simulator...! Thanks for the recommendation, Steam.

And who made this game...? Namaapa? That's an Indonesian game studio, it's from my own country! How is this even possible?! A match made in heaven! I didn't expect anyone would ever want to make another game similar to Princess Maker in US, let alone my country... So this is how Indonesian Princess Maker looks like.... Unbelievable. I'm gonna cry in happiness.... My life is complete now.

Ciel Maker: Princess Fledge
Wow. Okay. Now, let's see how the game turned out to be.

So, yeah, it's a Princess Maker game where you get to... well... raise your daughter, and then just do whatever you can do for your daughter to be good. Simple as that! Maybe....

Here's a twist: You're in the future! And it turns out our future looks just as boring as the present (can anyone with a time machine confirm this?). What a pathetic future. You also have this nice fighting minigame mechanics. Eh, the minigame is mediocre, the game would go off fine without the fighting minigame. Lastly, she looks just as cute as the other daughter from the Princess Maker series!

Since this is a simulation game (it's in their name!), it's supposed to be judged based on the accuracy of the simulation. Let's go.

It turns out, it's not that realistic. Truth to be told, Princess Maker 5 is still more realistic than this game. Your daughter (by default, named "Ciel") simply follows whatever schedule you make, just like in the older Princess Maker 2. The game does have completely different mechanics than Princess Maker 2, though. I'll give credits for that. Looking at their kickstarter page, it's explicitly stated that they wanted the game to be like Princess Maker 2. But still, the game is literally named "A Daughter Raising Simulator," so it should be a realistic simulation!

What about the story? The story is good if you don't mind the lore. I'd say the story is on par with present day life, except all the things from the present is now ancient. They didn't think much about the lore. There's many unexplained things (e.g. future with present technologies, non-existent water source, etc.).

To sum it all up, this game is not great, just good. I like realistic and advanced simulations, and this game didn't deliver up to my standards. I love every "daughter raising simulation" games, but this game is not that good. I guess I'll give a thumbs up because it's just a nice game with nice character arts.

So, uh, if you really like Princess Maker, buy this. If you don't know anything about Princess Maker, it's up to you whether you want it or not.

																TL;DR:

Better in almost every way compared to the first DreadOut, massive improvement overall (graphics, character design, story, gameplay fluidity, etc). We're seeing a side of Linda that's never shown before in addition to a new melee gameplay mechanic, which makes the game feel fresh. Overall a huge step up from the first game. One thing I'd like to see improved is the storytelling, it's still quite confusing especially towards the end. The major bugs are mostly patched as of version 1.1.0.

I'm recommending the game for those of you who want to try out a different horror experience / want to see a continuation of the first DreadOut and dive deeper into Indonesian horror. If you're into reading, my full thoughts are below.

----------

The first version (1.0.0) had plenty of bugs, but I didn't have the time to finish the game before the 1.0.1 update. At the time of writing, It's been a little over a week since release and we've received two major updates (currently on 1.1.0). It's great to know that the devs are actively working on improving the gameplay, squashing the bugs, even listening to user feedback and tweaked the boss fight behaviors. The final boss is still quite insane tho, and some still quite OP.

The melee gameplay mechanic is interesting, although I feel like the first game (and Keepers of the Dark) has more variation and cool ideas with the boss fights since you need to get creative with only a camera as your weapon. The storytelling in the last two acts could be improved because it's still confusing to figure out what's happening, English subtitles can be improved (there's quite a lot of grammatical errors), low-poly character models with nonexistent animation in some areas can be improved, support for other languages would be nice (I'm assuming it's being worked on).

Just about everything that you know and love from the first DreadOut is present in DreadOut 2, in addition to the charge-shot if you hold the shutter button and melee battles. The red and blue vignette is replaced by a bracelet, which is not as convenient as the vignette in terms of alerting the players if an enemy or item is nearby, but it works. It's got a more intense roller coaster of atmosphere compared to the first game. Sometimes it's cheery, silly, and funny, most other times it's dark, excitingly scary, and it just makes you feel anxious. That's another good thing about this game: it's not something that tries so hard to be scary all the time. Despite all the bugs in version 1.0.0 & 1.0.1 and sometimes quirky gameplay mechanics, I really enjoyed playing DreadOut 2. 

Many might compare this to Fatal Frame or Silent Hill. But while this is certainly like an homage to them, DreadOut 2 is NOT those games. It's a thing of its own which has its own gameplay rules and mechanics, whether you like it or not. The core gameplay of the DreadOut universe has always revolved around introducing people to the lore that exists in Indonesia through Linda's adventure, with her abilities to channel her powers through a medium (in this case a smartphone). The lore is what sets it apart from any other games, with both DreadOut and DreadOust 2 doing a pretty good job at that. You just can't compare this to other games, especially those done by non-indie developers. I can be hypercritical and nitpick about every little details in the game and it certainly has its flaws, but you just have to remember that DreadOut 2 is made and maintained by a very small team of devs. Thinking what they're able to pull off when you have that in mind is quite something.

I'm left with a void after finishing DreadOut 2, which is a sign that the game does a good job at making you attached to the characters (or in this case just the main character, Linda). If you can't tell already, I've been a fan since the first DreadOut and am plenty happy to see a continuation of Linda's journey. I'm hoping to see more of her, hopefully another continuation (Dr3adout, maybe? And Dre4dOut for the 4th game? Seriously, the title is awfully convenient for numerical releases). The ending tho, raises so many questions and I feel like I'm not all that satisfied with it, as if it's set up for a sequel. I'm hoping that's the case, fingers crossed, otherwise I'd just feel like crying in the corner wondering what happens to Linda after the final battle. No worries, I'll wait, please don't rush because this one does feel a bit rushed.

I'm recommending this game overall.

----------

To the devs at Digital Happiness: if you're reading this, keep doing what you're doing, and most importantly, keep improving. I'll be looking forward to seeing your next games.

																Nusakana makes for a nice little island getaway of a game.  It has strengths and weaknesses, and all in all I'd say the pros outweigh the cons.

What's good?
Open world to explore at your own pace
Eighteen ladies to recruit, each with their own story that progresses as you befriend them
Ambush or avoid the local wildlife
Characters full of personality
Day/night cycle and weather patterns
Survivalist mechanics including hunger and sleep deprivation
Multiple game modes that affect mechanics and difficulty
Handy in-game encyclopedia that adds information as you discover it
What are the problems?
Game gets easier instead of more challenging as you progress
Main plot is poorly paced with underwhelming resolution
Learning weapon skills is mindlessly repetitive
Loads of Engrish (aside from when it's meant to be poorly spoken in dialogue)
Fishing at sea is easy to glitch into softlocking
Fishing gameplay lacks depth and challenge
Basically, the idea is you've come to a remote tropical island because someone sent you a letter saying they could reveal to you your mysterious past (you were raised in foster care and never knew your parents).  Starting as a dumb tourist, you learn to live on the island and slowly become a familiar and admired fixture in the native community.  You forage and hunt for food and crafting materials, get paid for fulfilling requests posted across four request boards, camp in the wilderness, and meet and befriend girls ranging from little kids to mature women.

You can have up to three ladies accompanying you at any given time--one fights beside you in battle and the other two provide support effects unique to each character.  You can equip them with accessories, and eventually power up their swimsuits/armor to your preferred specifications.  They also automatically learn certain weapon skills that you unlock for yourself.

The game is at it's hardest when you're just starting out, with basically no money, no decent equipment, and wildlife that can tear you a new one.  Then, once you figure out how to make a bunch of money, the game's difficulty evaporates.



All in all, when you play this game, you play it to explore the island, soak in the atmosphere, and get to know the girls, all at whatever pace you feel.  Don't worry too much about the main excuse plot or being heavily challenged and play the game like it's a big playground for adventure.

Despite knowing the ending from the beginning, I still felt the sadness towards the end especially when I believed there was a plot twist during the after credits only to be taken back.

 Gameplay This game utilizes the point and click as it's main style for it's puzzles. The puzzles itself are not that difficult in the beginning unlike other point and click based puzzle storyline games, the only challenging parts are mediocre at best as this game serves to be relaxing suggested from its game speed pace. The only problem is how there's a lightbulb at the top right corner of the screen which supposedly serves as a helping hand for players, except that it shows only the things that you're able to click on and not actually giving you directions or advice to help you clear the puzzles. This might be troublesome for certain younger players who might be slow in puzzles and would have to rely on outside resources for help instead. The bad point is that when you're finished with the first run through and for people who are beginning their achievement hunting run through, clicking on the wrong chapter and trying to return to the front page after going through all the cutscenes might take awhile due to it's long pace in panning out.

 Graphics The graphics are hand drawn and animated exceptionally well in a simplistic way whereby it's not overbearing to the eyes. The colours used throughout the game is well expressed which falls along nicely with the emotions of the characters and readers that they're trying to bring out throughout the storyline. The graphics are dark when it's meant to be mysterious or grim, light and purple when it's meant to make you feel at awe, it's just amazing in a simplistic way overall.

 Soundtracks The main soundtrack felt very lighthearted and serves as the main focal point of this game as it's the way of how it all begins. Likewise with the graphics, the soundtrack has different tunes meant to let readers know when it's expected to be sad, the tone of the soundtrack when it's far away and what not. The sound effects itself is rather done well and pleasing to hear with a pinch of reality in the objects and animal interactions used. Despite all this, the main background soundtrack may still be rather repetitive with the occasional different tunes here and there.

 Pros Simple Puzzles
Adorable graphics
Lovely soundtrack
Relaxing gameplay
Great deal for money
Realistic bittersweet storyline

 Cons No help hints given
Repetitive soundtrack
Storyline felt too short

 Conclusion I extremely love the way the characters and storyline was portrayed which coincidentally felt like going through the six stages of grief before learning to love yourself independently again. I just wish that they expanded more on the middle chapters but with the way it is right now, it's still a great playthrough. I'd recommend anyone that would love to relax to try out this short game of no words to just enjoy the storyline and graphics.

Coffee Talk is a game that clearly responds to modern trends in more than one way. While the writing, the character construction and the graphics/music selection truly represent a vision, it is the topics that this game touches that are truly the core of the game. 

This game brought me back to 10 years or more ago, when after work I would meet with my friends, once every 2 weeks in a coffee shop to talk about life. We would discuss our life, our career decisions, our significant others (or lack of), our families, politics, and of course the future. This is exactly what this game does. It throws you in daily conversations with a grain of fantasy about every day topics of conversations. The characters are interesting, each one very unique in their personality, even though I am sure some will be cherished more than others, but in general, it is their conversations that you are truly invested on. 

And it was a refreshing experience. It was a very relaxing experience that took me most of my evening. The game even made me take a break to go and brew me a cup of coffee to continue playing in the same mood as the characters. 

If you are looking for a "slice of life" kinda game, and you are not worried about reenacting some conversations you may have had about... the usual stuff, then, this game will most likely is for you.

																With almost 15 hours under my belt, here's my thoughts.

The game is setup in an RTS meets deck-builder. This gives the game a different feel than your straight up deck builders (like Slay the Spire or Banners of Ruin). Since the battle is semi-automated, you just have to manage your resources. But don't call it easy, because there is a great challenge sometimes in keeping up with the various levels; especially with the "survive for xxx seconds" maps.

You get commanders with different playstyles. One is a straight-up combat deck and the other is a toy-box style deck with few normal units. You can also unlock alternate decks for the commanders for even more variation at the start. The upgrade paths for the cards can be a bit random, so the rogue-like element is there and can either flummox you or really help you.

There are a few oddities which can frustrate a player. The hit detection on placing the toy cards from the toy box deck is frustrating as it will often not place even though it is on what should be a legal spot on the field. The weird angles of some of the maps can make it hard to see everything without frequent rotations, which could bother people sensitive to constant motion. One of the decks you unlock is especially frustrating as it is all hammers which can be hard to deal with as you don't get much to add to your deck for awhile. There is also the oddity where hitting escape will cancel several screens at once and it forces you to hit the back button on the screen (this is especially true when starting a new game).

I do like the boosting cards that allow you to strengthen your deck before you play cards. This can help, provided you can survive the extra mana cost and time. The haunting of villages to improve your mana pool is another nice touch, although some maps have more villages than is reasonable to conquer. And of course we can't forget the relic system which gives you all sorts of perks and interesting affects.

Overall this is quite the enjoyable experience and is a fun game to mess with and figure out how to squeeze performance out of your deck to maximize your effectiveness. The cost might seem high to some, but the game has updates planned as well as a third commander, which will add some more variety to how the game plays out so I feel it is appropriate for what you are getting.
