																Cute and charming little PM clone.

Gameplay: Similar to the PM games. You fill her schedule up and she performs whatever you have her do. Then she gains skills that help out during her explorations and influence what ending you get. You can also have her work to earn money, you don't get a stipend so it is strongly suggested that you do this.  You can also befriend everyone you meet to an extent but your schedule allows you to talk to a specific person on the weekend to raise your friendship points with them. But, during the week, Ciel can encounter anyone and you will gain some friendship points with them.

Controls/UI: The controls and battle system are very simple. Unlike PM, your daughter does a weekly schedule instead of a monthly one. You have a slot called "parent activity" where you can have her work part time jobs, overtime, supervise her activities, or spoil her. The part time jobs net you 150 bucks a day while overtime nets you a little bit more. However, forcing her to work ot jobs will lower her affection for you. Each one tells you what stats go up and what lower. The next is her weekly meal plan. You start off with basic, scarce, and lavish. Basic is average, scarce lowers her height/weight, and lavish increases her height/weight. Like in the PM games, there are shops and you can actually purchase other meal plans for her. They are extremely expensive but worth the money as they will boost other specific stats. Under the meal plan, you have the days of the week, Mon-Sat. In these slots, you can have her attend school, rest, shop, socialize, work additional jobs, vacation, or do something otherwise fun. But, be aware that if her stamina and mood are down, she won't be overly productive. On her avatar she will have status indicators, such as sick or depressed. And those happen when she is stressed, her mood is low, or her stamina is low. You can easily get rid of them and I would strongly suggest that you do as soon as they appear because your daughter can get taken away from you and you can go to jail in game...and I assume it is game over there. The exploration system is way more simple than in the PM games. You choose where to go and you and your party move on their own through the zone. You can encounter traders and monsters. If your daughter's health or stamina reach zero, then she will be returned home. HOWEVER. There are some zones where if your daughter loses all her health/stamina, she will die. The game does tell you what zones these are so don't go into them unless you are very prepared. And save before you do. As for the battle system, it is extremely simple and easy to get a hang of. You basically pick matching cards until one of your abilities light up to use it. Your daughter will attack each time you pick 3 matching cards. You also have 3 companions with you who will attack and you can call on them to attack out of turn when their avatar lights up. Each companion has different boosts. Unfortunately, from my understanding, there is no romance in the game. So, I don't think there are any marriage endings.

Audio/Visuals: Art is nice and anime style, the colors are easy on the eyes, and gives you plenty of indicators on what you can do, where you can go, and e.c.t. I also like during the exploration that the chibis will hold their weapons. It's hilarious seeing them with knives and guns. Lol. I have heard that the sound track is amaze but I keep my game music muted so you would just have to listen and see for yourself. If you end up not liking the music, you can turn it off with ease.

Story: The story is very simple. It's set in a dystopian futuristic setting where humanity lives in these colonies called Arks to protect them/keep them away from the monsters that plague the earth. They don't get a ton into the story, just some cut scenes here and there since the main focus of the game is your daughter and her every day life. Although, as of this review, my daughter is only 14 years old so, how much the story plays into her life is still yet to be seen.

Characters: You, your daughter, and everyone else. You: Your age is unknown but you can pick your sex, name, where/how you were born, your main stat, and your profession. These have an affect on your daughter and her skill gains. You can also select how you speak to your daughter and whether you want to be a harsh parent, normal one, or a soft/doting one. Your daughter: You influence her life, what skills she gains, and how she turns out. Personality-wise, she seems to be a caring and curious girl. I don't know if she can go through a personality change or not. My daughter is extremely spoiled but has high discipline and doesn't act any differently. Everyone else: There are at least 12 different characters with their own unique personalities and quirks. You can actually have your daughter befriend them. I don't know if any of them play any huge roles in her endings though. But, you can take at least 3 of them with you on your explorations. They also change as the years pass by. Their clothes will change, the children will get taller, hair will get longer, and e.c.t. On the weekends you can socialize with one of them for a major increase in friendship but, you can and will sometimes encounter them during the week either through cut scenes or while just performing your duties and gain friendship points that way. Exploring with them also nets you friendship points as well.

The only downsides I've seen so far are: Clothes are expensive and get even more expensive later in the game. You will end up having to work for a month or two in order to afford at least one piece of clothing. The game sometimes lags when you speed up her activities. You will also need to increase her stamina if you don't want her resting 2 to 3 days a week and if you want to get through the exploration too. But once that is increased, you can get away with having her rest only 1 day a week.

All in all, I would recommend this game. It's fun and cute and worth the price.

They're so vacuous and vapory in every way (except maybe in game design which CAN be stellar). Even regarding FFXV, I hate its guts enough (oh spikey-haired emo lead what a surprise) especially with the pingpong-ball-frenetic fighting so alien to the FFI thru X continuity, I'm not even interested. With this taste, I enjoyed the indie Shadows of Adam but for the downright cardboard cast of characterrs.

So what do you get with this game, in a nutshell?:

- Generally familiar sort of JRPG plot. Nothing too different from anything you've probably got down pat as a concept from the many similar games LL takes its inspiration from.
- Great combat system, especially after the recent update. You get enough input in the advancement system to feel like choices matter, at the same time it's far more limiting than say, a job system or materia. Characters feel highly distinct this way, not vaguely stat-distinguished containers for your choices in the advancement system. Happily, encounters are mostly optional and can be avoided (obviously not a groundbreaking thing like it was in '95, but a good decision in an RPG instead of random encounters). The implementation of hair-trigger reflexes to improve the effectivity of attacks and guard stance in battle is generally a good way to make it more engaging because otherwise this is FULLY turn based... but what is already challenging to your reaction time is rendered unnecessecarily so by the fact that this system requires any of your four gamepad main buttons and it is random. Why not just one of them, at least as an option? You shouldn't have to brace yourself for which button on your PC gamepad corresponds to A, B, X and Y if that gamepad isn't even an XBOX pad.
- Fair graphics. This is an indie game released in 2018 but honestly, its graphics wouldn't have passed as AAA even in 2008. Don't play this for graphics. The hand-painted static backgrounds are, I believe, a way for this game's small development crew to massively cut down on the overhead of rendering and texturing field graphics. Yes, I noticed.
- Fair music. Although some of the tracks in the game are good, like the overworld music, even that isn't super strong compositionally, just serviceable. This is not Uematsu and Mitsuda-tier game music by any means, and of course every note of it is synthetic.
- Meh dialogue. The main characters never feel like they're friends especially because they keep arguing at every major juncure of the game.
- A good contender for the WORST ending in entertainment history. I mean, bad in every way. I mean, makes the ending of Matrix Revolutions look decent. Bad in terms of being a downer. Bad in terms of not wrapping up anything or answering anything. Bad in terms of confusing. Bad in terms of too short. Bad in terms of being a cliffhanger as an ending. BAD. If someone plays this game for 60 hours and it ends like that, and you don't even find out why the main character got amnesia in the first place, you'd be pissed too!

Not a lot to expect forthcoming, with this admittedly narrow taste in the JRPG. Edge of Eternity once it gets out of Early Access, Final Fantasy VII remake once it decides to finally come out of hiding, and maybe FFXVI. Depending on what exactly that end ends up being.

																Introduction
My Lovely Daughter is the third Steam title from GameChanger Studio, published by Toge Productions and Another Indie.

In My Lovely Daughter you assume the role of Faust, an amnesiac alchemist who wakes in a somewhat dilapidated mansion / castle not far from the village of Salach, a haven for criminals, outcasts, and other unsavoury types.

Exploring the large house you soon discover the recently dead body of a girl. You remember she is your daughter, Arhea, though you've no idea how she died. You also discover what you know to be her disembodied soul in a special container nearby, along with some brief research notes on soul removal and insertion, and the raising of alchemical homunculi.

Determined to save your daughter before she decays and you lose her forever, you set about raising and sacrificing all manner of homunculi in an effort to restore her soul to its former state, and thence to her body.

Presentation
The game is presented very simply, but quite beautifully, with hand-drawn graphics in a consistent style from a rather small, but appropriate mostly neutral colour palette. The whole game is played on only a few screens, with a number of pop-up dialogs used to allow choices and control and to present information to the player.

Background graphics portray the rooms of Faust's mansion and the map of the nearby village in a simple sketched style using minimal colours. Some flavour animations are included to help set the scene and these add a nice touch of extra atmosphere to the game.

Each basic homunculus type has a unique personality that comes across well in the scripted dialog and letters they write to you, as well as in their sketched, cartoon-like character art. It's hard to not become attached to some of them as they learn and grow through their few short weeks of life before you cruelly butcher them for resources and soul affinities. The script is very well written, both thematically and grammatically.

The interface is very easy to use. The game includes a brief guided tutorial section when you first begin, as well as on-screen help available for most dialogs and screens. The village interface could use a couple of tweaks to reduce pointless clicking, though: displaying available homunculus portraits (with affinity tooltips) in the job selection dialogs would prevent needing to swap back to the homunculus screen over and over, and similarly displaying available resources and those already assigned to contracts on the contract selection screen would prevent needing to swap back to the inventory screen all the time to evaluate contracts. But these are only minor issues.

Music is haunting and lovely, though can be repetitive with only a few tracks available. Sound effects are few and far between, too, but are appropriate for the game. There are no voices, but the crying and screaming when you murder one of your girls is truly horrifying ... and heart breaking.

Gameplay
The core gameplay loop in My Lovely Daughter is exceptionally simple. You begin each week in your castle, where you can create, sacrifice, or interact with your homunculi; consult your experimental notes and journal; and talk to your dead daughter and examine her soul. Then you head into Salach for the rest of the week.

In the village you click on locations on the map to buy basic homunculi materials, gifts, and a few special upgrade items from the local shop; talk to the locals; negotiate contracts to deliver higher-tier materials; and, most importantly, send your homunculi out to do jobs for the villagers. Then you return back home for the next week.

These jobs provide you with income in the form of gold and also increase the homunculis' experience, while usually also decreasing their intimacy with you (they don't like being treated like slaves). Each job is also geared towards one of the four affinities which a homunculus may have: anger, sadness, fear, and joy. Give a homunculus a job that matches her affinity and she'll do better and dislike you less; give her one that opposes it and she'll do poorly and hate you more.

Every fourth week there is a full moon, which allows you to perform the magical ritual that may restore your daughter's soul. In order for this to have a chance of success, however, you must sacrifice your hard-working, and sometimes even loving, homunculi to imbue Arhea's soul with their affinities. If you get the right affinity balance then your daughter is returned to you and it's game over. Otherwise your poor homunculi died for nothing more than a narrowing down of the affinity ranges for your next attempt; Arhea's soul is once more stripped of all affinities and you start the next month from scratch.

Sacrificing a homunculus not only imbues your daughter's soul with the homunculus's affinity, it also provides a chance to receive higher tier materials, which you can then use either to fulfil contracts with the villagers or to create other homunculi. A higher-level homunculus not only provides more affinity points to Arhea's soul when sacrificed, but also has a greater chance of dropping higher-tier materials.

There are something like 30 different homunculus types, but if you look at it from a purely practical point of view, then you really only care about their affinities, of which there are only four.

And that's it. The task of balancing income against the costs of homunculus creation and intimacy maintenance is an easy one, particularly as the game appears to have no time limit -- which is a very good thing. The mechanics are very simple, but the story and characters bring the game to a weird sort of life, and they do an excellent job of it.

The game's challenge isn't so much a gameplay challenge as an emotional one. While it may be easy to cast off your grumpy failed Enmity homunculus to free up her room and scavenge what meagre resources you can from her corpse, it's much less pleasant to do the same to a beautiful, sweet Titanium homunculus who's been writing you letters and whom you've been talking to every week and showering with gifts, especially when she pleads for her life and starts crying.

The life of an alchemist is a tough one, indeed.

Pros and ConsPros:
+ Thought-provoking story with likeable (and hateable) characters
+ Beautiful hand-drawn art
+ Great music and simple, but excellent, sound effects

Cons:
- Replayable only for achievement hunters
- Core gameplay becomes repetitive very quickly


Verdict
When you begin My Lovely Daughter you're greeted with a screen explaining that, though it is a work of fiction, it is dark and depressing, and may make you think and feel certain things. The gameplay is extremely simple and becomes repetitive quickly, but the story and characters carry the game through to its bittersweet end.

My Lovely Daughter is a very simple game that only takes a handful of hours to complete, but will haunt you for much, much longer.

																The game has a great concept. Great art, great music, great premise, but for a 15 dollars I can't recommend it. I even regret the purchase.

My problem is that there's really no substance. I beat the game in 8 hours and the rest was just gtrying to get all the other endings. The protagonist is delightfully sick and twisted and jerkish, but other than his minimal interactions with the towns folk you don't really get to see it. The very brief interactions are the only cutscenes in the game other than the very beginning and end, which the true end didn't have as big an impact as I feel like it was trying to go for.

Even after all the grinding and slog that is the repeated weeks, I felt very unfulfilled. You're supposed to feel bad for the children you're sacrificing but there's nothing to really do to engage with them other than the one-way communication of letters. Maybe if the "spend time with" option had some story panels like the other stuff centered around Faust, or if there were some cutscenes that influence affection depending on your choice of words/actions, it would have been much more engaging. It all feels so monotonous, even with the sparse village interactions. 

There is a great setting in this game, and it's a real shame that we won't ever get to know more about it other than what's relevant to the protagonist's one-track mind or what's told to him by the townsfolk. It leaves me hungry for more, but not in a good way. 

One mild nitpick I would like to say is that the inventory and the magic book are hard to navigate.
-The inventory squares are checkered, which made searching for anything hard, especially when the objects are black and white while the squares are in shades of yellow/brown/tan. And anything that you have once had in your inventory stays in your inventory, albeit with a x0 on it. It makes navigation hard and really turned me off from doing requests because I had to keep checking to see what I was missing or what I don't have.

-In the book, the homunculi are listed in order of discovery, instead of say, dominant material or by affinities.

-None of these issues can be opted out of/changed in the settings. A basic "sort by" option or a "hide items you don't have" option would solve everything but the unfriendly design of the checkerboarded slots.

If this game wasn't so expensive, I would recommend it. But I can't. 8 hours is too short of a gameplay, and relying on completionist tendencies is the only way to pad out the game and maybe satisfy the void. There's lots of achievements and combinations and letters so doing 100% can be fun, if you can handle the flat execution and the mechanics.

Regardless, I'm extremely interested in the developer, and I hope there's another game like this from them, but better.

																I'm really sorry, but I have to give this game a thumb down and I really didn't want to do this.

I loved the first Dreadout, which played like Project Zero, you had a camera and you got to make pictures of ghosts to defeat them. The game was really enjoyable, the locations were cool and the ghost were fun to fight.

Now we got Dreadout 2 and after playing this game at the GamesCom, I was hyped to see, how they wanted to improve on Dreadout 1, because the game now features melee combat besides the camera function.

Unfortunately, this game is not nearly as good as the first one.

Like I said, you now got 2 Options to engage in combat (The game decides, in which level you have to use either melee or your phone-camera).

First the Camera:
This is nothing like I remember from the first Dreadout. The first one was responsive and you are actually able to do well in fighting ghost,
In Dreadout 2, the hitboxes, where you can actually damage a ghost while making pictures are so extremely tiny, I even thought at one boss, he doesn't even have a hitbox and I had to do something else.
Ghosts are moving really fast in this game and the places where you fight them often doesn't give you enough room to maneuver, well okay, even if, you can't really dodge the ghosts, because they are too fast.
So you have to hit the perfect pixels, while the ghosts go circles around you and that's just annoying unfortunately.

At one specific Boss, I had to look for that magic pixel, where I could damage it for 5 minutes and I only beat it, because I glitched the fight, so the boss wouldn't move and I could savely search for that pixel. That's not good combat and it's nothing like I remember from the first one, it's a downgrade and that's really a shame :(

The Melee Combat:
The melee combat on the other hand was actually enjoyable at times! While not perfect, there is potential.
You get to use Axes or Knives at some points in the game and your cameras functions get removed except for the flash, which can now stun enemies, if you load it up and flash those zombie-thingys right in their face!
So yeah, you don't fight ghosts with axes, if there is melee, you are going to fight Zombies, Demons, anything touchable.
You get a 3-4 hit combo, aiming is pretty easy with the mouse, so hitting the enemy is fine.
You also get to do a backstab if you stunned the enemies with a flash, but I don't know, if it does more damage, than your standard combo. I also want to say, I really liked the melee combat animations!
It just felt good killing stuff with the axe :)

And sure I first had to get used to the combat, because it can be a bit tricky in the beginning, but the more I played, the more I liked it and in the end, I just mowed through the enemies... unless they gang up on you and don't ever get hit in that situation!
If you get hit, the enemies can actually stunlock you, because their attacks are faster than yours!
The best way to get out of a stunlock for me was to spam the mousebutton to go for a fast counter attack if you're lucky to get out of the stunlock, while the enemy is still winding up an attack, but most of the time, you are done for if you're not careful.
The Bosses, where you had to use melee combat are much more doable than the ghost bosses.
They may look random in their movement or kinda unfair, I thought so too, but actually you can outplay most of the melee bosses, but at this point just let me tell you - the bosses in this game ARE HARD - even unfair in most cases and yes I said you can outplay them, which doesn't mean, the fights are easy. If you don't know how to outplay them, god bless your soul.

The Enviroment:
The locations you visit all look cool, but still after playing Dreadout 1, I was expecting more. You mostly follow linear pathes, even if some locations look more open ended. But the locations as they are presented are well done and I liked the atmosphere of the places.
It all had a bit of a silent hill feeling for me.

The things you have to do:
Most of the time, if you are in a more open ended place, you are looking for a key to open a lock. The key and the lock can be replaced with any kind of object. But what I want to say is, you always have to find A at place B and bring it to C so you can get back to A to proceed.
If there are enemies involved, then it's most of the time a linear path you have to follow, while fighting those enemies, or evading / hiding from them.
Later on in the game, you will encounter a few puzzles. they are fine and I think this level, where the puzzles are placed is one of the best in the game, it got a fine balance between combat, exploration and puzzles.

But I have to say, many times in this game I was completely clueless, what I had to do to, because the game won't tell you, what you have to do often times. Sure I don't like handholding or big arrows showing me, where to go, like all of you guys, but sometimes it was just incomprehensible, like for example, one time, I had to look through one specific window (one of many) to proceed in the game and it only worked, while looking through the window while looking through the camera while standing exactly in front of it!
It just didn't worked, if i was just one step further away, I looked in there so many times until I've read online "yeah you have to look inside that window".
And remember, nothing in this game tells you, that this one window is special!
This was not the only part in the game, where I was kinda stuck or didn't know what to do, often I just trial and errored my way through.

The Bugs:

And you gotta love the devs take on Hell in this game. It's basically a vertical tower-like place which you have to ascend in order to make your way out of this demons infested nightmare. Pretty creative in my opinion. So I guess that makes it a vertical action platformer where you fight through hordes of demons trying to ascend higher and higher.

The gameplay is pretty addictive. You smash demons left and right while trying to get to the top of some weird hellish tower. Every tower has its own boss which is pretty strong so make sure to get enough power ups on your way. It might sound simple but in reality the devs made it insanely replayable by adding the portal system. That means that every tower (sub level) in this game ends with two portals which you have to choose between in order to progress. Every portal leads to a unique tower with its own specific traps and trials. Think of them as circles of Hell I guess. Sometimes it's poison, sometimes its blades or lava (oh yeah BTW the devs seem to be familiar with the whole "Floor is lava" thing LOL). So every time you get to the top of a tower and see two portals you keep thinking where is it gonna take me now?

One thing that absolutely nailed this game for me is the awesome perk system. Yeah I know you call them talents but I like the word perks more. So yeah you earn currency as you progress and every once in a while you get to choose between 3 new talents/perks which give you a small buff. And OMG they are SOOOO MANY. And it's soooo cool choosing between them trying to come up with the most optimal OP build to simply smash the boss to pieces.

And of course you simply can't forget about the crazy metal soundtrack. I don't know how to best describe it. I'm just gonna say that this mixture of Gothic Metal, Power Metal and Black Metal is absolutely what this game needs.

Don't get me wrong I'm not trying to say this game is flawless. I see a lot of room for improvement here: for example the combat system could use some variety like combos or something. 																What can I say about Coffee Talk... Well, let's start at the beginning - and I promise to be spoiler free (beyond mentioning a few character names).

Coffee Talk is an indie Visual Novel style game, following in the footsteps of the likes of VA-LL Hall-A. In short, you're slinging drinks and having conversations with characters. For some, that's enough of a recommendation (it was for me) and, for some, that's enough to send you running. That's also fair. For those still on the fence, let me tell you why this quickly peaked to one of my favourite games.

Firstly, the game oozes the comfiest vibes. The entire development team - from artists, to writers, to audio - fundamentally nailed the sensation of a warm coffee shop on a rainy day, with hushed conversations and steamy drinks. The game is just downright pleasant to play - enough that it was something to look forward to experiencing a day or two after a long work day.

Secondly, the game's setting is intriguing - carrying that feeling where you're simply paddling on the surface of a great, deep lake. I'd love to see more set within this world - engaging with the races and their 'politics', as you sorta do with characters (like Gala, or Lua/Baileys.)

Thirdly, the characters themselves are a sheer joy to experience. From best girl Freya (who will be your stalwart companion the entire time), to the love stories, the forgiveness-seekers, the children playing adults (and adults playing children), to... some things a little out of this world. There wasn't a single soul I was unhappy to see cross my door, there wasn't a single story I was excited to see through - and with the promise of multiple endings (some better than others), I'm hoping my 9 hours turns into more.

If I can make a recommendation - don't do what I did, and spoil the 'correct' drinks and options for yourself. Experiment - you have five chances per drink to screw up, so try and determine what they might want. Failure is an option - and there's always another try. 

From a simple concept came a fantastic place to spend my time, phenomenal characters to interact with and some secrets to explore, even when you're done. For the price point, so long as you're comfortable with Visual Novels, light urban fantasy and some good ol' fashioned LGBTQA+ good vibes... what's not to love?

Coffee Talk is a serious contender for my Indie Game of the Year, and it's only February. That's how much I love and recommend it. 

So, consider it. There's a free demo. 

And, if you do purchase it, maybe I can order a drink, yeah?

The art and design are beautiful and the game embodies that cosy feeling of being tucked up somewhere warm when it's raining outside well. Unfortunately, though, the gameplay annoyed me.
For the most part, this game falls solidly under graphic novel. The story is structured around a month in the Fall of 2020 in a Bright-style take on Seattle, complete with octopus-people (that's not a mermaid), WoW orcs, and succubi. There are apparently 5 instances where your choice of drink branches the story - at least two of them are fairly clear - but there is no conscious decision-making in the dialogue. Since the major gameplay is making the drinks, that's what I'll focus on here. 

Drinks
When a customer orders a drink, you make it - which I think is pretty well described by other reviewers and in the screenshots of the game itself. What was NOT clear to me on first playthrough however was that you have ~244 permutations of the ingredients and very little help as to how to combine them. The base is always 1 of 5 ingredients (e.g coffee, tea) and then the second and third ingredients can be that same base and/or any of the other six ingredients (ginger, mint, lemon, etc). And the order matters! 

Main sequence
So a customer may come in asking for 'that special spicy chocolate drink' (fake example) and chocolate+cinnamon+milk will work but chocolate+milk+cinnamon will NOT. You can see how this quickly becomes quite frustrating, particularly since many of the customers are very elusive as to what they actually want.

Sometimes they ask for a speciality drink you haven't unlocked yet in your drink menu, and often it has a name that gives no clues, e.g. Bitter Heart, The Grinch. But the game, knowing you haven't unlocked it, doesn't give you any options to figure it out other than brute-forcing on the spot (and you only have 5 tries in which to do this) or playing one of the endless-mode games to unlock the menu item. So, let's talk about the endless modes.

Unlocking the drinks
Free-play is great for brute-forcing combinations. 
 The timed endless mode is probably the best if you don't want to brute-force your way through all 244 options (which I ended up doing to figure out the last few drinks). It has increasing levels of difficulty. 
The first stage of timed mode is essentially a reading comprehension test in which the customer asks for drinks with a specific set of ingredients. Again, important to pay attention to order here, e.g. if they ask for a 'lemon and honey tea' you have to input tea+lemon+honey and not tea+honey+lemon or you won't get the point. 
In the second stage you have to quickly read menu items off the recipe cards you've unlocked. If a customer asks for one you haven't figured out yet - tough! Unless its name is particularly descriptive you'll have no way of figuring it out and probably time out. 
The third stage infuriated me. Here customers will ask for drinks with specific attributes, e.g. a COOL and SWEET drink. The problems arise when you get a request such as NOT TOO COOL, BITTER, and VERY WARM. In reading that I would assume that maxing out on an espresso would pass all the criteria (it's both hot and bitter) but they actually want something that has a rating of 2-3 on COOL && BITTER and maxed out on WARM. Confusing, right? And because there's no feedback mechanism other than a character looking grumpy it's hard to know where exactly you've gone wrong when a drink gets returned. 


Story
The stories are sweet but a little hollow. I'm very amused that many reviewers found them 'too political', if you think in 2020 that segregation is a valid stance in inter-racial relations or mixed-race couples are making a strong political statement... then you're way behind the times anyway to put it lightly. Unless you think werewolves are political? Or indie-game dev?
 In general I wanted the game to be a little bolder with the story, since that's the bulk of the time you'll spend with it. I found the lead character, the journalist that lies to her boss, to be quite immature and rude at times but an unlikeable protagonist is sometimes more entertaining than not, so I wasn't mad about it. 


tl;dr
If there was a better feedback system for the drinks other than 'ugh, this isn't what I ordered' and a smarter way to unlock menu items I would have loved this game! As it is, it's too frustrating to play. A good time-killer and beating endless is satisfying if you figure out how to please the customers but ultimately not quite there for me.

Audio Available at: 
	
	
		YouTube™ Video: Andy Plays Indies - My Lovely Daughter 
		
			Views: 128		
		
			Andy reviews indie horror dating sim, My Lovely Daughter.		
	

Do you remember how in Assassin's Creed Brotherhood, you had to raise up your own little team of Assassin Cub Scouts, sending them off on missions and watching their stats grow? Imagine, if you will, that you found out, halfway through the game, that you were, in fact, training them up so that the Assassin Order could send them off to do kamikaze dives with those rickety Da Vinci gliders. Imagine further, that instead of burly Italian thugs and saucy wenches, your squad of Renaissance suicide bombers was being recruited from innocent ten-year-old girls.  

That's the position we find ourselves placed in by My Lovely Daughter, a crafting/relationship sim, out this year from GameChanger Studios. 
Upon starting the game, we find ourselves in the shoes of an amnesiac alchemist, unimaginatively named Faust. The game's primary challenge is then quite efficiently presented to us, in the form of an empty house, a magic book, and a dead daughter.
As Faust, we quickly learn that in order to revive our dead daughter we must infuse her preserved soul with those harvested from home-made little monster-girls called homunculi. Each homunculus has a single emotional stat, which has to be groomed in order to make them effective sacrifices. This is achieved by sending them off to do jobs in the neighboring village, and by giving them presents. At the same time, we have to make sure that our artificial children don't run away before we can murder them, and that our daughter's body doesn't decompose, before we figure out how to resurrect her. 
The game interface reminds one strongly of those NewGrounds point-and-click flash games from the early 2000s, and the art style reminds one of a webcomic from the same era. That flash game attitude carries on into the gameplay, which largely consists of acquiring resources and seeing what you can combine them into, and the affection and personality measures are reminiscent of those flash RPG dating sims, where you have to court each character according to their one personality trait.

The concept is kind of interesting, though. The process of raising up your home full of nightmarish little digipets is lent some extra weight by the fact that the game will eventually force you to kill them. The minimalistic approach means that you won't constantly be interrupting the experience to look at walkthroughs. The stylized animation is capable of delivering some genuinely striking imagery, while avoiding the slip into sleazy torture porn.

On the flip-side, though, the limited number of game mechanics means that it tends to drag on a bit, and the impact of the imagery quickly gets lost in the sheer drudgery of the stat management.  Despite the interesting concept, the storytelling is kind of weak, too. The only scripted events seem to occur at the beginning and end of the game, and the game world isn't reactive enough to allow for any kind of an emergent story, along the way.  

This is a game that I think might have benefited from being formatted more like a conventional adventure game. You'd lose a some of the autonomy in the gameplay, but as it stands, the game doesn't really have the story structure that its highbrow concept is crying out for. 

You see, in the mythology of this game, the homonculi are a bit like Blade Runner's replicants: It's left open to what extent these artificial creations are real people. The game takes some serious effort to characterize them, and makes a point of the fact that the development of their personalities is necessary to Faust's plan. Buried in the premise is the idea that each homonculus gets closer to becoming a fully realized, conscious individual, as they get closer to their inevitable death at the protagonist's hands. That could set up a pretty serious moral dilemma, asking the audience to consider what constitutes a sentient life, and whether one life can genuinely be more important than another. 

The only problem with that, is that the game seems to be completely insensitive to the issue, as does our main character. He never shows even a scrap of remorse over killing his creations, and his regard for any for the human characters begins and ends with worrying about them interfering with his evil scheme. 

Ironically, --because it seems to be an accident-- the game isn't a bad exploration of a certain kind of evil. Faust has an objective that he thinks is justified, and as far as he's concerned, everyone else is either a tool or an obstacle toward that goal. Through his perspective, the line between the homonculi and the human characters is irrelevant. He regards everyone not himself as an object, and that's about as good a definition of evil as I can think of. 

So what we have here is a game in which you play as what is unquestionably the villain, an interesting concept in itself, but without a hero to offset you, the game's moral universe feels incomplete. Consequently, while the ambience of the game can be unsettling, the story lacks much in the way of a satisfying payoff. 

The lack of a more structured story leads to some other missed opportunities, too. There's never much of a sense of threat in this game. Yeah, if you fail to buy a preservative for your daughter's corpse, it will deteriorate and eventually lead to game a game over, but the item necessary is in infinite supply at the shop,  and I never found myself short on cash. The bigger mistake is that there doesn't seem to be any chance of the villagers catching on to what you're up to. Another thing this game is crying out for is a "Young Frankenstein"-esque nosy police inspector, to periodically come poking around and asking questions. 

Without wishing to spoil, the endings aren't up to much, either. Particularly the "true" ending, which throws the established tone overboard with a ham-fisted analogy about becoming trapped in a spiral of negative behavior.  

GameChanger's self-declared intent, at least as far as can be inferred from the game's -- frankly pretentious -- Steam page,  is to use the game as an exploration of a variety of personal and social ills, including "child labor, abusive parenting, and ignorant societies". On that level, its an unmitigated failure, just because every single character is so one-dimensionally miserable and depressing, that any attempt at social commentary is hard to take seriously. It's also claiming to be a serious portrayal of grief, but the protagonist isn't much deeper than the average mad scientist, and he never seems to undergo any kind of emotional change or development. 

In fact, after playing the game, the Steam page for it is starting to remind me of the information cards at modern art exhibits: desperately trying to preemptively convince you that if you don't like it, it's just too artistic and serious for you. 

Would I recommend it? Well, it's certainly a more clever subversion of its genre than Doki Doki Literature club, but it also isn't free. My Lovely Daughter isn't as disturbing as the developers clearly think it is, and it's not terribly immersive, either. The game sucked me in initially, but the repetitive nature of its slow-paced, and sometimes obscure management gameplay will probably undercut your investment in the story. The concept is worthwhile, and it'll be plenty different from anything else on your Steam list, but there just isn't enough game here to carry it for me.

In this day of Steam Sales and free downloads, It seems a little gutsy to me, to charge $15 for what is essentially a glorified flash game, especially when you can get most of the experience from watching a few YouTube videos. But I also have to admit that I don't like crafting games or relationship sims, so your mileage may vary. If you like that kind of thing, you'll have to decide if the concept is worth the money to you.

																Sometimes visual novel games fall a bit flat. Either they're too much story, or too much game, not striking the balance that makes the best of the genre work. When the Past Was Around does both well and provides some evocative music besides. Evocative? Yes, this is an emotional game, for those who think and feel. Shallow people and human robots, this is not the puzzlefest you are looking for. 

Now, for specifics. The artwork is top-notch, manga-like without being excessively 2-D. The graphics effectively communicate the character's emotions without being over-the-top. There is an aching gentleness that suffuses the game, from its artwork, to its story, to its music. And the music? Not the most diverse of soundtracks, but it will stay with you. But back to the feel for a moment. The feel can be heavy at times (not for me but for some) -- think emotional intensity, not horror. As for story, the game is paced well and brings it all to a satisfying close without being cheesy or predictable. The characters are relatable. Although the two main characters' relationship isn't specified exactly (I don't recall rings), that is the only possible downer. 

Now for the puzzles. The puzzles are occasionally too difficult (think: the tic-tac-toe problem -- argh), but by the end you will probably be in tune with the developers and they will become easier. They're not too numerous and they're not cruel. 

Overall, you get a memorable experience that is both story and puzzle that's not too short nor too long, and it's something that you want to remember. Charming and timeless -- When the Past Was Around is a solid 8.5.
